questions.question: Under CARs Part IX, which pilot certificate is required to conduct Advanced RPAS operations?
choices: Pilot Certificate – Small RPAS (Basic Operations)
Pilot Certificate – Small RPAS (Advanced Operations)
Pilot Certificate – Small RPAS (VLOS)
No certificate is required if under 25 kg
questions.rationale: Advanced operations (e.g., in controlled airspace, near or over people, near aerodromes) require the Pilot Certificate – Small RPAS (Advanced Operations), obtained by passing the advanced exam and flight review.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Subpart 901 – Advanced Operations pilot certification requirements
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot wants to operate a small RPAS within 3 NM of the centre of an uncontrolled aerodrome. Under Advanced Operations rules, what is generally required before doing so?
choices: Nothing, as long as the flight stays below 400 ft AGL
Notification to, or coordination with, other aerodrome users/operators and confirmation the operation will not create a hazard to aviation safety
A Special Flight Operations Certificate (SFOC) in all cases
Written permission from NAV CANADA only
questions.rationale: Operating near an aerodrome requires the pilot to ensure the flight won't interfere with aircraft operations, which typically involves coordinating with aerodrome users/operators rather than defaulting to an SFOC.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – aerodrome proximity operating rules (Advanced Operations)
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Which of the following operations would require a Special Flight Operations Certificate – RPAS (SFOC-RPAS), even for a pilot holding an Advanced Operations certificate?
choices: Flying over bystanders at a controlled special event or advertised event
Flying within 30 metres horizontally of a bystander not involved in the operation, under the reduced-distance Advanced privileges
Flying in Class G airspace below 400 ft AGL
Flying beyond 3 NM from an uncontrolled aerodrome
questions.rationale: Operating over or near an advertised/controlled event with bystanders present falls outside standard Advanced Operations privileges and requires an SFOC-RPAS due to the elevated public-safety risk.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the maximum takeoff weight limit for an RPAS operated under the standard Basic/Advanced Operations rules in CARs Part IX?
choices: Less than 5 kg
Less than 25 kg
Less than 150 kg
No weight limit applies
questions.rationale: CARs Part IX standard Basic/Advanced Operations rules apply to RPAS with a maximum takeoff weight of less than 25 kg; heavier systems generally require an SFOC or fall under different provisions.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Subpart 901 – applicability/weight threshold
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Under CARs Part IX, what must a pilot do before conducting a flight in controlled airspace under Advanced Operations privileges?
choices: Nothing additional if flying below 400 ft AGL
Obtain an air traffic control (ATC) authorization for the specific operation
File a NOTAM only, without ATC contact
Obtain a Basic Operations certificate upgrade
questions.rationale: Advanced Operations privileges permit flight in controlled airspace, but only with a specific ATC authorization for that operation, since controlled airspace involves manned traffic separation requirements.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – controlled airspace authorization requirement
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot's ATC authorization for controlled airspace specifies a maximum altitude of 250 ft AGL and a defined lateral boundary. If the pilot needs to briefly exceed 250 ft AGL to avoid an obstacle, what must they do?
choices: Proceed since obstacle avoidance is always permitted
Contact ATC and obtain an amended authorization before exceeding the approved limits
Land immediately and file an incident report
Descend below 100 ft AGL instead of climbing
questions.rationale: An ATC authorization is specific to the parameters requested (altitude, lateral limits, time window). Any deviation outside those parameters requires contacting ATC for an amendment before proceeding.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – terms and limitations of ATC authorizations
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Which document must an Advanced Operations RPAS pilot carry or have accessible during flight?
choices: Only the aircraft's purchase receipt
Proof of pilot certificate, and if applicable, the RPAS operator's operating certificate/documentation for the flight
A copy of the Aeronautics Act in full
Nothing is required to be carried
questions.rationale: Pilots must be able to demonstrate valid certification (pilot certificate, and any required operational authorizations) when requested by an inspector or authority.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the general maximum altitude for RPAS operations under CARs Part IX, absent a specific authorization?
choices: 100 ft AGL
400 ft AGL
1000 ft AGL
No limit
questions.rationale: The default operating ceiling under CARs Part IX is 400 ft AGL, unless operating within a defined distance of a structure (with an added buffer) or under a specific authorization allowing otherwise.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – general altitude limit
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An Advanced Operations pilot is conducting a flight over a bystander who is not involved in the operation, using the reduced horizontal distance permitted under Advanced privileges. What additional requirement typically applies to enable this?
choices: The RPAS must be registered as Basic only
The RPAS must meet the declared compliance requirements (e.g., Standard 922) for operating closer to people
No additional requirement applies beyond holding the Advanced certificate
The flight must occur only at night
questions.rationale: Reduced-distance operations near people under Advanced privileges require the RPAS to meet the applicable technical/declaration requirements (Standard 922) demonstrating it's safe to operate at the reduced distance.
questions.source: CARs Part IX Standard 922 – RPAS operating near people
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot loses positive control of an RPAS during an Advanced Operations flight and it strikes a parked vehicle, causing damage. What is the pilot's primary regulatory obligation afterward?
choices: No obligation if the damage is minor
Report the occurrence as required (e.g., to the operator/organization and, where applicable, per incident reporting requirements) and retain records of the event
Only inform the vehicle owner verbally
Destroy the flight logs to avoid liability
questions.rationale: Pilots/operators are expected to document and report RPAS incidents/accidents as required, retaining records to support any investigation and demonstrate compliance with safety management obligations.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – incident/occurrence reporting and recordkeeping
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between Basic and Advanced Operations certificates under CARs Part IX?
choices: They are unrelated and require entirely separate aircraft registrations
Advanced Operations privileges include everything permitted under Basic Operations plus additional privileges (controlled airspace, near people, near aerodromes) subject to further requirements
Basic Operations allows more privileges than Advanced Operations
Advanced Operations only applies to aircraft over 25 kg
questions.rationale: The Advanced Operations certificate builds on Basic privileges, adding the ability to operate in controlled airspace, closer to people, and near aerodromes, subject to additional certification/authorization requirements.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – certificate privilege structure
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Before conducting an Advanced Operations flight in Class F Special Use Airspace, what must the pilot do?
choices: Nothing, since Class F airspace is uncontrolled
Check the status and restrictions (e.g., active periods, NOTAMs) for that airspace and obtain any required authorization before entry
File a flight plan with NAV CANADA only
Assume it is always closed to RPAS
questions.rationale: Class F airspace may be restricted, advisory, or danger areas with specific active periods and entry conditions; pilots must check current status/NOTAMs and obtain any required authorization before entering.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TC AIM – Class F airspace operating considerations
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is 'operating weight' as used in CARs Part IX intended to capture?
choices: Only the empty airframe weight
The total weight of the RPA at takeoff, including all fuel, batteries, and payload
The manufacturer's advertised maximum weight regardless of configuration
The weight of the ground control station only
questions.rationale: Operating weight refers to the actual all-up weight of the RPA as flown, which determines the applicable weight category and rule set.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot wants to fly a medium RPA (25–150 kg) under the 2025 CARs amendments. Which statement is correct?
choices: Medium RPA are always prohibited regardless of certification
Medium RPA operations are permitted under the amended Part IX framework, subject to declaration and applicable operating division requirements
Medium RPA may only be flown under a Basic Operations certificate
Medium RPA require no additional certification beyond a Basic certificate
questions.rationale: The 2025 amendments extended Part IX to cover RPA up to 150 kg, introducing new declaration and divisional requirements rather than simply applying Basic rules.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – 2025 amendments, medium RPA provisions
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An operator wants to conduct BVLOS operations below 400 ft AGL over a sparsely populated area with a small RPA. Which regulatory pathway is most appropriate?
choices: Standard Basic Operations certificate only
Standard Advanced Operations certificate only
Level 1 Complex Operations under Division VI, with the required declaration and pilot certificate
No certificate is required over sparsely populated areas
questions.rationale: BVLOS operations below 400 ft AGL over unpopulated/sparsely populated areas, away from aerodromes, fall under Division VI Level 1 Complex Operations, which has its own declaration and certification requirements.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division VI – Level 1 Complex Operations

questions.question: A Level 1 Complex operation is planned over an area initially assessed as sparsely populated, but a small seasonal campground opens nearby during the operation window. What must the pilot do?
choices: Continue as planned since the original site survey is still valid
Reassess population density and site survey assumptions, since a change in ground conditions may invalidate the original risk assessment
Only worry about population density at the moment of takeoff
Population density is irrelevant to Level 1 Complex operations
questions.rationale: Site surveys and population density assessments must reflect current conditions; a change like a seasonal campground opening can materially change the risk profile and must be reassessed.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division VI – site survey currency

questions.question: What is the purpose of an RPAS Operator Certificate (ROC)?
choices: It replaces the need for a pilot certificate
It authorizes an organization to conduct specified RPAS operations under defined conditions, roles, and safety management processes
It is only required for recreational flying
It certifies the airworthiness of a single aircraft
questions.rationale: An RPAS Operator Certificate authorizes an organization (not just an individual pilot) to conduct certain operations, with defined crew roles, training, and safety management requirements.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – Requirement for RPAS Operator Certificate
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Under Division II general operating rules, what restriction applies near a forest fire area or police/safety agency site?
choices: No restriction applies to RPAS in these areas
RPAS operations are generally restricted near these sites unless specific circumstances/coordination permit it
Only manned aircraft are restricted, not RPAS
Restrictions apply only above 1000 ft AGL
questions.rationale: CARs Part IX restricts RPAS operations in the vicinity of forest fire areas and police/safety agency sites due to interference risk with emergency response aircraft, except under specific permitted circumstances.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division II – general operating and flight rules
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Which of the following best describes when Standard 923 may be used in lieu of a declared detect-and-avoid (DAA) system for a Level 1 Complex operation?
choices: Standard 923 can never substitute for a declared DAA system
Standard 923 provides an alternative means of compliance for specific lower-risk BVLOS scenarios where a full declared DAA system is not required
Standard 923 only applies to manned aircraft
Standard 923 replaces the need for any site survey
questions.rationale: Standard 923 sets out alternative means of compliance that may apply to certain lower-complexity BVLOS scenarios, allowing operators to forgo a fully declared DAA system under defined conditions.
questions.source: CARs Part IX Standard 923 – alternative means of compliance

questions.question: What must a pilot do if they believe their RPA is no longer airworthy after a pre-flight inspection?
choices: Fly it anyway if the mission is time-sensitive
Not conduct the flight until the airworthiness concern is resolved
Only report it after the flight
Ignore minor findings regardless of severity
questions.rationale: Pilots are responsible for determining airworthiness before flight and must not fly an RPA they believe is unsafe.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – pre-flight airworthiness responsibility
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Under CARs Part IX, who may demand to inspect aviation documents related to an RPAS operation?
choices: Only the aircraft manufacturer
A person authorized under the Aeronautics Act/CARs, such as a Transport Canada inspector or peace officer acting within their authority
Any member of the public
No one may inspect these documents
questions.rationale: CAR 103.02(1)-(2) requires the owner/operator of an aircraft, and any holder of a Canadian aviation document or other RPAS record, to make it available for inspection to the Minister (e.g., a Transport Canada inspector) on reasonable notice.
questions.source: CARs 103.02 – Access to aircraft, aerodrome facilities, records and documents
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: May computer-stored records be used in place of paper records for RPAS documentation?
choices: No, paper records are always mandatory
Yes, provided measures are taken to protect the records from loss or unauthorized alteration
Only for maintenance records, never for training records
Only if approved individually by Transport Canada each time
questions.rationale: CAR 103.04 permits recording systems (computer records, microfiche, etc.) in place of paper entries, provided the records are protected against inadvertent loss, destruction or tampering and can be printed for the Minister on reasonable notice.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS operator wants to modify their aircraft in a way not covered by the manufacturer's declaration for Division VI operations. What is required?
choices: No action needed if the modification seems minor
The operator must assess whether the modification is within permitted modifications or requires a new/updated declaration before continued Division VI use
Modifications are always prohibited under Division VI
Only a verbal notification to Transport Canada is required
questions.rationale: Division VI operations rely on declared technical requirements; modifications outside the permitted scope can invalidate the declaration and require reassessment before further use.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division VI – permitted modifications
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What must a Level 1 Complex pilot certificate holder do to maintain recency?
choices: Nothing; the certificate never expires or requires recency
Meet the recency requirements defined for the Level 1 Complex Pilot Certificate (e.g., periodic flight review or activity)
Retake the Basic exam annually
Recency only applies to RPAS Operator Certificates, not individual pilots
questions.rationale: Like other pilot certificates, the Level 1 Complex certificate has defined recency requirements the holder must satisfy to remain current.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division VI – recency requirements

questions.question: What is the general prohibition regarding RPAS use for commercial air service under CARs Part IX?
choices: RPAS may never be used commercially under any circumstance
RPAS operations that meet the definition of 'commercial air service' are subject to additional restrictions/prohibitions beyond standard RPAS rules
Commercial use is unrestricted as long as the pilot holds an Advanced certificate
Commercial air service rules do not apply to RPAS at all
questions.rationale: CARs Part IX includes prohibitions/restrictions around RPAS operations that would meet the definition of commercial air service, distinct from general commercial RPAS work like inspections or photography.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division II – commercial air service restrictions
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A training provider wants to train candidates who do not yet hold a Level 1 Complex Pilot Certificate. What must the training provider satisfy?
choices: No special requirements beyond having any RPAS pilot on staff
The training provider must meet the defined Level 1 Complex training provider requirements before conducting such training
Only Transport Canada itself may provide this training
Training providers cannot train uncertified candidates under any circumstances
questions.rationale: CARs Part IX sets specific requirements for organizations providing Level 1 Complex training to candidates who are not yet certificated.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division VI – training provider requirements

questions.question: Which type of RPAS operation would require a Special Flight Operations Certificate–RPAS (SFOC-RPAS) rather than standard Basic/Advanced/Level 1 Complex rules?
choices: A standard VLOS flight below 400 ft AGL in Class G airspace
An operation that falls outside the scope defined for Basic, Advanced, and Level 1 Complex operations (e.g., certain BVLOS profiles, heavier RPA, or unusual risk conditions)
Any flight conducted with an Advanced certificate
Any operation using a declared DAA system
questions.rationale: Operations that don't fit within the defined Basic/Advanced/Level 1 Complex frameworks continue to require an SFOC-RPAS issued by Transport Canada.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Subpart 3 – Special Flight Operations – RPAS, section 903.01
questions.carsQuote: No person shall conduct any of the following operations using a remotely piloted aircraft system unless the person complies with the provisions of a special flight operations certificate — RPAS issued by the Minister under section 903.03:

questions.question: What must be established for all small or medium RPA operating under Division VI before flight?
choices: Nothing beyond the pilot certificate
Procedures for normal and emergency operations
A commercial insurance policy only
A public notification campaign
questions.rationale: Division VI requires that procedures be established for both normal and emergency operations prior to conducting the flight.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division VI – operating procedures
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What document describes crew roles and responsibilities before, during, and after a Level 1 Complex flight?
choices: The pilot certificate itself
The operator's documented crew roles/responsibilities as required under the RPAS Operator Certificate
The aircraft flight manual only
No such document is required
questions.rationale: The RPAS Operator Certificate requires documentation defining crew roles and responsibilities throughout all flight phases.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division XII – RPAS Operator Certificate

questions.question: What must an RPAS Operator Certificate holder describe regarding their training program?
choices: Nothing; training is left entirely informal
Training program requirements appropriate to each crew member's assigned duties
Only pilot training, not visual observer or crew training
Only initial training, with no recurrent requirements
questions.rationale: The operator must define training requirements appropriate to each crew member's assigned duties, not just the pilot's role.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division XII – training program requirements
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What reporting requirements apply to an RPAS Operator Certificate holder under Division XII?
choices: No reporting requirements exist
The operator must comply with defined occurrence/incident reporting requirements as part of their certificate obligations
Reporting is only required if the incident is publicized in the media
Only reportable if damage exceeds a specific dollar threshold set by the operator
questions.rationale: RPAS Operator Certificate holders are subject to defined reporting requirements for occurrences/incidents as part of their regulatory obligations.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division XII – reporting requirements
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is a 'visual observer' as defined in CARs Part IX?
choices: Any bystander watching the flight
A trained crew member assisting the pilot by maintaining visual contact with the RPA and surrounding airspace/environment
A camera mounted on the RPA
An air traffic controller
questions.rationale: A visual observer is a designated, trained crew member who assists the pilot with situational awareness, not simply any onlooker.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division I – definitions
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: How does 'command and control link' (C2 link) relate to RPAS regulatory definitions?
choices: It only refers to the physical remote controller hardware
It is the defined communication link used to transmit commands to, and receive telemetry/status from, the RPA
It refers exclusively to radio frequencies below VHF
It has no formal regulatory definition
questions.rationale: The C2 link is a formally defined term describing the communication path for command/control and telemetry between the control station and the RPA.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division I – definitions
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What must an RPAS pilot do regarding 'mandatory action' items defined in CARs Part IX?
choices: Mandatory actions are optional recommendations only
Mandatory actions must be defined and followed as specific required responses to particular flight conditions or system states
Mandatory actions apply only to manned aircraft
Mandatory actions only apply after an accident has occurred
questions.rationale: 'Mandatory action' is a defined regulatory term representing required responses to specific conditions, and must be built into operating procedures.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division I – definitions
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is a 'populated area' intended to capture under CARs Part IX?
choices: Only areas with more than 1 million residents
An area with a density of human occupancy sufficient to create a higher risk profile for people/property on the ground
Only urban downtown cores
Areas within controlled airspace only
questions.rationale: 'Populated area' is a defined risk-related term distinguishing higher-density human occupancy areas from sparsely populated or unpopulated ones, driving different rule sets.
questions.source: CARs Part IX, Division I – definitions
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What defines Class G airspace?
choices: Controlled airspace requiring ATC clearance
Uncontrolled airspace where ATC services are not provided
Airspace reserved exclusively for RPAS
Airspace above FL600 only
questions.rationale: Class G is uncontrolled airspace; ATC does not provide separation services there, though flight information services may still be available. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-3
questions.source: CARs Part VI / TC AIM – airspace classification
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Which airspace classes are considered 'controlled airspace' in Canada?
choices: Class A, B, C, D, E only
Class G only
Class F only
All classes are controlled
questions.rationale: Classes A through E are controlled airspace; Class F is special use (may or may not be controlled depending on type); Class G is uncontrolled. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-4
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot wants to operate in Class D airspace surrounding a controlled aerodrome. What is required?
choices: Nothing beyond an Advanced certificate
A specific ATC authorization for the operation
Only a NOTAM filing
Class D airspace is always closed to RPAS
questions.rationale: Class D is controlled airspace; RPAS operations require a specific ATC authorization under Advanced Operations privileges. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-5
questions.source: CARs Part IX – controlled airspace authorization + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot's controlled airspace authorization is valid for a specific time window and altitude. Weather delays the flight past the window. What must the pilot do?
choices: Fly anyway since the delay wasn't the pilot's fault
Request a new or amended authorization before flying outside the approved window
Assume the authorization automatically extends
Only notify ATC after landing
questions.rationale: ATC authorizations are valid only for their specified parameters; operating outside the approved time window requires a new/amended authorization. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-6
questions.source: CARs Part IX – terms and limitations of authorizations + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What symbol/color typically represents Class F Special Use Airspace on a VFR chart?
choices: A solid blue line
A distinct border with an identifying code (e.g., CYR, CYA, CYD) and associated legend entry
No representation; Class F is never charted
A green dashed line only
questions.rationale: Class F areas are charted with defined boundaries and identifier codes (Restricted, Advisory, Danger) referenced in the chart legend. CARs 601.01 lists 'restricted airspace', 'advisory airspace' and 'danger areas' as recognized airspace types, and 601.02 classifies them as Class F Special Use Restricted or Class F Special Use Advisory, with exact boundaries specified in the Designated Airspace Handbook. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-7
questions.source: CARs 601.01–601.02 (airspace types/classification); boundaries specified in the Designated Airspace Handbook + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the difference between a CYR (Restricted) and CYA (Advisory) Class F area?
choices: There is no difference; both are identical
CYR entry is prohibited/restricted without specific permission, while CYA is advisory only, alerting pilots to activity without prohibiting entry
CYA is always more restrictive than CYR
CYR only applies to RPAS, CYA only applies to manned aircraft
questions.rationale: CARs 601.02 classifies Class F airspace as either 'Special Use Restricted' or 'Special Use Advisory'. CARs 601.04(2) then states the enforceable rule for the Restricted type: 'No person shall operate an aircraft in Class F Special Use Restricted airspace unless authorized to do so by the person specified for that purpose in the Designated Airspace Handbook.' No equivalent prohibition exists for Advisory areas — they simply alert pilots to activity (e.g., parachute jumping) without legally barring entry. The Designated Airspace Handbook is the document CARs itself designates for the exact boundaries and the specific authorizing person/agency for each named area. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-8
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the standard default RPAS altitude limit in uncontrolled Class G airspace absent specific authorization?
choices: 100 ft AGL
400 ft AGL
1000 ft AGL
18,000 ft ASL
questions.rationale: The default RPAS ceiling is 400 ft AGL unless operating near a structure with the applicable buffer, or under specific authorization. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-9
questions.source: CARs Part IX – general altitude limit + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Within 100 ft laterally of a structure, how much additional altitude buffer above the structure may an RPAS pilot generally use without further authorization?
choices: No buffer is permitted
Up to 100 ft above the structure's height, subject to remaining within 200 ft AGL overall or per applicable rule
Unlimited altitude near any structure
Only 10 ft of buffer is permitted
questions.rationale: CARs permits a limited additional altitude buffer above a nearby structure's height when operating close to it, without exceeding overall applicable ceilings. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-10
questions.source: CARs Part IX – structure proximity altitude rule + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot wants to fly at 350 ft AGL directly beneath a Class C airspace floor of 700 ft AGL. Is an ATC authorization required?
choices: No, since 350 ft AGL is below the Class C floor and in uncontrolled airspace below it
Yes, always required regardless of altitude relative to the Class C floor
Only required if flying at night
Only required if crossing the lateral boundary of Class C, not the floor
questions.rationale: If the RPAS remains below the floor of the overlying controlled airspace and within uncontrolled airspace, no ATC authorization is required for that controlled airspace layer. [AIM] AIM Section 2.2, p. 2-11
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part IX – vertical airspace boundaries
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What does a Control Zone (CZ) typically surround?
choices: A weather reporting station only
A controlled aerodrome, providing controlled airspace for arriving/departing traffic
A national park
A military exercise area exclusively
questions.rationale: A Control Zone is controlled airspace established around an aerodrome to protect IFR/VFR traffic during arrival and departure. [AIM] AIM Section 2.2, p. 2-12
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is a Terminal Control Area (TCA) generally associated with?
choices: A small uncontrolled grass strip
Busy terminal airspace around one or more major airports requiring higher levels of ATC service
An area exclusively for RPAS training
International airspace boundaries only
questions.rationale: TCAs are established around busy terminals to manage higher volumes of controlled traffic with appropriate ATC services. [AIM] AIM Section 2.3, p. 2-13
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot wants to operate within a Control Zone that has multiple satellite aerodromes. What must the pilot verify?
choices: Nothing beyond the primary aerodrome's ATC unit
Which ATC unit or agency has jurisdiction over the specific area/altitude being used, since satellite aerodromes may have different authorization points
Satellite aerodromes are always excluded from the Control Zone
Only the CFS listing for the primary aerodrome matters
questions.rationale: Complex Control Zones may have multiple aerodromes and delegated authorities; pilots must confirm the correct authority for their specific operating area. [AIM] AIM Section 2.3, p. 2-14
questions.source: TC AIM / CFS – Control Zone structure
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the vertical extent typically associated with low-level airspace referenced by RPAS operations?
choices: Surface up to 18,000 ft ASL (the altimeter setting region boundary)
Only 0-100 ft AGL
Only above FL600
There is no defined vertical extent for low-level airspace
questions.rationale: The altimeter setting region extends from the surface up to 18,000 ft ASL, above which the standard pressure region and flight levels apply. [AIM] AIM Section 2.4, p. 2-15
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is it important for RPAS pilots to know the altimeter setting region boundary?
choices: It has no operational relevance to RPAS
It affects how altitude references (e.g., local altimeter setting vs standard pressure) should be applied and interpreted for airspace/traffic purposes
It only matters for aircraft above FL600
It determines RPAS registration requirements
questions.rationale: Understanding which altimetry reference applies helps pilots correctly interpret altitude information relative to other traffic and airspace boundaries. [AIM] AIM Section 2.4, p. 2-16
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot near an international border sees airspace on a chart change classification without an obvious visual marker on the ground. Why does this matter?
choices: Airspace classification is irrelevant if there's no visible ground feature
Airspace boundaries are defined by lateral/vertical coordinates on charts, not ground features, so pilots must reference charts/GPS rather than visual cues alone
Only manned aircraft need to consider airspace boundaries
Airspace never changes classification near borders
questions.rationale: Airspace boundaries are defined geographically and vertically per charts, independent of visible ground features, requiring careful chart/GPS cross-reference. [AIM] AIM RPA Section, p. 2-40
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What information source shows the current status of a Class F Restricted Area (active/inactive)?
choices: The pilot's own guess based on time of day
NOTAMs and/or the controlling agency, since restricted area activity can vary by schedule
The RPA's onboard GPS only
There is no way to determine this
questions.rationale: Restricted area activation schedules can vary; pilots must check NOTAMs or contact the controlling/using agency for current status. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-3
questions.source: Designated Airspace Handbook / NOTAM system + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the purpose of an Air Defence Identification Zone (ADIZ)?
choices: To mark RPAS-only flying areas
To require aircraft entering/operating within it to identify themselves for national security/defence purposes
To indicate uncontrolled airspace exclusively
To define weather reporting boundaries
questions.rationale: An ADIZ requires aircraft to file identification/flight plan information for national security purposes when operating within its boundaries. [AIM] AIM Section 2.2, p. 2-11
questions.source: TC AIM – Air Defence Identification Zones
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS operation is planned within an ADIZ near a border area. What additional consideration applies compared to a similar flight elsewhere?
choices: None; ADIZ rules do not apply to RPAS
The operator should consider whether ADIZ identification/notification requirements affect the operation, in addition to standard RPAS airspace rules
ADIZ automatically prohibits all RPAS flight
ADIZ only affects flights above FL600
questions.rationale: While RPAS operations are typically low-level and localized, operators near ADIZ boundaries should assess whether any identification/notification obligations apply. [AIM] AIM Section 2.3, p. 2-13
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What does MF stand for in the context of uncontrolled aerodrome airspace procedures?
choices: Mandatory Frequency
Minimum Fuel
Multi-Function
Maximum Flight
questions.rationale: MF (Mandatory Frequency) areas require aircraft to monitor/communicate on a specified frequency near certain uncontrolled aerodromes. [AIM] AIM Section 2.4, p. 2-15
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: How does an MF area differ from an ATF (Aerodrome Traffic Frequency) area?
choices: They are identical concepts with different names
MF areas have a regulatory requirement to communicate on the specified frequency, while ATF is a recommended frequency without the same mandatory regulatory backing
ATF is more restrictive than MF
MF only applies to RPAS, ATF only applies to manned aircraft
questions.rationale: MF carries a regulatory requirement for radio communication procedures, while ATF is recommended practice at aerodromes without an MF designation. [AIM] AIM RPA Section, p. 2-40
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot without a radio wants to operate near an MF aerodrome. What must they consider?
choices: Nothing; MF requirements don't apply if you don't have a radio
How they will maintain situational awareness and avoid conflicts with manned traffic despite not being able to monitor/transmit on the MF, potentially adjusting the operation area/timing
MF procedures are only advisory and can be ignored
RPAS are automatically prohibited near any MF aerodrome regardless of distance
questions.rationale: Even without a radio, the pilot must still manage the risk of operating near an MF aerodrome's traffic, since the underlying safety concern remains regardless of equipment. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-3
questions.source: CARs Part IX – aerodrome proximity risk management + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: On a VFR Navigation Chart (VNC), what typically indicates the base and top of controlled airspace?
choices: Colored shading with numbers indicating altitudes (e.g., in hundreds of feet)
There is no way to determine this from a VNC
Only text descriptions in a separate manual
A single universal altitude applies everywhere
questions.rationale: VNCs use shading/boundary lines with numeric altitude values to depict the vertical limits of controlled airspace. [AIM] AIM Section 2.2, p. 2-11
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What does a number like '25' inside a controlled airspace boundary typically represent on a VNC (in the context of altitude)?
choices: 25 statute miles
2,500 ft ASL (in hundreds of feet)
25 knots wind speed
25 nautical miles from the aerodrome
questions.rationale: Chart altitude figures are typically expressed in hundreds of feet, so '25' represents 2,500 ft (commonly ASL unless otherwise noted). [AIM] AIM Section 2.3, p. 2-13
questions.source: NAV CANADA VNC/VTA chart conventions + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A VTA chart shows overlapping Class C and Class D segments with different floor altitudes around a busy terminal. What should the pilot do before flight?
choices: Assume the lowest floor applies everywhere in the area
Carefully identify which specific segment and floor altitude applies to their intended flight location, since floors can vary by segment
Ignore chart segment differences since RPAS fly low anyway
Only check the highest floor value shown on the chart
questions.rationale: Complex terminal airspace often has multiple segments with different floors; pilots must identify the specific segment applicable to their location. Correctly reading VNC/VTA charts is a TP 15263 Section 5 (Maps and charts) knowledge objective; the underlying regulatory driver is knowing controlled airspace boundaries for site survey (CAR 901.27) and controlled airspace authorization (CAR 901.71/901.73) purposes — no CARs section mandates the VTA chart product by name.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Maps and charts (VNC/VTA chart interpretation); VNC/VTA are paid NAV CANADA products (no free copy). The free, regulatory-recognized equivalent for airspace boundary/floor data is the NAV CANADA Designated Airspace Handbook (DAH).

questions.question: What is the general purpose of the Canada Flight Supplement (CFS)?
choices: A weather forecasting tool only
A reference publication providing detailed aerodrome, communications, and airspace facility data
A pilot logbook
An RPAS registration database
questions.rationale: The CFS is a comprehensive reference for aerodrome data, frequencies, and facility information used alongside charts. [AIM] AIM RPA Section, p. 2-40
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: How can the CFS help identify the correct ATC authority for a controlled airspace authorization request?
choices: It cannot help with this
It lists aerodrome/airspace facility contact and frequency information which can help identify or confirm the responsible ATC unit
It only lists RPAS operators
It replaces the need to contact ATC entirely
questions.rationale: CFS entries include facility and frequency data useful for identifying the correct authority, though direct confirmation with ATC/NAV CANADA is still required.
questions.source: NAV CANADA CFS – facility data + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot cross-references the CFS with a VNC and finds a discrepancy in an aerodrome's published elevation. What should the pilot do?
choices: Use whichever value seems more convenient
Treat the discrepancy as a flag to verify with the most current official source and, if unresolved, contact the aerodrome operator or NAV CANADA for clarification
Ignore both and estimate elevation visually
Always trust the VNC over the CFS without further checking
questions.rationale: Discrepancies between official sources should prompt verification against the most current publication and, if needed, direct confirmation from the responsible agency.
questions.source: TC AIM – reconciling official data sources + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What generally defines a Water Aerodrome as charted in the Canada Water Aerodrome Supplement (CWAS)?
choices: Any body of water regardless of use
A designated area of water used for aircraft takeoff/landing, published with relevant operational data
Only ocean-based aerodromes
Water aerodromes are not published anywhere
questions.rationale: The CWAS publishes designated water aerodromes with relevant operational information, similar to the CFS for land aerodromes.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might an RPAS pilot planning an operation near a lake need to check the CWAS?
choices: The CWAS is irrelevant to RPAS operations
The lake may be a designated water aerodrome with associated float plane traffic, affecting risk and airspace considerations
The CWAS only applies to scuba diving areas
Water aerodromes are always closed to RPAS by default
questions.rationale: If a body of water is a designated water aerodrome, float plane traffic patterns and associated risks must be factored into the operation.
questions.source: NAV CANADA CWAS – operational relevance + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot plans a flight adjacent to an unregistered private aerodrome not listed in the CFS. What should the pilot do?
choices: Assume it does not exist since it isn't listed
Use a site survey (and any available imagery/local knowledge) to identify unregistered aerodromes and account for them in risk assessment, since not all aerodromes are formally registered
Ignore any aerodrome not listed in official publications
Only worry about aerodromes with runways over 3000 ft
questions.rationale: Site surveys are specifically meant to catch unregistered/uncharted aerodromes that official publications may miss, increasing situational awareness.
questions.source: TP 15530 – site survey / unregistered aerodrome awareness + DAH

questions.question: What is Class E airspace generally used for?
choices: Uncontrolled airspace only
Controlled airspace not otherwise classified as A, B, C, or D, often used for transition areas and airways
Airspace exclusively above FL600
Airspace reserved for military use only
questions.rationale: Class E is controlled airspace that doesn't fit the other controlled categories, commonly used for airways and transition areas. [AIM] AIM Section 2.1, p. 2-3
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might Class E airspace be less obvious to RPAS pilots compared to Class B/C/D?
choices: Class E is always identical to Class G and requires no special attention
Class E often has less prominent charted boundaries/shading in some areas and lower minimum floors, making it easy to overlook as controlled airspace
Class E never exists near RPAS operating altitudes
Class E is only found outside Canada
questions.rationale: Class E airspace, especially at lower floors, can be easy to miss on a chart if a pilot isn't specifically checking for it, despite being controlled airspace requiring authorization. [AIM] AIM Section 2.2, p. 2-11
questions.source: TC AIM / NAV CANADA VNC – Class E awareness
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot plans a flight at 300 ft AGL in an area where Class E airspace has a floor of 700 ft AGL, with Class G below it. Is ATC authorization required?
choices: Yes, since any Class E in the vicinity requires authorization regardless of altitude
No, because the flight remains below the Class E floor, in uncontrolled Class G airspace
Only required at night
Only required if the flight exceeds 10 minutes duration
questions.rationale: As long as the RPAS remains below the floor of the controlled airspace above it, it is operating in uncontrolled airspace and does not require authorization for that layer. [AIM] AIM Section 2.3, p. 2-13
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What information does the Designated Airspace Handbook (DAH) primarily provide?
choices: Weather forecasts for specific regions
Detailed listings of Class F Special Use Airspace boundaries, altitudes, and controlling/using agencies
A directory of drone pilot schools
Aircraft maintenance schedules
questions.rationale: The DAH details Class F airspace boundaries, vertical limits, and the agencies responsible for or using each designated area. [AIM] AIM Section 2.4, p. 2-15
questions.source: NAV CANADA Designated Airspace Handbook + AIM
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot needs to determine if a CYA area requires coordination before flight. Where should they check?
choices: Only a general internet search
The Designated Airspace Handbook and any associated NOTAMs for that specific CYA identifier
The Aeronautics Act text only
Their RPA's user manual
questions.rationale: The DAH entry for a specific CYA identifier, cross-referenced with current NOTAMs, provides the authoritative details on coordination needs. [AIM] AIM RPA Section, p. 2-40
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Two adjacent Class F areas have overlapping altitude ranges but different controlling agencies. What is the operational implication for an RPAS pilot?
choices: Only one agency needs to be contacted, whichever is more convenient
The pilot may need to coordinate with both controlling agencies depending on which portion of the overlapping airspace the flight will use
Overlapping Class F areas are not possible in Canada
Overlapping areas automatically default to Class G rules
questions.rationale: When areas overlap with different responsible agencies, the pilot must identify and coordinate with the correct agency (or both) based on the specific area of operation.
questions.source: Designated Airspace Handbook – overlapping Class F areas + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is a NAV CANADA Flight Information Region (FIR) boundary used for?
choices: Marking international waters only
Defining the area within which a specific Flight Information Centre/ATC unit provides flight information and related services
Marking RPAS-only airspace
Marking weather radar coverage only
questions.rationale: FIR boundaries define the area of responsibility for flight information and related air traffic services provided by a specific unit.
questions.source: TC AIM – Flight Information Regions + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why would an RPAS pilot need to know which FIR they are operating in?
choices: It has no operational relevance for RPAS
It identifies which Flight Information Centre to contact for services like NOTAM briefings or flight information relevant to the operation
It only matters for international flights
FIR boundaries determine RPAS registration fees
questions.rationale: Knowing the FIR helps identify the correct FIC or ATC unit to contact for briefings and relevant flight information.
questions.source: TC AIM – FIR operational relevance + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS operation is planned very close to the boundary between two FIRs. What should the pilot verify?
choices: Nothing; FIR boundaries never affect ground-level airspace users
Which FIR (and associated FIC/ATC authority) is responsible for the specific operating location, in case cross-boundary coordination or differing services apply
FIR boundaries automatically merge for low-altitude RPAS flights
Only the FIR named after the province matters
questions.rationale: Operating near an FIR boundary may create ambiguity about which unit is responsible; pilots should confirm the correct authority for their specific location.
questions.source: TC AIM – FIR boundary considerations + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What does a dashed magenta line typically represent around some uncontrolled aerodromes on a VNC?
choices: A Mandatory Frequency (MF) or ATF area boundary
A restricted military zone
An international border
A no-fly zone for all aircraft
questions.rationale: Dashed boundary symbology is commonly used to depict MF/ATF area boundaries around certain uncontrolled aerodromes.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: How should a pilot interpret a chart note showing 'BY NOTAM' next to an airspace boundary?
choices: The airspace parameters shown are fixed and never change
The airspace's active status/parameters may be modified by NOTAM, so current NOTAMs must be checked before relying solely on the chart
It means the airspace has been permanently decommissioned
It only applies to military aircraft
questions.rationale: 'By NOTAM' indicates that current activation or parameter changes are communicated via NOTAM, requiring the pilot to check current NOTAMs rather than relying on the chart alone. [AIM] AIM Section 2.2, p. 2-11
questions.source: TC AIM / NAV CANADA chart conventions
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot is unsure whether their planned altitude places them inside or just below a shelf of Class C airspace shown on a VTA. What is the safest approach?
choices: Assume they are below the shelf and proceed without confirmation
Treat the situation conservatively: verify the exact floor value from the chart/CFS and, if in doubt, obtain an ATC authorization or reduce planned altitude with margin
Only worry about it if ATC contacts them first
Fly higher to be clearly inside controlled airspace instead
questions.rationale: When uncertain about proximity to a controlled airspace boundary, the safe practice is to verify exact figures and build in margin or obtain authorization rather than assume. [AIM] AIM Section 2.3, p. 2-13
questions.source: TC AIM – airspace boundary risk management
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the general function of a Flight Service Station (FSS)?
choices: It provides ATC separation services identical to a tower
It provides flight information, advisory services, and aerodrome advisory service at certain locations, without providing full ATC separation
It only sells fuel to aircraft
It replaces the need for NOTAMs
questions.rationale: FSS units provide flight information and advisory services (including aerodrome advisory service at some locations) but do not issue ATC clearances/separation like a tower. [AIM] AIM Section 2.4, p. 2-15
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might an RPAS pilot contact an FSS before a flight near an uncontrolled aerodrome with an FSS presence?
choices: FSS units have no relevant information for RPAS pilots
To gain situational awareness of known traffic, weather, and aerodrome conditions that could affect coordination near the aerodrome
FSS contact is legally required for every RPAS flight regardless of location
Only to request permission to takeoff, similar to an ATC tower
questions.rationale: Contacting the FSS can provide useful situational awareness (traffic, weather, aerodrome status) supporting safe coordination, even though FSS doesn't issue clearances. [AIM] AIM RPA Section, p. 2-40
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot receives conflicting information: the FSS advises of no known traffic, but a NOTAM indicates a temporary parachute jumping area nearby. What should the pilot do?
choices: Trust the FSS exclusively and disregard the NOTAM
Treat both sources as relevant and reconcile them, giving weight to the NOTAM's specific temporary hazard information alongside the FSS's general traffic picture
Disregard both and proceed regardless
Only NOTAMs matter; FSS advisories are irrelevant
questions.rationale: FSS advisories and NOTAMs serve different but complementary purposes; a specific NOTAM about a hazard should not be dismissed simply because a general advisory didn't mention it.
questions.source: TC AIM – reconciling aeronautical information sources + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What does 'transponder-mandatory airspace' generally imply for manned aircraft?
choices: All aircraft must carry an operating transponder to operate within that airspace
Transponders are optional in that airspace
It only applies to helicopters
It is unrelated to airspace classification
questions.rationale: Transponder-mandatory zones require aircraft to carry and operate a transponder, relevant to understanding traffic detectability in that airspace.
questions.source: TC AIM – transponder airspace requirements + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is knowledge of transponder-mandatory airspace relevant to RPAS pilots even though most RPAS don't carry transponders?
choices: It is not relevant at all
It signals areas with likely higher-density controlled traffic, informing risk assessment and the need for ATC authorization/coordination
It means RPAS are automatically permitted without restriction
It replaces the need for any DAA considerations
questions.rationale: Transponder-mandatory airspace often correlates with busier or more sensitive controlled traffic environments, which is useful context for RPAS risk planning.
questions.source: TC AIM – airspace risk context + DAH

questions.question: A pilot plans a flight that will briefly clip the corner of a Class C shelf at exactly the published floor altitude. How should this be handled?
choices: Assume flying exactly at the floor altitude is automatically safe without authorization
Treat operating at or above the published floor as being within controlled airspace, requiring authorization, and add a safety margin below the floor if authorization is not obtained
Only altitudes strictly above the floor require authorization; exactly at the floor is exempt
Class C shelves cannot have corners
questions.rationale: Operating at or above a published floor altitude is generally treated as within the controlled airspace; prudent practice is to maintain a margin below the floor unless authorized.
questions.source: TC AIM – controlled airspace floor interpretation + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of NAV CANADA as an organization relevant to airspace?
choices: A private drone manufacturer
Canada's civil air navigation service provider, responsible for air traffic control, flight information, and aeronautical publications
A government regulatory body that writes the CARs
An airline operator
questions.rationale: NAV CANADA is the country's air navigation service provider, distinct from Transport Canada (the regulator), providing ATC services and aeronautical publications.
questions.source: TC AIM – roles of NAV CANADA vs Transport Canada + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A pilot assumes Transport Canada issues real-time ATC authorizations for controlled airspace. Why is this a misconception?
choices: It is correct; Transport Canada issues all ATC authorizations
NAV CANADA, not Transport Canada, operates air traffic services and issues real-time ATC authorizations; Transport Canada is the regulator setting the rules
Neither organization is involved in airspace authorizations
Only provincial authorities issue ATC authorizations
questions.rationale: Transport Canada regulates aviation safety and sets the rules, while NAV CANADA operates air navigation services including issuing real-time ATC authorizations.
questions.source: TC AIM – regulator vs service provider distinction + DAH
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the default minimum distance an Advanced Operations RPAS must maintain from an uncontrolled aerodrome without further coordination?
choices: 0.5 NM
3 NM
10 NM
There is no defined distance
questions.rationale: Standard Advanced Operations rules define a proximity threshold (3 NM) from an aerodrome's centre within which additional coordination/consideration is required.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – aerodrome proximity rule
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is a heliport, as distinct from an aerodrome generally?
choices: A term used only for military airfields
A facility specifically designed/designated for helicopter takeoff and landing
Any open field usable by any aircraft
A water aerodrome exclusively
questions.rationale: A heliport is a facility specifically intended for helicopter operations, which may have different proximity/procedural considerations than fixed-wing aerodromes.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might operating near a heliport require extra caution compared to a fixed-wing aerodrome?
choices: Helicopters never fly below 400 ft AGL
Helicopters can operate at low altitudes, arrive/depart from varied directions, and use non-standard patterns, increasing the chance of unexpected proximity to an RPAS
Heliports are always co-located with major airports
There is no meaningful difference
questions.rationale: Helicopters often fly at low altitude with flexible approach/departure paths, creating less predictable traffic patterns that RPAS pilots must account for.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A hospital rooftop heliport is not listed in the CFS. What should a pilot planning a nearby urban flight do?
choices: Assume it doesn't matter since it isn't in the CFS
Use a thorough site survey (visual inspection, local knowledge, satellite imagery) to identify unregistered/rooftop heliports and account for possible emergency medical helicopter traffic
Only worry about heliports listed in official publications
Rooftop heliports never have active traffic
questions.rationale: Hospital heliports may operate with time-critical emergency traffic and aren't always fully captured in standard publications, making a site survey essential for urban operations.
questions.source: TP 15530 – site survey / unregistered facility awareness

questions.question: What information in the CFS helps identify an aerodrome's runway orientation?
choices: The aerodrome's elevation only
Runway designators (e.g., 09/27) and associated headings/lengths
The aerodrome's radio frequency only
The CFS does not include runway information
questions.rationale: CFS entries list runway designators, headings, and lengths, useful for understanding aircraft approach/departure directions.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is runway orientation relevant to RPAS site surveys near an aerodrome?
choices: It is not relevant
It helps predict likely approach/departure flight paths of manned traffic, informing where RPAS operations pose the greatest conflict risk
It only matters for determining wind direction
It determines the RPAS pilot's certificate level required
questions.rationale: Knowing runway orientation helps anticipate where manned aircraft will typically be on approach/departure, informing risk assessment for nearby RPAS operations.

questions.question: An aerodrome has two crossing runways with different active configurations depending on wind. How should this affect an RPAS pilot's proximity risk assessment?
choices: Only the longer runway needs to be considered
The pilot should account for the range of possible approach/departure paths across all active runway configurations, not just the current one
Crossing runways eliminate the need for proximity consideration entirely
Only one configuration is ever used regardless of wind
questions.rationale: Since active runway configuration can change with wind, a thorough risk assessment should consider all plausible traffic patterns, not just the one observed at a single moment.

questions.question: What does 'circuit' or 'traffic pattern' refer to at an aerodrome?
choices: The electrical wiring of runway lights
The standard flight path aircraft follow around the aerodrome for takeoff/landing sequencing
A type of RPAS flight formation
The boundary of controlled airspace
questions.rationale: A traffic pattern/circuit is the standard rectangular flight path used by aircraft near an aerodrome to organize arrivals/departures.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why should an RPAS pilot understand the typical traffic pattern altitude at a nearby aerodrome?
choices: It has no bearing on RPAS operations
It identifies the altitude band where manned aircraft are likely concentrated during circuits, helping avoid conflicts
It determines the RPAS registration category
It only matters for jet aircraft
questions.rationale: Circuit altitude is where manned traffic concentrates near an aerodrome; RPAS pilots should factor this into vertical risk assessment.
questions.source: TC AIM / TP 15530 – traffic pattern awareness

questions.question: A pilot wants to fly at 250 ft AGL, 2 NM from an uncontrolled aerodrome whose circuit altitude is 1000 ft AGL. What should the pilot still consider?
choices: Nothing, since 250 ft AGL is well below circuit altitude
Departing/arriving aircraft transiting through lower altitudes en route to/from the circuit, plus practice approaches or low passes that may occur below normal circuit height
Circuit altitude makes proximity irrelevant below it
Only helicopters need to be considered at this distance
questions.rationale: Aircraft transit through lower altitudes during initial climb/final approach, and practice or emergency scenarios may bring traffic below normal circuit height, so proximity risk isn't eliminated simply by being below circuit altitude.

questions.question: What is an 'apron' at an aerodrome?
choices: The area used for aircraft parking, loading, and servicing
The main runway surface
A type of RPAS launch pad
The control tower building
questions.rationale: The apron is the designated area for aircraft parking, loading/unloading, fueling, and servicing.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might ground vehicle and aircraft movement on an apron be relevant to an RPAS operation flying nearby?
choices: Apron activity is irrelevant to airborne RPAS risk
Ground movement areas can indicate active aircraft operations and additional low-altitude hazards, informing overall risk awareness near the aerodrome
Aprons are always located far from any RPAS operating area
Only runway activity matters, never apron activity
questions.rationale: Apron activity signals overall aerodrome activity level and potential for low-altitude aircraft movement, relevant to comprehensive risk assessment.

questions.question: What visual indicator commonly shows wind direction at an uncontrolled aerodrome?
choices: A windsock
A runway numbering system
A radio beacon
An apron marking only
questions.rationale: A windsock is the standard visual indicator of wind direction (and rough speed) at many aerodromes.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: How can observing an aerodrome's windsock help an RPAS pilot planning nearby operations?
choices: It has no relevance to RPAS operations
It helps confirm which runway/direction is likely active, supporting prediction of traffic patterns
It only indicates precipitation, not wind
It replaces the need to check weather reports
questions.rationale: Wind direction informs which runway is likely in use, helping the RPAS pilot anticipate traffic flow near the aerodrome.

questions.question: A pilot observes the windsock indicating a runway different from the one implied by recent radio calls. What should the pilot do?
choices: Ignore the discrepancy and proceed with the original plan
Reconcile the discrepancy by continuing to monitor for updated information and treating the situation with increased caution until traffic patterns are clarified
Assume the windsock is broken and disregard it entirely
Immediately land the RPA regardless of circumstances
questions.rationale: Conflicting cues about active runway/traffic flow should increase caution and prompt further monitoring rather than being dismissed.

questions.question: What is the general purpose of Aerodrome Traffic Frequency (ATF) procedures?
choices: To coordinate ground vehicle traffic only
To provide a common frequency for pilots to self-announce position/intentions near an uncontrolled aerodrome
To replace the need for visual scanning
To control international flights only
questions.rationale: ATF procedures allow pilots at uncontrolled aerodromes to self-announce and coordinate via a shared frequency, supporting situational awareness.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Should an RPAS pilot without a radio still be concerned about ATF procedures at a nearby aerodrome?
choices: No, ATF is irrelevant if you lack a radio
Yes, since manned traffic will still be using ATF-coordinated patterns; the RPAS pilot must account for that traffic even without direct radio participation
ATF procedures only apply to jets
ATF eliminates all risk of conflict automatically
questions.rationale: Even without a radio, RPAS pilots must consider the traffic patterns and activity that ATF-coordinated aircraft will be following.
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part IX – aerodrome risk awareness
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS operator wants to establish standing coordination procedures with a nearby uncontrolled aerodrome's users. What is a reasonable approach?
choices: No coordination is possible at uncontrolled aerodromes
Establish direct contact with known aerodrome users/operators to agree on notification procedures, timing, and safe operating practices for recurring RPAS activity
Only coordinate once per year regardless of operation frequency
Assume coordination is unnecessary since the aerodrome is uncontrolled
questions.rationale: Direct coordination with aerodrome users/operators is a recognized way to establish safe recurring operating procedures near an uncontrolled aerodrome.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15263 – aerodrome coordination
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What does the CFS entry for an aerodrome typically include regarding lighting?
choices: Nothing about lighting
Details on runway/approach lighting availability and type, relevant for night operations
Only street lighting near the aerodrome
Lighting information is only in the DAH
questions.rationale: The CFS lists lighting facilities available at an aerodrome, useful context for understanding night operational capability.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might a well-lit aerodrome be a factor in RPAS night operation risk assessment nearby?
choices: Lighting is irrelevant to any risk assessment
Increased lighting may indicate potential for greater nighttime manned aircraft activity, which should be factored into risk near the aerodrome
Lighting always means the aerodrome is permanently closed
Lighting only matters for RPAS taking off, not landing
questions.rationale: Aerodrome lighting availability can correlate with nighttime traffic capability, relevant to assessing risk of an RPAS operation conducted after dark nearby.

questions.question: What is a 'displaced threshold' on a runway?
choices: A section of runway not available for landing but possibly usable for takeoff/taxi
The exact midpoint of the runway
A designated RPAS-only landing area
An area reserved for helicopter operations only
questions.rationale: A displaced threshold moves the landing point further down the runway, though the surface before it may still be usable for other purposes like takeoff roll.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why would understanding a displaced threshold matter for RPAS operations very close to a runway?
choices: It has no bearing on RPAS risk
It affects where manned aircraft touchdown/rotation actually occurs, which can shift the zone of highest low-altitude activity along the runway
It only matters for water aerodromes
Displaced thresholds eliminate all aircraft activity nearby
questions.rationale: The displaced threshold changes where aircraft are actually descending/touching down, shifting the practical zone of concern for nearby low-altitude operations.
questions.source: TC AIM / TP 15530 – runway feature awareness

questions.question: An RPAS operation is planned adjacent to a runway with a significant displaced threshold. How should the site survey account for this?
choices: Ignore the displaced threshold entirely
Map the actual usable landing/takeoff zone (post-displacement) rather than assuming the full physical runway length is uniformly used for touchdown
Assume touchdown always occurs at the very start of the physical runway
Displaced thresholds are irrelevant unless the RPAS crosses the runway
questions.rationale: A proper survey should reflect where aircraft actually operate given the displaced threshold, not just the nominal runway length.

questions.question: What does 'aerodrome elevation' refer to in the CFS?
choices: The height of the control tower
The elevation above sea level (ASL) of the highest point on the landing area
The average cruising altitude of aircraft using the aerodrome
The elevation of the nearest mountain
questions.rationale: Aerodrome elevation is defined as the elevation ASL of the highest point of the landing area, used as a reference for AGL/ASL conversions.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is knowing aerodrome elevation useful for an RPAS pilot planning a flight near that aerodrome?
choices: It's not useful for RPAS planning
It allows accurate conversion between AGL and ASL altitudes when comparing RPAS operating altitude to manned traffic pattern altitudes referenced to aerodrome elevation
It only matters for filing flight plans
It determines RPAS registration fees
questions.rationale: Traffic pattern and circuit altitudes are often referenced relative to aerodrome elevation; knowing this value supports accurate AGL/ASL comparisons.

questions.question: An RPAS pilot at a site with significant terrain slope near the aerodrome must relate their GPS altitude to circuit altitude referenced from aerodrome elevation. What is the key risk if this isn't done carefully?
choices: There is no risk; GPS altitude is always directly comparable
Terrain elevation differences between the RPAS launch site and the aerodrome reference point can cause a miscalculated vertical separation from manned traffic if not properly accounted for
GPS altitude is never usable near aerodromes
Terrain slope only affects RPAS battery life, not altitude calculations
questions.rationale: Since circuit altitudes are referenced to aerodrome elevation, launch-site elevation differences must be carefully reconciled to avoid misjudging actual vertical separation from traffic.

questions.question: What is a 'movement area' at an aerodrome?
choices: Only the parking apron
The part of the aerodrome used for takeoff, landing, and taxiing of aircraft, excluding aprons in some definitions
The area used exclusively by ground vehicles
A designated wildlife area
questions.rationale: The movement area typically comprises runways and taxiways used for takeoff, landing, and taxi operations.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why would an RPAS pilot want to avoid overflying an aerodrome's movement area even at low altitude?
choices: There is no reason to avoid it
Aircraft taxiing, taking off, or landing use this area, and any RPAS presence there creates a direct collision/interference risk
Movement areas are always closed and empty
Only helicopters use the movement area
questions.rationale: The movement area is where active aircraft operations occur; RPAS presence there creates significant direct conflict risk.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – aerodrome hazard avoidance

questions.question: A site survey shows the planned RPAS operational volume does not overlap the movement area, but the contingency volume does. What is the appropriate response?
choices: No action needed since only the operational volume matters
Treat this as a significant risk requiring mitigation (e.g., adjusting flight geography, buffers, or contingency procedures) since a contingency event could bring the RPA into the movement area
Contingency volume overlap is never a concern
Only worry about this if an accident has already occurred
questions.rationale: Contingency volume represents where the aircraft could go during an abnormal event; overlap with a movement area is a serious risk requiring mitigation, not just the nominal operational volume.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – contingency volume risk assessment

questions.question: What is an 'obstacle limitation surface' near an aerodrome generally intended to protect?
choices: RPAS operating corridors
Airspace needed for safe aircraft approach/departure by limiting the height of nearby obstacles/structures
Ground vehicle parking areas
Wildlife habitats near the aerodrome
questions.rationale: Obstacle limitation surfaces define height restrictions on structures/obstacles near an aerodrome to protect safe approach and departure paths.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: How is an obstacle limitation surface relevant to an RPAS pilot planning to fly a tethered or elevated structure-mounted operation near an aerodrome?
choices: It is not relevant to RPAS at all
The RPAS itself, if operating at height near the approach/departure path, could represent an obstacle-like hazard similar to what these surfaces are meant to protect against
Obstacle limitation surfaces only apply to buildings, never to aircraft
It only matters for aircraft over 150 kg
questions.rationale: Even though RPAS aren't fixed obstacles, operating within these protected surfaces creates a similar hazard to manned aircraft using the approach/departure path.
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part IX – approach/departure path protection
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot wants to fly a survey mission that would place the aircraft briefly within the obstacle limitation surface of a nearby runway's approach path. What should the pilot do?
choices: Proceed without any special consideration since RPAS are not 'obstacles' by definition
Treat this as a high-risk scenario requiring specific coordination/authorization given the direct approach-path conflict potential, and consider redesigning the flight geography to avoid it
Only avoid this if flying above 400 ft AGL
This is never a concern for VLOS operations
