questions.rationale: Operating within a protected approach surface creates meaningful risk to arriving/departing traffic and warrants redesign or specific coordination rather than being dismissed.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – aerodrome proximity risk management
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the purpose of NOTAMs related to aerodromes?
choices: To advertise aerodrome services to the public
To communicate temporary or time-critical information affecting aerodrome operations (e.g., runway closures, obstacles, hazards)
To replace the CFS entirely
To set aerodrome landing fees
questions.rationale: NOTAMs communicate temporary, time-critical changes to aerodrome status not yet reflected in permanent publications.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A CFS entry lists an aerodrome as active, but a NOTAM indicates the runway is closed for construction. Which should the pilot rely on?
choices: The CFS, since it is the primary publication
The current NOTAM, since it reflects the most up-to-date operational status
Neither; assume normal operations
Only rely on visual observation on the day of flight
questions.rationale: NOTAMs override the static CFS entry when there's a temporary change, since they represent the most current operational information.
questions.source: TC AIM – NOTAM precedence over static publications
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: A runway closure NOTAM near a planned RPAS site actually increases RPAS risk rather than decreasing it. Why might this be the case?
choices: Runway closures always eliminate all aircraft activity nearby
Closed-runway construction activity may bring additional ground vehicles, temporary structures, or diverted traffic patterns to alternate runways that increase overall aerodrome-area activity
NOTAMs about closures are never relevant to RPAS risk
A closed runway means the aerodrome itself is permanently shut down
questions.rationale: Runway closures can shift traffic to other runways or introduce construction-related ground activity, which may increase rather than decrease overall risk near the aerodrome.

questions.question: What is a 'certified aerodrome' generally distinguished by?
choices: Any aerodrome used at least once a year
An aerodrome that has met specific standards and been issued an aerodrome certificate by the regulator
An aerodrome only usable by certified pilots
A synonym for any registered aerodrome regardless of standards met
questions.rationale: Certified aerodromes have met defined regulatory standards and hold a certificate, generally associated with higher levels of activity/scrutiny (e.g., airports serving commercial air service).
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might a certified aerodrome warrant extra caution for nearby RPAS operations compared to a registered but uncertified aerodrome?
choices: There is no meaningful difference in risk
Certified aerodromes are often associated with higher traffic volumes/commercial air service, increasing the likelihood and consequence of an encounter
Certified aerodromes are always closed to non-commercial traffic
Only certified aerodromes have runways
questions.rationale: Certification standards are often tied to higher-activity aerodromes (e.g., serving commercial air service), correlating with increased traffic density and risk.
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part III – aerodrome certification context
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot assumes a small registered (uncertified) aerodrome poses negligible risk due to low traffic volume. What could make this assumption incorrect?
choices: Low traffic volume always means zero risk

Even low-traffic aerodromes can have unpredictable, unannounced flights (e.g., private aircraft, flight training, medevac diversions) that a pilot might not anticipate from traffic-volume assumptions alone
Uncertified aerodromes are never used by real aircraft
This assumption is always safe to make
questions.rationale: Low overall traffic doesn't eliminate the possibility of unpredictable individual flights; risk assessment shouldn't rely solely on assumed traffic volume.
questions.source: TP 15530 – risk assessment beyond traffic volume assumptions

questions.question: What does a Water Aerodrome Supplement entry help identify near a lake used by float planes?
choices: Wildlife protection zones only
Designated water aerodrome boundaries and operational information relevant to float plane activity
Fishing regulations
Recreational boating speed limits
questions.rationale: The CWAS provides designated water aerodrome information relevant to float plane operations, similar to how the CFS covers land aerodromes.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: How might float plane traffic patterns differ from fixed-wing land-based traffic patterns in a way relevant to RPAS?
choices: They are identical in every respect
Float planes may use longer, less confined approach/departure paths over open water, and can operate from multiple directions depending on wind/water conditions
Float planes never operate below 1000 ft AGL
Float planes only operate at night
questions.rationale: Float plane operations on open water may have more flexible/variable approach and departure paths compared to fixed runways, requiring broader risk consideration.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS survey mission is planned over a large lake also used as a water aerodrome. What is a prudent risk mitigation approach?
choices: No mitigation needed since float planes rarely use lakes
Coordinate timing/location with known float plane operators, monitor for radio calls if equipped, and design flight geography to minimize time spent within likely approach/departure paths
Only fly at night to avoid float plane traffic
Assume all lakes are automatically off-limits to RPAS
questions.rationale: Coordination, monitoring, and thoughtful flight-path design are practical mitigations for operating near active water aerodrome traffic.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an aerodrome's 'segmented circle' visual aid?
choices: To indicate fuel prices
To convey traffic pattern information (e.g., pattern direction) to pilots at uncontrolled aerodromes
To mark RPAS-only landing zones
To indicate the aerodrome's exact elevation
questions.rationale: A segmented circle with associated indicators conveys traffic pattern direction and related information at some uncontrolled aerodromes.
questions.source: TC AIM – visual traffic pattern indicators
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why would an RPAS pilot benefit from checking whether an aerodrome has a segmented circle indicating a non-standard traffic pattern (e.g., right-hand circuits)?
choices: It has no operational relevance
It helps the pilot correctly anticipate where manned traffic will actually be, since a non-standard circuit direction changes the expected pattern location
All traffic patterns are always left-hand, so this never matters
It only affects RPAS pilots flying above 1000 ft AGL
questions.rationale: Non-standard circuit direction changes where traffic is expected relative to the aerodrome, which is important for accurate risk assessment.
questions.source: TC AIM / TP 15530 – circuit direction awareness

questions.question: A pilot's site survey assumed a standard left-hand circuit, but on arrival, the segmented circle indicates a right-hand circuit is in effect. What should the pilot do?
choices: Proceed with the original flight plan regardless
Update the risk assessment and flight geography to reflect the actual right-hand circuit before proceeding, since the assumed traffic pattern location was incorrect
Assume the segmented circle is outdated and ignore it
Cancel the mission permanently without further evaluation
questions.rationale: The site survey and flight plan should be updated to reflect actual observed conditions rather than proceeding on an incorrect assumption about traffic pattern direction.
questions.source: TP 15530 – adapting plans to observed conditions

questions.question: What does 'final approach' refer to in the context of aerodrome traffic?
choices: The last leg of an aircraft's flight path aligned with the runway before landing
The initial climb after takeoff
A ground taxi route
A type of RPAS flight termination procedure
questions.rationale: Final approach is the last segment of an aircraft's approach, aligned with the runway, immediately prior to landing.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is the final approach path considered one of the highest-risk zones for RPAS proximity near an aerodrome?
choices: It isn't a high-risk zone
Aircraft are typically low, slow, and in a fixed configuration with limited maneuvering ability during final approach, making any conflict there especially hazardous
Aircraft are at their highest altitude during final approach
Final approach only occurs at controlled aerodromes
questions.rationale: Aircraft on final approach are low, slow, and committed to landing with limited ability to maneuver, making this a particularly hazardous zone for RPAS conflicts.

questions.question: A site survey identifies that the planned RPAS flight geography does not cross the final approach path, but the ground risk buffer does. What is the appropriate conclusion?
choices: No further action needed since the flight geography itself is clear
The ground risk buffer overlap still represents meaningful risk that should be mitigated, since it reflects the margin for potential deviation, not just the nominal flight path
Ground risk buffers only apply to people on the ground, never to other aircraft
This scenario is impossible in practice
questions.rationale: The ground risk buffer represents a margin for deviation; overlap with the final approach path is a legitimate risk that should be addressed even if the nominal flight geography avoids it directly.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – buffer-zone risk assessment

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'go-around' procedure for manned aircraft?
choices: A scenic detour requested by passengers
An aborted landing where the aircraft climbs away to attempt another approach or divert
A ground taxi shortcut
A type of aerobatic maneuver
questions.rationale: A go-around is executed when a landing cannot be safely completed, resulting in the aircraft climbing away to reattempt or divert.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why should RPAS pilots operating near an aerodrome consider the possibility of a go-around?
choices: Go-arounds never happen in practice
A go-around can put an aircraft into airspace/altitude it wouldn't otherwise occupy, potentially bringing it closer to an RPAS operating area than a normal landing profile would suggest
Go-arounds only occur at night
Go-arounds are irrelevant since they only happen at controlled aerodromes
questions.rationale: A go-around changes the aircraft's flight path unpredictably compared to a standard landing, so RPAS risk assessments should account for this possibility.

questions.question: A pilot argues that since their RPAS operation is timed for a period with 'no scheduled traffic,' aerodrome-related risk mitigations aren't necessary. Why is this reasoning flawed?
choices: It is correct; scheduled traffic is the only risk that matters
Aerodromes can have unscheduled, private, training, medevac, or diverted traffic at any time, so absence of scheduled traffic doesn't eliminate risk
Aerodromes without scheduled traffic are always permanently closed
Only jet aircraft need to be considered in this scenario
questions.rationale: Unscheduled and unpredictable traffic (private flights, training, medevac, diversions) can occur regardless of a published schedule, so risk mitigation should not depend solely on scheduled activity.
questions.source: TP 15530 – risk assessment beyond scheduled traffic

questions.question: What does NOTAM stand for?
choices: Notice to Airmen
National Operations Tracking and Monitoring
Notification of Terrain and Altitude Measurement
Navigation Operations Technical Advisory Memo
questions.rationale: NOTAM stands for Notice to Airmen, communicating time-critical aeronautical information. [AIM] AIM Section 5.1, p. 5-1

questions.question: What is the general purpose of a NOTAM?
choices: To advertise new aviation products
To provide timely information about changes to aeronautical facilities, services, procedures, or hazards essential to flight safety
To replace pilot certification requirements
To set airline ticket prices
questions.rationale: NOTAMs exist to communicate essential, time-critical safety information not yet reflected in permanent publications. [AIM] AIM Section 5.1, p. 5-2

questions.question: What does the 'Q-line' of a NOTAM primarily encode?
choices: The pilot's name and license number
Standardized coded information including subject, condition, altitude limits, and geographic scope
Only the weather forecast for the area
The aircraft's registration number
questions.rationale: The Q-line is a coded summary line providing standardized data (subject/condition codes, altitude limits, coordinates/radius) for automated processing and quick reference. [AIM] AIM Section 5.2, p. 5-3

questions.question: A NOTAM Q-line shows altitude limits '005/025'. What do these values represent?
choices: 5 and 25 nautical miles from the reference point
Lower and upper limits in hundreds of feet (500 ft and 2,500 ft), typically ASL unless otherwise specified
5% and 25% probability of the hazard occurring
5 and 25 minutes duration of the NOTAM
questions.rationale: Q-line altitude limits are expressed in hundreds of feet; '005/025' indicates a vertical band from 500 ft to 2,500 ft. [AIM] AIM Section 5.2, p. 5-4
questions.source: TC AIM – NOTAM Q-line altitude coding

questions.question: A pilot misreads a NOTAM Q-line altitude band of '010/025' as being in flight levels (FL) rather than hundreds of feet AGL/ASL. What is the risk of this error?
choices: No risk; the values are identical either way
The pilot could grossly misjudge whether their low-altitude RPAS operation actually falls within the NOTAM's affected vertical band, leading to an unintended violation or missed hazard
Q-line altitudes are never expressed in feet
This error would only matter for high-altitude jet traffic
questions.rationale: Correctly interpreting whether Q-line values represent feet vs flight levels is critical; misinterpretation can cause a pilot to wrongly conclude a NOTAM doesn't apply to their low-level operation. [AIM] AIM Section 5.3, p. 5-5

questions.question: Where can a pilot obtain current NOTAMs for a planned flight?
choices: Only from a printed newspaper
Through NAV CANADA's official NOTAM/flight planning services (e.g., online briefing tools or FIC)
From social media posts only
NOTAMs are not available to RPAS pilots
questions.rationale: NAV CANADA provides official channels (online tools, Flight Information Centres) for obtaining current NOTAMs. [AIM] AIM Section 5.3, p. 5-6

questions.question: Why should an RPAS pilot check NOTAMs even for a familiar, frequently-used flying site?
choices: NOTAMs never change for familiar sites
Temporary hazards, restrictions, or changes can appear at any time, even at sites flown regularly, so currency of information must be reverified before each flight
Checking NOTAMs is only required for first-time flights at a site
NOTAMs only apply to controlled airspace
questions.rationale: NOTAMs reflect the latest temporary conditions, which can change at any time regardless of how familiar a pilot is with a site. [AIM] AIM Section 5.4, p. 5-7
questions.source: CARs Part IX – pre-flight information requirement + AIM

questions.question: A pilot checks NOTAMs the night before a flight and finds none affecting the area. On the morning of the flight, is this check still sufficient?
choices: Yes, a single check is always sufficient regardless of timing
Not necessarily; NOTAMs can be issued at any time, so a fresh check closer to the actual flight time is prudent, especially for time-sensitive hazards
NOTAMs are only issued once per week
Only the initial check matters; new NOTAMs don't apply retroactively to the pilot's plan
questions.rationale: Since NOTAMs can be issued at any time, a check performed well before the flight may not capture last-minute changes; rechecking closer to flight time is best practice. [AIM] AIM Section 5.4, p. 5-8

questions.question: What type of hazard would commonly be published via NOTAM relevant to RPAS operations?
choices: Permanent changes to CARs regulations
Temporary obstacles, airspace restrictions, aerodrome closures, or unmanned aircraft activity in the area
Long-term weather climate trends
Pilot certificate renewal deadlines
questions.rationale: NOTAMs typically cover temporary/time-critical items like obstacles, restrictions, closures, and other aircraft activity. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-9

questions.question: A NOTAM describes a temporary 500 ft crane erected near a planned RPAS survey site. What must the pilot do?
choices: Ignore it since cranes are ground obstacles, not aircraft hazards
Incorporate the crane's location and height into the flight plan/risk assessment, adjusting the flight geography or altitude to maintain safe clearance
Only worry about the crane if it appears on the VNC as well
Assume the NOTAM is outdated if the crane isn't visible from a distance
questions.rationale: Temporary obstacles like cranes represent direct hazards to low-altitude RPAS operations and must be incorporated into planning. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-10

questions.question: A pilot finds two overlapping NOTAMs for the same area: one indicating a temporary restricted area for a special event, and another indicating routine runway maintenance nearby. How should these be handled?
choices: Only the more recently issued NOTAM matters; the other should be disregarded
Both NOTAMs should be considered together since they represent separate, potentially compounding hazards/restrictions affecting the same area
Overlapping NOTAMs cancel each other out
NOTAMs about maintenance never need to be considered for airborne risk
questions.rationale: Multiple active NOTAMs for an area can compound risk and must all be factored into planning, not just the most recent one.
questions.source: TC AIM – multiple concurrent NOTAMs + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does a NOTAM's 'valid from/until' timeframe indicate?
choices: The period during which the described condition/hazard is in effect
The period during which the pilot must file a flight plan
The pilot's certificate validity period
The manufacturer's warranty period for the RPA
questions.rationale: NOTAMs specify a validity period defining when the described condition or restriction applies.
questions.source: TC AIM – NOTAM validity period + NAV CANADA

questions.question: A NOTAM's validity period ends at 2300Z, but the pilot's mission is expected to run until 2330Z local planning error aside. What must the pilot verify?
choices: Nothing; NOTAM expiry times are irrelevant once a mission begins
Whether the mission timeline, once correctly converted to the same time reference (UTC/Zulu vs local), actually falls within or outside the NOTAM's validity window
The NOTAM will automatically extend to match the mission length
Only the start time of a NOTAM matters, not the end time
questions.rationale: Correctly converting and comparing timeframes (often UTC vs local) is essential to know whether a NOTAM's restriction actually applies during the planned mission window. [AIM] AIM Section 5.1, p. 5-1
questions.source: TC AIM – time reference conversion for NOTAMs

questions.question: Why is confusing UTC (Zulu) time with local time a common and dangerous NOTAM interpretation error?
choices: It is never a real risk since NOTAMs always use local time
It can cause a pilot to believe a NOTAM restriction has expired (or not yet started) when it actually still applies, or vice versa, due to the time zone offset
UTC and local time are always identical in Canada
This error only affects flight planning software, not human interpretation
questions.rationale: NOTAMs are typically expressed in UTC; failing to convert correctly to local time can lead to a pilot misjudging whether a restriction is currently active. [AIM] AIM Section 5.2, p. 5-3

questions.question: What is a common abbreviation used in NOTAMs to indicate 'until further notice'?
choices: UFN
TBD
N/A
EOD
questions.rationale: UFN (Until Further Notice) is a standard NOTAM abbreviation indicating no defined end date. [AIM] AIM Section 5.3, p. 5-5

questions.question: A NOTAM marked 'UFN' affecting a planned operating area is found during pre-flight planning. What should the pilot conclude?
choices: The NOTAM will expire automatically within 24 hours
The restriction/condition remains in effect indefinitely until a cancelling NOTAM is issued, so the pilot must treat it as currently active
UFN NOTAMs can be safely ignored
UFN only applies to weather-related NOTAMs
questions.rationale: A NOTAM marked UFN remains in effect until specifically cancelled by a subsequent NOTAM, so it must be treated as currently active. [AIM] AIM Section 5.4, p. 5-7

questions.question: A pilot assumes an old UFN NOTAM from months ago is no longer relevant simply due to its age. Why is this risky?
choices: Age is the only factor that matters for NOTAM relevance
A UFN NOTAM remains active regardless of age until explicitly cancelled; assuming it has lapsed due to time alone could mean missing an active restriction/hazard
UFN NOTAMs automatically expire after 90 days
Old NOTAMs are always replaced by new ones covering the same area
questions.rationale: UFN NOTAMs do not expire based on elapsed time; only a specific cancelling NOTAM ends their validity, so age alone is not evidence of irrelevance. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-9

questions.question: What does a NOTAM referencing 'RPAS' or 'UAS' activity in an area typically indicate?
choices: That RPAS/UAS flights are permanently banned in that area
That another RPAS/UAS operation is planned or ongoing in that airspace, relevant to deconfliction with the pilot's own operation
That the area is reserved exclusively for RPAS with no other traffic
That the area requires a special radio frequency exclusive to drones
questions.rationale: NOTAMs about other RPAS/UAS activity inform pilots of potential deconfliction needs with other unmanned operations in the same airspace. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-10
questions.source: TC AIM – NOTAM content for RPAS activity

questions.question: A pilot finds a NOTAM describing another operator's RPAS BVLOS activity overlapping their planned area and time. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Proceed without any coordination since NOTAMs don't require a response
Attempt to coordinate with the other operator or adjust the flight plan/timing to avoid conflict, given the overlapping activity
Assume the other NOTAM is inaccurate and disregard it
File a complaint with Transport Canada instead of adjusting the plan
questions.rationale: Overlapping RPAS activity notified via NOTAM should prompt coordination or a plan adjustment to avoid conflict between operations.
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part IX – deconfliction practice + NAV CANADA

questions.question: Two NOTAMs describe overlapping RPAS BVLOS operations in adjacent, but not identical, geographic areas with a shared boundary. What must the pilot assess?
choices: No assessment is needed since the areas aren't identical
Whether the operational and contingency volumes of each operation could realistically overlap near the shared boundary, requiring coordination or added buffer even though the nominal areas differ
Only exact geographic matches ever require coordination
The NOTAMs automatically resolve any conflict without pilot action
questions.rationale: Even non-identical but adjacent operating areas can have overlapping contingency volumes near their shared boundary, requiring careful assessment and possible coordination.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – multi-operator deconfliction + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does a NOTAM typically use to describe the geographic area affected?
choices: A general regional name only, with no coordinates
Coordinates and/or a radius from a reference point, sometimes supplemented by a plain-language description
A photograph of the area
The nearest city's postal code
questions.rationale: NOTAMs typically use coordinates and radius (Q-line) plus plain-language description to define the affected area. [AIM] AIM Section 5.1, p. 5-1

questions.question: A NOTAM's radius is centered on a reference point 8 NM from the pilot's planned launch site, with a 5 NM radius. Does the NOTAM affect the operation?
choices: No, since 8 NM is a large distance
It could, since the radius (5 NM) extends 5 NM from the reference point in all directions; the pilot must check if their operating/contingency volume falls within that combined area
NOTAM radii never overlap with a launch site itself
Only the exact reference point coordinates matter, not the radius
questions.rationale: Because the NOTAM's radius extends outward from its reference point, a launch site 8 NM away is still 3 NM inside the NOTAM's 5 NM boundary and must be evaluated. [AIM] AIM Section 5.2, p. 5-3

questions.question: A pilot calculates that their planned flight geography just barely falls outside a NOTAM's radius, based on a straight-line distance calculation. What additional consideration is important?
choices: No additional consideration is needed once outside the radius
Margin for GPS/position error, wind drift, and the RPAS's ground risk/contingency buffers should be considered, since 'just barely outside' leaves little safety margin
NOTAM radii are always rounded up automatically for safety
This calculation is unnecessary since NOTAMs don't use precise radii
questions.rationale: A marginal clearance from a NOTAM boundary leaves little room for position error or deviation; prudent planning should include margin rather than relying on an exact boundary calculation. [AIM] AIM Section 5.3, p. 5-5

questions.question: What is a 'SNOWTAM'?
choices: A NOTAM specifically reporting snow/ice conditions affecting a movement area
A NOTAM about a snowstorm forecast
A type of RPAS designed for winter operations
A seasonal pilot certificate renewal notice
questions.rationale: A SNOWTAM is a specialized NOTAM format reporting snow, ice, or other contaminants on a movement area. [AIM] AIM Section 5.4, p. 5-7

questions.question: Why might a SNOWTAM be relevant to an RPAS operation even though RPAS don't use runways for winter contaminant purposes the same way manned aircraft do?
choices: It's never relevant to RPAS
It indicates winter conditions and potentially heightened activity/attention around an aerodrome (e.g., snow removal vehicles), relevant to nearby RPAS risk awareness
SNOWTAMs replace the need for weather checks entirely
SNOWTAMs only matter for helicopters
questions.rationale: A SNOWTAM can indicate increased ground vehicle activity (snow removal) and winter operational conditions relevant to overall aerodrome-area risk awareness. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-9

questions.question: A pilot ignores a SNOWTAM near a planned flight site because 'it's not about airspace.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: No flaw; SNOWTAMs are indeed irrelevant to airspace risk
NOTAM types beyond pure airspace/altitude restrictions (like SNOWTAMs) can still signal relevant ground-level activity and operational context that affects overall situational awareness
SNOWTAMs are always cancelled before RPAS flights
SNOWTAMs only apply to jet aircraft operations
questions.rationale: Dismissing a NOTAM based solely on its category name misses the broader situational awareness value it can provide, even if not a direct airspace restriction. [AIM] AIM Section 5.1, p. 5-1
questions.source: TC AIM – comprehensive NOTAM review practice

questions.question: What does a NOTAM code beginning with a hazard/subject like 'obstruction' typically alert pilots to?
choices: A change to radio frequencies only
A new or changed obstacle (e.g., crane, tower, temporary structure) that could affect flight safety
A change in fuel prices at a nearby aerodrome
A pilot certificate expiry
questions.rationale: Obstruction-related NOTAMs alert pilots to new or modified obstacles affecting flight safety in the area. [AIM] AIM Section 5.2, p. 5-3

questions.question: A pilot sees an obstruction NOTAM listing a new tower at a height described only in metres, while their planning tools use feet. What must the pilot do?
choices: Assume the units are automatically the same
Correctly convert the units (metres to feet or vice versa) before comparing the obstacle height to planned RPAS operating altitude
Ignore the obstacle since units differ
Only use whichever unit is more convenient without converting
questions.rationale: Unit mismatches between NOTAM data and planning tools must be reconciled through correct conversion to avoid misjudging obstacle clearance. [AIM] AIM Section 5.3, p. 5-5
questions.source: TC AIM – unit conversion for obstacle data

questions.question: An obstruction NOTAM gives a tower height 'AGL' relative to its own base elevation, but the RPAS operating altitude is being planned relative to the pilot's own launch site elevation, which differs by 50 ft. What must be done?
choices: No adjustment needed; AGL always means the same absolute altitude everywhere
Reconcile the different reference elevations (tower base vs launch site) to accurately compare actual heights/altitudes on a common vertical reference
Always assume the tower is shorter than stated to be safe
AGL measurements are never comparable between different locations
questions.rationale: AGL is relative to local ground elevation, so comparing obstacle height to RPAS altitude requires reconciling different reference elevations onto a common vertical datum (e.g., ASL). [AIM] AIM Section 5.4, p. 5-7

questions.question: What is the general recommended practice for retaining NOTAM briefing records for a flight?
choices: No record needs to be kept
Retain a record of the briefing/NOTAM check as part of good operational practice and potential incident investigation support
Only keep records if requested by a passenger
Records should be destroyed immediately after each flight
questions.rationale: Retaining a record of pre-flight NOTAM/weather briefings supports good operational practice and can be valuable if an incident investigation occurs. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-9

questions.question: What is a practical way for an RPAS operator to demonstrate compliance with the requirement to consult aeronautical information before flight?
choices: Relying on memory alone with no documentation
Saving or logging the NOTAM briefing output (e.g., screenshot, printout, or briefing reference number) as part of flight records
Assuming compliance is automatic once a certificate is held
Verbally telling a colleague what was checked, with no record kept
questions.rationale: Saving or logging briefing outputs provides documented evidence that the aeronautical information consultation requirement was met.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – documentation practice + NAV CANADA

questions.question: An operator's SMS review after an incident finds that NOTAM briefings were performed but not documented for several prior flights. What is the appropriate corrective action?
choices: No action needed since briefings were performed
Implement a documented process (e.g., standard checklist/logging requirement) to ensure NOTAM briefings are consistently recorded going forward, closing the gap identified
Discontinue NOTAM briefings since they clearly aren't valued
Only document briefings after future incidents occur
questions.rationale: A safety management system should identify gaps (like inconsistent documentation) and implement corrective processes to prevent recurrence.
questions.source: AC 107-002 – SMS corrective action practice + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does a NOTAM referring to a 'GPS outage' or 'GNSS interference' typically warn about?
choices: A permanent shutdown of all satellite navigation
A temporary degradation or unavailability of GPS/GNSS signals in a specified area, which can affect RPAS navigation/autopilot performance
A change in radio frequencies only
A ban on all RPAS use nationwide
questions.rationale: GPS/GNSS outage NOTAMs warn of temporary signal degradation that could affect navigation and autopilot systems relying on satellite positioning. [AIM] AIM Section 5.1, p. 5-1

questions.question: A NOTAM warns of GPS interference testing near a planned RPAS BVLOS mission relying heavily on GNSS for navigation. What should the pilot do?
choices: Proceed as planned since GPS interference rarely affects RPAS
Reassess the mission's reliance on GNSS, consider alternate navigation/contingency procedures, or reschedule to avoid the affected period
Ignore the NOTAM since it's likely intended only for manned aircraft
Increase RPAS altitude to avoid the interference automatically
questions.rationale: GNSS-reliant RPAS missions face direct risk from interference testing; the pilot should reassess navigation contingencies or reschedule accordingly. [AIM] AIM Section 5.2, p. 5-3

questions.question: A GNSS interference NOTAM covers a large area, but the pilot's RPA claims 'redundant' non-GPS positioning (e.g., visual/inertial). Should the NOTAM still be a concern?
choices: No, redundant systems fully eliminate any risk from GPS interference
Yes; redundant systems may have their own limitations (e.g., drift over time, degraded accuracy) and the interference could still affect safety margins, autopilot behaviour, or fallback modes
GNSS interference NOTAMs never actually affect real operations
Redundant systems automatically extend flight range to avoid the area
questions.rationale: Backup navigation systems have their own limitations and may not fully replace GNSS performance, so interference risk should still be carefully evaluated rather than dismissed. [AIM] AIM Section 5.3, p. 5-5

questions.question: What is a 'Class I' NOTAM distribution generally associated with?
choices: International distribution of significant NOTAMs
Only local aerodrome bulletin board postings
NOTAMs relevant only to weather balloons
A now-retired system with no modern equivalent
questions.rationale: NOTAM distribution classes distinguish between wider (international) and more localized distribution scopes. [AIM] AIM Section 5.4, p. 5-7

questions.question: Why does NOTAM distribution scope matter to an RPAS pilot using an automated briefing tool?
choices: Distribution scope is irrelevant to briefing completeness
Some briefing tools/services may not automatically include every distribution class, so pilots should confirm their briefing source captures all NOTAMs relevant to their specific operating area
All briefing tools always include every possible NOTAM regardless of distribution class
Distribution scope only matters for international flights
questions.rationale: Not all briefing sources may capture every NOTAM distribution class, so pilots should verify their tool's coverage is adequate for their operating area. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-9

questions.question: A pilot relies solely on a third-party mobile app for NOTAM briefings, which later turns out to have missed a locally-distributed NOTAM. What lesson does this illustrate?
choices: Third-party apps are always fully reliable and need no verification

Pilots should verify that their briefing source is authoritative and complete, and consider cross-referencing with NAV CANADA's official briefing services, especially for less common distribution scopes
NOTAMs with limited distribution are never legally binding
This scenario cannot occur in practice
questions.rationale: Reliance on unofficial or incomplete tools can create gaps in situational awareness; cross-referencing official sources helps mitigate this risk. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-10

questions.question: What does a NOTAM cancellation notice typically indicate?
choices: That the original NOTAM's condition/restriction is no longer in effect
That the pilot's certificate has been cancelled
That the aerodrome has permanently closed
That a new permanent regulation has been enacted
questions.rationale: A cancellation NOTAM formally ends the validity of a previously issued NOTAM's condition or restriction.
questions.source: TC AIM – NOTAM cancellation + NAV CANADA

questions.question: A pilot sees a NOTAM listed as active in an older briefing but finds no corresponding cancellation NOTAM in a fresh briefing. What should the pilot conclude?
choices: The NOTAM automatically expired since it wasn't mentioned again

If it isn't in the current briefing and the system indicates it has ended (e.g., past its stated end time or shown as cancelled/expired), it's no longer active; if uncertain, verify directly with the briefing source
All NOTAMs are permanent unless the pilot personally confirms otherwise via letter
The absence of any mention means the pilot should assume it's still active indefinitely
questions.rationale: Whether a NOTAM has lapsed should be confirmed by checking its stated validity period or an explicit cancellation, ideally cross-checked against a current, complete briefing.
questions.source: TC AIM – NOTAM lifecycle verification + NAV CANADA

questions.question: A pilot's briefing tool shows a NOTAM as 'active' past its stated expiry time due to a system delay. What is the safest course of action?
choices: Trust the tool's 'active' status over the NOTAM's own stated expiry time in all cases
Rely on the NOTAM's actual stated validity period as authoritative, and if there's ambiguity or system lag, seek direct confirmation from an official briefing source before proceeding
Assume all briefing tools are always perfectly synchronized in real time
Ignore both the tool and the stated NOTAM period, and just fly cautiously
questions.rationale: The NOTAM's own stated validity period is authoritative; tool display lag shouldn't be blindly trusted, and direct confirmation should be sought if there's doubt. [AIM] AIM Section 5.1, p. 5-1
questions.source: TC AIM – resolving briefing tool discrepancies

questions.question: What is the purpose of a pre-flight self-briefing checklist item specifically for NOTAMs?
choices: To ensure the pilot has checked and understood all NOTAMs relevant to the planned flight before departure
To confirm the aircraft's registration number
To verify battery voltage only
To confirm payload weight distribution
questions.rationale: A NOTAM checklist item ensures the pilot has systematically reviewed relevant NOTAMs as part of standard pre-flight preparation. [AIM] AIM Section 5.2, p. 5-3

questions.question: Why is it good practice to brief a visual observer or crew member on relevant NOTAMs before flight, not just the pilot?
choices: It is unnecessary since only the pilot needs to know
Shared awareness improves overall crew situational awareness and supports better collective decision-making if conditions change during the flight
Visual observers are legally barred from knowing NOTAM content
NOTAMs are irrelevant to visual observer duties
questions.rationale: Shared crew awareness of NOTAMs supports better collective situational awareness and decision-making, consistent with crew resource management principles. [AIM] AIM Section 5.3, p. 5-5
questions.source: TP 15530 – crew resource management / shared awareness + AIM

questions.question: During a mission, a visual observer notices new construction equipment that seems inconsistent with the pre-flight NOTAM briefing. What should occur?
choices: Ignore the observation since the NOTAM briefing was already completed

The observer should report it to the pilot, who should reassess the current situation and consider whether new information (e.g., a since-issued NOTAM) or an unreported hazard now affects the operation
Only post-flight reports need to capture this kind of observation
Construction equipment is never relevant to RPAS safety
questions.rationale: Real-time observations inconsistent with pre-flight information should prompt reassessment during the flight, reflecting good crew communication and adaptive risk management. [AIM] AIM Section 5.4, p. 5-7

questions.question: What generally triggers Transport Canada or NAV CANADA to issue a new NOTAM?
choices: Only a fixed weekly publication schedule
A reported change or event affecting aeronautical facilities, airspace, or hazards that requires timely pilot notification
Only pilot complaints
A change in aircraft manufacturing standards
questions.rationale: NOTAMs are issued in response to reported changes/events needing timely notification, not on a fixed publication schedule. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-9

questions.question: An RPAS operator identifies a new permanent hazard (e.g., a newly built tower) near their frequent flying area. What should the operator do regarding NOTAMs?
choices: Nothing; only Transport Canada/NAV CANADA can identify hazards
Report the observed hazard through appropriate channels so it can be verified and, if warranted, published (e.g., as an obstacle NOTAM or chart update) for the benefit of all aviation users
Keep the information private to maintain a competitive advantage
Assume all new towers are automatically already known to authorities
questions.rationale: Reporting newly observed hazards supports the broader aviation safety system, potentially leading to NOTAM issuance or chart updates. [AIM] AIM Section 5.5, p. 5-10

questions.question: A pilot wants to determine whether a temporary drone restriction they read about online is officially reflected as a NOTAM. What is the correct verification step?
choices: Trust the online source without further verification
Check official NAV CANADA/Transport Canada NOTAM services directly to confirm whether an official NOTAM corresponding to the reported restriction actually exists
Assume any online report is automatically an official restriction
Only verify if the restriction seems inconvenient to the pilot's plans
questions.rationale: Official verification through authoritative NOTAM services is necessary since unofficial online reports may be inaccurate, outdated, or unofficial.
questions.source: TC AIM – verifying restrictions through official sources + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What is a common reason a temporary flight restriction (TFR) NOTAM might be issued?
choices: A VIP movement, major public event, or emergency response requiring temporary airspace restriction
A routine daily weather forecast update
A pilot certificate renewal
A change in RPAS registration fees
questions.rationale: TFRs are commonly issued for VIP movements, major events, wildfires/emergency response, or similar situations requiring temporary airspace control.
questions.source: TC AIM – temporary flight restrictions + NAV CANADA

questions.question: A TFR NOTAM is issued for a wildfire response near a planned RPAS survey mission. What is the correct pilot action?
choices: Proceed since RPAS are small and unlikely to interfere

Do not operate within the TFR area, since firefighting aircraft operate at low altitude and RPAS presence creates a serious collision/interference risk, potentially grounding the firefighting response
Only avoid the TFR if flying above 400 ft AGL
TFRs for wildfires only apply to manned aircraft, not RPAS
questions.rationale: Wildfire TFRs exist specifically because RPAS incursions have historically grounded firefighting aircraft; compliance is critical for both legal and life-safety reasons.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TC AIM – forest fire area restrictions + NAV CANADA

questions.question: A pilot's planned survey area is adjacent to, but not within, a wildfire TFR boundary. The pilot assumes this is automatically safe. What additional factor should be considered?
choices: Nothing; being outside the exact boundary is always fully safe

Firefighting aircraft may transit near or just outside the TFR boundary, and smoke/visibility conditions could extend beyond the mapped area, so extra caution and possibly a larger buffer are warranted
TFR boundaries are always drawn with enormous excess margin, so no caution is needed
Wildfire TFRs never affect areas outside their exact mapped boundary in any way
questions.rationale: Real-world firefighting operations and smoke conditions can extend beyond the exact mapped TFR boundary, so prudent risk management includes additional caution near the edge.
questions.source: TC AIM – TFR boundary risk margin + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does a METAR primarily report?
choices: A forecast of future weather conditions
Current/actual observed weather conditions at an aerodrome at a specific time
A pilot's personal weather opinion
Only wind speed and nothing else
questions.rationale: METAR (Meteorological Aerodrome Report) provides actual observed conditions at a specific time, distinct from a forecast.

questions.question: What does a TAF represent?
choices: A current observation
A Terminal Aerodrome Forecast predicting expected weather conditions over a defined future period
A type of radar image
A record of past weather only
questions.rationale: TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast) provides a forecast of expected conditions at an aerodrome over a stated period, distinct from an observed METAR.

questions.question: A METAR reports 'BKN008'. What does this indicate?
choices: Broken cloud layer with a base at 800 ft AGL
Broken cloud layer with a base at 8,000 ft AGL
8% cloud coverage
Wind gusting to 8 knots
questions.rationale: Cloud group codes in METAR give amount (e.g., BKN=broken) followed by height in hundreds of feet, so '008' equals 800 ft.

questions.question: An RPAS operation requires a minimum 500 ft AGL ceiling per operating procedures. A METAR shows 'OVC004'. Should the flight proceed?
choices: Yes, since OVC004 refers to distance, not ceiling
No, since OVC004 indicates an overcast ceiling at only 400 ft AGL, below the required 500 ft minimum
Yes, because overcast layers don't count as a ceiling
It depends only on visibility, not cloud height
questions.rationale: OVC004 indicates an overcast ceiling at 400 ft, which is below a stated 500 ft minimum ceiling requirement, so the flight should not proceed as planned.
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part IX – ceiling minimums

questions.question: What is 'visibility' as reported in a METAR intended to represent?
choices: The distance a pilot can see and identify prominent objects/lights
The percentage of sky covered by cloud
Wind speed only
Runway length
questions.rationale: Reported visibility represents the greatest distance at which prominent objects can be seen and identified.

questions.question: An RPAS operating procedure requires 3 statute miles minimum visibility for VLOS flight. A METAR shows visibility '2SM'. What should the pilot conclude?
choices: The flight can proceed since 2SM is close enough
The flight should not proceed as planned, since 2SM is below the stated 3SM minimum requirement
Visibility requirements don't apply to RPAS operations
2SM refers to 2 nautical miles, which meets the requirement
questions.rationale: 2SM (2 statute miles) is below the stated 3SM minimum, meaning the operation should not proceed under that specific visibility minimum.
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part IX – visibility minimums

questions.question: A METAR shows good visibility (10SM) but also reports 'FG' with patchy areas nearby not captured by the single-point observation. What should the pilot consider?
choices: The METAR fully represents conditions everywhere in the operating area
METAR is a point observation and may not represent localized variations (e.g., patchy fog) across the entire operating area; the pilot should supplement with direct observation
Fog reports in a METAR are never relevant if visibility is good
FG codes only apply to airports with control towers
questions.rationale: METARs are point observations at the aerodrome; localized conditions like patchy fog elsewhere in the operating area may not be captured, requiring supplemental direct observation.
questions.source: TC AIM – limitations of point weather observations

questions.question: What does a GFA (Graphic Area Forecast) primarily depict?
choices: A textual report of past weather only
A graphical forecast of expected weather (clouds, turbulence, icing, etc.) over a region and time period
A single aerodrome's current METAR
Only surface wind direction
questions.rationale: GFAs provide a graphical depiction of forecast weather conditions across a wider region, useful for broader route/area planning.

questions.question: Why might a GFA be more useful than a single METAR for an RPAS BVLOS mission spanning a larger area?
choices: GFAs are never useful for RPAS planning
A GFA covers a broader region and forecast period, better matching the wider geographic scope of a BVLOS mission compared to a single point-based METAR
METARs always cover larger areas than GFAs
GFAs replace the need for any NOTAM checks
questions.rationale: GFAs are designed for broader regional/route planning, complementing point-based METAR/TAF data for missions spanning a wider area.

questions.question: A GFA shows marginal VFR conditions across a large region, but the nearest METAR shows good conditions. How should a pilot reconcile this for a BVLOS mission extending beyond the METAR's immediate vicinity?
choices: Trust only the METAR since it's a direct observation

Recognize that conditions can vary across the mission area; use the GFA to understand the broader trend and consider that parts of the route beyond the METAR's immediate area may experience the forecast marginal conditions
Trust only the GFA and disregard the METAR entirely
Assume conditions are uniform across the entire GFA region
questions.rationale: Reconciling point observations with regional forecasts helps identify where conditions might differ across a mission's extended area, supporting better risk assessment.
questions.source: TC AIM – reconciling weather sources for extended operations

questions.question: What atmospheric phenomenon is primarily responsible for reduced air density at higher density altitude?
choices: Increased temperature and/or altitude reducing air density
Increased humidity always increasing air density
Lower temperature always reducing air density
Wind speed alone determines density altitude
questions.rationale: Density altitude increases (air becomes less dense) with higher temperature and/or higher pressure altitude.

questions.question: How does high density altitude typically affect RPAS performance?
choices: It has no effect on RPAS since they don't use propellers
It can reduce lift and propulsion efficiency, requiring more power and reducing overall performance margins
It always improves battery endurance
It only affects fixed-wing RPAS, never multirotor
questions.rationale: Reduced air density at high density altitude reduces aerodynamic and propulsion efficiency for both multirotor and fixed-wing RPAS, requiring more power for the same performance.
questions.source: TP 15530 – density altitude effects on performance

questions.question: A hot summer afternoon at a high-elevation site produces a density altitude significantly higher than the pressure altitude. What operational adjustment should a pilot consider?
choices: No adjustment needed; density altitude only matters for jets
Plan for reduced climb performance, reduced payload capacity, and increased power demand, potentially adjusting mission timing to cooler parts of the day or reducing payload
Always fly at maximum payload regardless of density altitude
Density altitude only affects landing, not takeoff or cruise performance
questions.rationale: High density altitude conditions reduce performance margins; mitigations include adjusting timing to cooler conditions or reducing payload/weight to preserve performance margins.
questions.source: TP 15530 – performance planning under high density altitude

questions.question: What generally causes fog to form?
choices: Air cooling to its dew point near the surface, causing condensation
Strong winds mixing dry air near the surface
High-altitude jet stream activity
Volcanic activity exclusively
questions.rationale: Fog forms when air near the surface cools to its dew point, causing water vapor to condense into visible droplets.

questions.question: Why is early morning often a higher-risk time for fog-related RPAS visibility issues?
choices: Fog only forms at night and dissipates before sunrise
Overnight radiative cooling can bring temperature close to the dew point, and fog often persists into early morning before solar heating dissipates it
Morning conditions never involve fog
Fog risk is unrelated to time of day
questions.rationale: Radiation fog commonly forms overnight due to surface cooling and can persist into early morning until solar heating raises temperatures enough to dissipate it.

questions.question: A pilot plans an early morning mission near a river valley known for persistent fog. What is a prudent planning approach?
choices: Proceed exactly as scheduled regardless of local fog patterns
Build in a delayed start time or flexible launch window to allow for local fog to dissipate, and monitor current conditions rather than relying solely on a general forecast
Assume forecasts always precisely predict local microclimate fog timing
Fog is never a factor for RPAS since they fly at low altitude anyway
questions.rationale: Local microclimates (like river valleys) can have fog patterns not perfectly captured by general forecasts, so flexible timing and direct monitoring are prudent.
questions.source: TC AIM / TP 15530 – microclimate risk awareness

questions.question: What is the general risk posed by icing conditions to an RPA?
choices: Icing has no impact on small RPA
Ice accumulation can add weight, disrupt aerodynamics, and impair sensors/control surfaces, degrading performance and safety
Icing only affects large jet aircraft
Icing always improves aerodynamic efficiency
questions.rationale: Ice accumulation adversely affects weight, aerodynamics, and sensor/control performance, posing a real risk to RPA of all sizes.

questions.question: Under what general temperature/moisture conditions is icing most likely to form on an RPA in flight?
choices: Warm, dry conditions well above freezing
Near or below freezing temperatures combined with visible moisture (e.g., cloud, freezing rain, or freezing drizzle)
Only in clear skies with no moisture present
Only during summer months
questions.rationale: Icing generally requires temperatures at or below freezing combined with the presence of visible moisture such as cloud or precipitation.

questions.question: A pilot's RPA is not certified/declared for flight in known icing conditions. A GFA shows a layer of freezing drizzle at the pilot's planned altitude. What must the pilot do?
choices: Proceed anyway since RPAS are lightweight and unaffected
Avoid operating in or through the identified icing conditions, since the aircraft is not approved for known icing and the risk to control/performance is significant
Only avoid icing if operating above 1000 ft AGL
Assume freezing drizzle never actually produces ice on small aircraft
questions.rationale: Operating an aircraft not approved for known icing conditions into forecast freezing drizzle creates unacceptable risk and should be avoided.
questions.source: TP 15530 – icing limitations and manufacturer approval

questions.question: What is mechanical turbulence primarily caused by?
choices: Wind flow disrupted by terrain, buildings, or other obstacles
Only thunderstorm activity
Solar radiation heating the ground
High-altitude jet stream winds exclusively
questions.rationale: Mechanical turbulence results from wind flow being disrupted as it passes over or around terrain, buildings, or other obstacles.

questions.question: Why can RPAS flight controllers sometimes mask the true level of turbulence being experienced by the aircraft?
choices: Flight controllers cannot compensate for turbulence at all
Active stabilization/control corrections may smooth out visible aircraft motion, making the actual turbulence intensity less apparent to the pilot observing the aircraft or camera feed
Turbulence never affects small RPA
Camera stabilization always accurately reflects raw turbulence levels
questions.rationale: Flight controller stabilization and camera gimbal correction can visually smooth out aircraft motion, potentially masking the actual severity of turbulence being encountered.

questions.question: A pilot notices increased battery/power consumption and control input activity on the telemetry display, despite the RPA appearing visually stable via camera feed. What might this indicate?
choices: Nothing of concern; visual stability is the only relevant indicator
The flight controller may be actively compensating for turbulence not visually apparent, and the pilot should factor this into risk/endurance planning even though the aircraft looks stable
This pattern indicates a GPS malfunction exclusively
Increased power consumption is unrelated to turbulence
questions.rationale: Telemetry indicators like increased power draw or control activity can reveal turbulence compensation not obvious from a visually smoothed camera feed, informing better risk awareness.
questions.source: TP 15530 – interpreting telemetry vs visual cues

questions.question: What generally causes a wind gust?
choices: A rapid, short-term increase in wind speed above the sustained wind value
A permanent increase in average wind speed
A decrease in wind speed only
A change in wind direction with no change in speed
questions.rationale: A gust is a rapid, brief increase in wind speed above the sustained/average value.

questions.question: A METAR reports 'wind 270 at 12 gusting 22'. How should a pilot interpret the gust value for risk planning?
choices: Ignore gusts and plan only for the sustained 12-knot value
Plan for the possibility of wind gusts up to 22 knots, since gusts can significantly affect control and stability even if brief
The gust value only matters for manned aircraft
Gust values indicate direction changes, not speed changes
questions.rationale: Gust values represent real, if brief, peak wind speeds that can significantly affect RPAS control and should be included in risk planning, not just the sustained value.
questions.source: TC AIM – interpreting wind gust reports

questions.question: A manufacturer's maximum demonstrated wind limit for an RPA is 20 knots sustained. A METAR shows wind '15 gusting 28'. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The flight is within limits since sustained wind (15 kt) is below the 20 kt limit
The gust value (28 kt) exceeds the demonstrated limit and should be treated as exceeding safe operating margins, even though sustained wind is within limits
Gust values are never compared to manufacturer limits
Only average wind speed over the full day matters, not instantaneous METAR values
questions.rationale: Gusts represent real peak wind conditions the aircraft could encounter; a gust exceeding the demonstrated wind limit should be treated as exceeding safe operating margins.
questions.source: TP 15530 – wind limit interpretation including gusts

questions.question: What generally characterizes 'urban airflow' effects relevant to RPAS operations in cities?
choices: Uniform, predictable wind patterns identical to open terrain
Turbulent, gusty, and variable wind patterns caused by buildings channeling and disrupting airflow
Complete absence of wind in urban canyons
Urban airflow is identical to airflow over water
questions.rationale: Buildings and urban structures disrupt and channel airflow, often producing turbulent, gusty, and unpredictable wind patterns compared to open terrain.

questions.question: Why might a reported airport wind reading not accurately represent conditions for an RPAS flying between tall buildings several kilometres away?
choices: Airport wind readings are always representative of the entire region
Urban structures can create localized wind acceleration, channeling, and turbulence not captured by an airport's more open-terrain wind sensor
Wind conditions never vary by location
RPAS are unaffected by wind regardless of location
questions.rationale: Airport wind sensors are typically located in open terrain and may not capture the localized turbulent effects of urban structures elsewhere in the city.
questions.source: TP 15530 – urban airflow vs official wind reports

questions.question: An RPAS pilot plans an urban BVLOS mission and relies solely on the nearest airport's METAR for wind data. What is the risk, and what mitigation should be applied?
choices: No risk; airport METARs are always fully representative of urban wind conditions
Urban wind effects can differ significantly from the airport reading; mitigation includes consulting urban airflow guidance material and considering on-site wind observation before and during flight
The mission should always be cancelled if any buildings are present
Only wind direction matters in urban areas, not speed
questions.rationale: Relying solely on a distant airport METAR risks missing significant local urban wind effects; consulting urban airflow guidance and on-site observation mitigates this risk.
questions.source: TP 15530 – urban airflow operator guidance material

questions.question: What weather phenomenon is a weather front generally associated with?
choices: A boundary between two air masses with different properties, often bringing changes in weather
A single, unchanging air mass with no boundary
Only clear sky conditions
A permanent, unmoving weather feature
questions.rationale: A front is the boundary between two differing air masses, commonly associated with changing weather conditions as it passes.

questions.question: What weather conditions are commonly associated with the passage of a cold front?
choices: Gradual, gentle change with no notable weather activity
Potentially rapid onset of gusty winds, turbulence, and showers/thunderstorms along the frontal boundary
Only clear, calm conditions
Only fog, never precipitation
questions.rationale: Cold fronts can bring rapid weather changes including gusty winds, turbulence, and showers/thunderstorms as they pass.

questions.question: A forecast shows a cold front expected to pass through the planned RPAS operating area partway through a scheduled multi-hour BVLOS mission. What should the pilot do?
choices: Proceed with the full mission as scheduled regardless of the frontal timing

Plan contingencies for a significant weather change mid-mission (e.g., an earlier recovery time, updated go/no-go criteria, or splitting the mission) to avoid being airborne during the frontal passage
Assume fronts only affect manned aircraft, not RPAS
Cancel the entire mission permanently regardless of front timing accuracy
questions.rationale: A forecast frontal passage during a mission window should prompt contingency planning to avoid being caught in rapidly deteriorating conditions.

questions.question: What is the primary hazard associated with thunderstorms relevant to RPAS operations?
choices: Severe turbulence, strong wind shifts, lightning, and hail, all of which can severely affect small aircraft
Thunderstorms only affect visibility, nothing else
Thunderstorms have no effect on RPAS due to their small size
Thunderstorms only occur at night
questions.rationale: Thunderstorms present severe hazards including turbulence, wind shifts, lightning, and hail, all significant risks to small RPA.

questions.question: How should an RPAS pilot generally respond to signs of developing thunderstorm activity near a planned or ongoing operation?
choices: Continue the mission and only take action once lightning is directly overhead
Terminate or avoid the operation with a wide safety margin, since thunderstorm hazards can extend well beyond the visible storm cell
Thunderstorms are irrelevant unless rain is currently falling
Only avoid thunderstorms if the RPA lacks a rain cover
questions.rationale: Thunderstorm hazards (like outflow winds and lightning risk) can extend beyond the visible storm cell, so a wide safety margin and early avoidance/termination is appropriate.
questions.source: TC AIM / TP 15530 – thunderstorm avoidance practice

questions.question: A distant thunderstorm is visible on the horizon during an ongoing RPAS mission, with no rain yet at the operating site. What action is most appropriate?
choices: Continue the mission unchanged since the storm is still distant
Begin preparing to terminate the mission and recover the aircraft, since thunderstorm-associated gust fronts and hazards can arrive well before visible precipitation reaches the site
Only take action once thunder is heard directly overhead
Increase RPA altitude to fly above the approaching storm
questions.rationale: Thunderstorm hazards like gust fronts can precede visible precipitation by a significant distance and time, so early recovery planning is the safer response.

questions.question: What generally happens to air pressure with increasing altitude?
choices: Air pressure decreases with increasing altitude
Air pressure increases with increasing altitude
Air pressure remains constant at all altitudes
Air pressure only changes with temperature, not altitude
questions.rationale: Atmospheric pressure decreases as altitude increases, a fundamental principle underlying altimetry.
questions.source: TC AIM – atmospheric pressure and altitude

questions.question: Why does the rate of pressure change with altitude vary with temperature?
choices: Temperature has no effect on pressure/altitude relationships
Warmer air is less dense, so pressure decreases more gradually with height in warm air compared to cold, denser air where pressure decreases more rapidly
Pressure change rate is always identical regardless of temperature
Temperature only affects humidity, not pressure
questions.rationale: Air density (affected by temperature) influences how quickly pressure changes with altitude; warmer, less dense air has a more gradual pressure gradient with height.
questions.source: TC AIM – temperature effects on pressure lapse rate

questions.question: On a very cold day, an RPAS pilot uses a standard altimeter setting assumption without adjusting for actual cold-temperature error. What is the risk?
choices: No risk; temperature never affects altimeter accuracy
True altitude may be lower than indicated altitude in cold temperatures, meaning the aircraft could be closer to terrain/obstacles than the altimeter suggests
True altitude is always higher than indicated in cold temperatures
Cold temperature errors only affect aircraft above FL180
questions.rationale: In cold temperatures, true altitude tends to be lower than indicated altitude, creating a risk of reduced actual terrain/obstacle clearance if not accounted for.
questions.source: TC AIM – cold temperature altimetry error

questions.question: What does the term 'ceiling' refer to in aviation weather reporting?
choices: The height of the lowest layer of cloud reported as broken or overcast (or vertical visibility in obscured conditions)
The maximum altitude an aircraft is certified to fly
The highest cloud layer present
A synonym for visibility
questions.rationale: Ceiling is defined as the height of the lowest broken or overcast layer, or vertical visibility in obscured sky conditions.

questions.question: A METAR shows 'FEW015 SCT025 BKN040'. What is the reported ceiling?
choices: 1,500 ft (the FEW layer)
4,000 ft (the BKN layer, since it's the lowest broken/overcast layer)
2,500 ft (the SCT layer)
There is no ceiling reported in this METAR
questions.rationale: Ceiling is defined by the lowest broken or overcast layer; FEW and SCT don't count as ceiling, so the BKN040 layer at 4,000 ft defines the ceiling.

questions.question: An RPAS Level 1 Complex operation requires a defined minimum ceiling of 1,000 ft AGL for the operation to proceed. A METAR shows 'SCT008 BKN012'. Should the flight proceed?
choices: Yes, since the scattered layer at 800 ft doesn't count as a ceiling
No, since the broken layer at 1,200 ft AGL... actually the ceiling (BKN012, 1,200 ft) exceeds the 1,000 ft minimum, so the flight may proceed regarding ceiling, assuming other minimums are also met
No, because any cloud below 1,000 ft automatically cancels the flight regardless of coverage type
The flight cannot be assessed without wind data
questions.rationale: The ceiling is defined by the broken layer at 1,200 ft (BKN012), which exceeds the 1,000 ft AGL minimum; the scattered layer doesn't define ceiling, so this specific requirement is satisfied assuming other minimums are also met.
questions.source: TC AIM / CARs Part IX – ceiling requirement assessment

questions.question: What causes surface-based haze or smoke layers to reduce visibility?
choices: Suspended particulates (dust, smoke, pollutants) scattering/absorbing light near the surface
A sudden drop in air pressure
Excessive humidity alone with no particulates
Only occurs above 10,000 ft ASL
questions.rationale: Haze and smoke consist of suspended particulates that scatter and absorb light, reducing visibility near the surface.

questions.question: How can wildfire smoke specifically impact RPAS visual line-of-sight operations even when official visibility figures seem acceptable?
choices: Smoke never affects visibility figures or visual operations
Smoke density can vary significantly over short distances and time, so localized visibility for the pilot's specific vantage point/altitude may be considerably worse than a nearby official reading
Smoke only affects visibility above 5,000 ft ASL
Official visibility readings always perfectly match on-site smoke conditions
questions.rationale: Smoke conditions can vary significantly by location and time, meaning official readings from a different point may not reflect the pilot's actual local visibility for VLOS purposes.

questions.question: During wildfire season, a pilot notices deteriorating on-site visibility due to smoke that isn't yet reflected in the nearest official weather report. What should the pilot do?
choices: Continue relying solely on the official report since it's the authoritative source
Prioritize direct, current on-site observation over a potentially lagging official report, and terminate/adjust the operation if actual VLOS visibility requirements are no longer met
Wait for the official report to update before taking any action
Assume smoke never actually reduces visibility enough to matter
questions.rationale: Direct on-site observation should take priority when it reveals conditions that a potentially lagging official report hasn't yet captured, especially for VLOS visibility compliance.

questions.question: What is the general relationship between low-level cloud and legacy (manned) aircraft traffic patterns?
choices: Low cloud can force manned aircraft to fly at lower altitudes than usual, potentially closer to RPAS operating levels
Low cloud always causes aircraft to climb higher, away from RPAS
Low cloud has no effect on manned aircraft altitude choices
Low cloud only affects RPAS, never manned aircraft
questions.rationale: Low cloud ceilings can force manned aircraft to operate at lower altitudes to remain clear of cloud, potentially increasing proximity to RPAS operating levels.

questions.question: Why might a low ceiling day actually increase collision risk near an aerodrome despite reduced overall traffic volume?
choices: Low ceiling days always eliminate all manned traffic
Aircraft that do fly may be compressed into a narrower altitude band below the clouds, increasing the concentration of traffic at lower altitudes where RPAS also operate
Low ceilings only affect helicopters
There is no relationship between ceiling and traffic concentration
questions.rationale: A lower ceiling compresses manned traffic into a narrower altitude band, potentially concentrating aircraft closer to typical RPAS operating altitudes.
questions.source: TP 15530 – altitude compression under low ceilings

questions.question: A pilot plans a 300 ft AGL survey mission near an aerodrome on a day with a 600 ft AGL ceiling. What risk factor is most elevated compared to a high-ceiling day?
choices: No elevated risk; all traffic will be grounded on a low ceiling day

Manned traffic that continues operating may be flying lower than usual (closer to the RPAS altitude) to remain clear of cloud, increasing proximity risk despite the RPAS operating below the aerodrome's normal circuit height
Only RPAS icing risk increases, not manned aircraft interaction risk
The ceiling has no bearing on manned aircraft altitude choices
questions.rationale: Continuing manned traffic may need to fly lower than typical circuit altitude to stay clear of a lower ceiling, increasing the risk of proximity to RPAS operating at lower altitudes.

questions.question: What weather service is commonly used to determine local weather where no official reporting station exists?
choices: Direct observation, nearby unofficial sources, and interpolation from surrounding official reports/forecasts
There is no way to determine weather without an official station
Only satellite imagery, with no other methods used
Weather cannot be assessed at all in these locations
questions.rationale: In the absence of an official station, pilots use direct observation combined with nearby official reports/forecasts and other available tools to estimate local conditions.
questions.source: TP 15530 – determining weather without official reporting

questions.question: How can weather trend analysis (e.g., comparing successive METARs over a few hours) help an RPAS pilot?
choices: Trend analysis provides no useful information
It helps identify whether conditions (ceiling, visibility, wind) are improving, stable, or deteriorating, supporting better go/no-go and contingency decisions
Trend analysis is only useful for forecasting temperature
It replaces the need to check a TAF entirely
questions.rationale: Observing trends across successive reports helps assess whether conditions are improving or deteriorating, informing better operational decisions.

questions.question: Over three hours, successive METARs show ceiling dropping from 3,000 ft to 1,500 ft to 900 ft, with the TAF still forecasting VFR conditions for the mission window. How should the pilot weigh this conflicting information?
choices: Trust the TAF exclusively since forecasts are always more authoritative than observed trends
Give significant weight to the clear deteriorating trend in actual observations, since real-time trends can reveal that the forecast is not verifying, and adjust the go/no-go decision accordingly
Ignore both data sources and proceed based on visual assessment alone at the last possible moment
Deteriorating trends in METARs are never relevant if a TAF still shows better conditions
questions.rationale: When observed trends contradict a forecast, it can indicate the forecast is not verifying; prudent risk management gives weight to the real, deteriorating trend rather than blind trust in an outdated forecast.
questions.source: TP 15530 – reconciling forecast vs observed trend conflicts

questions.question: A pilot argues that since the RPA is small and lightweight, general aviation weather minimums (ceiling/visibility) developed for manned aircraft are overly conservative and don't need to be followed as strictly. Why is this reasoning flawed?
choices: It's correct; RPAS are exempt from weather-related risk considerations

RPAS weather minimums are set based on RPAS-specific operational and regulatory requirements, and small size doesn't eliminate risks like reduced situational awareness, control degradation, or conflict with traffic in poor weather
Weather minimums only exist for cosmetic/legal reasons with no real safety basis
Small aircraft are always immune to visibility and ceiling related risks
questions.rationale: RPAS-specific weather minimums reflect real operational risk factors (situational awareness, control, traffic conflict potential) independent of aircraft size, so they shouldn't be dismissed as overly conservative.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – rationale for weather minimums

questions.question: What is the primary role of a visual observer (VO) in an RPAS operation?
choices: To assist the pilot by maintaining visual contact with the RPA and surrounding airspace/environment
To operate the ground control station instead of the pilot
To act as a substitute pilot with full control authority at all times
To handle only post-flight paperwork
questions.rationale: A visual observer supports the pilot's situational awareness by maintaining visual contact with the aircraft and surrounding environment.

questions.question: What does EVLOS stand for?
choices: Extended Visual Line-of-Sight
External Visual Loss of Signal
Extended Vertical Limit Operating Space
Emergency Visual Landing Operating System
questions.rationale: EVLOS (Extended Visual Line-of-Sight) uses visual observers to extend the effective range beyond the pilot's own unaided VLOS.

questions.question: How does an EVLOS operation typically extend the pilot's effective range?
choices: By using one or more trained visual observers positioned to maintain continuous visual contact with the RPA beyond the pilot's own direct line of sight
By allowing the pilot to fly using only camera feed with no visual observers
By removing all visual contact requirements entirely
By requiring the RPA to fly higher than 400 ft AGL
questions.rationale: EVLOS relies on positioned visual observers maintaining continuous visual contact, effectively extending the coverage beyond the pilot's own direct sightline.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – EVLOS operational concept

questions.question: An EVLOS operation uses two visual observers positioned along the flight path. A gap in coverage exists between their fields of view. What must the pilot/operator do?
choices: Ignore the gap since some coverage exists
Redesign the observer placement or flight path to eliminate the coverage gap, since EVLOS requires continuous visual contact with the aircraft throughout the operation
Only worry about the gap if an incident occurs
Assume radio communication alone is sufficient to cover any visual gap
questions.rationale: EVLOS requires continuous visual contact; a coverage gap represents a period without required visual awareness and must be eliminated through redesign.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – EVLOS coverage requirements

questions.question: What key communication capability must a visual observer typically have with the pilot?
choices: Reliable, real-time two-way communication
No communication is required as long as the VO can see the RPA
Only written communication after the flight
Communication is only required if the VO is more than 5 km from the pilot
