questions.question: What is a typical aircraft behaviour following a propulsion system failure on a fixed-wing RPA?
choices: The aircraft continues climbing indefinitely with no change in behaviour
The aircraft will typically begin to lose altitude/glide, requiring the pilot to manage the resulting descent and select a safe landing area per contingency procedures
The aircraft automatically converts to a different aircraft type
Propulsion failure has no effect on fixed-wing aircraft behaviour
questions.rationale: A fixed-wing aircraft experiencing propulsion failure will generally begin descending/gliding, requiring the pilot to manage the descent and select a safe landing area.

questions.question: A fixed-wing RPA experiences a propulsion failure over a populated area where the pre-planned emergency landing sites are now unusable due to a recent event (e.g., a temporary event/crowd). What must the contingency plan account for?
choices: Nothing; the original plan should always be followed exactly as written regardless of new conditions

The plan should be dynamic enough to allow the pilot to select the best available option in real time, and site surveys should be updated when known changes affect previously identified emergency landing areas
Propulsion failure contingency planning is unnecessary if the aircraft has ever flown successfully before
The RPA should always be flown until battery/fuel exhaustion regardless of terrain below
questions.rationale: Contingency plans should allow for real-time adaptation when previously identified options become unusable, and site surveys should be updated to reflect known changes affecting planned emergency areas.

questions.question: What generally distinguishes 'payload' from the rest of an RPAS?
choices: Payload refers to equipment carried for a mission purpose (e.g., camera, sensor) distinct from the core systems needed to fly the aircraft
Payload refers to the aircraft's motors and propellers
Payload is a synonym for the aircraft's battery
Payload only refers to passengers, which RPAS never carry
questions.rationale: Payload refers to mission-specific equipment (like sensors or cameras) distinct from the aircraft's core flight systems.

questions.question: How can an integrated payload affect an RPA's performance compared to a lighter or no-payload configuration?
choices: Payloads never affect performance regardless of weight or integration
Integrated payloads can affect weight, center of gravity, aerodynamics, and power/fuel consumption, all of which should be accounted for in performance planning
Only external payloads affect performance; integrated payloads never do
Payload weight only matters for ground handling, not in-flight performance
questions.rationale: Integrated payloads can affect weight, balance, aerodynamics, and power consumption, all relevant to performance planning.

questions.question: An operator wants to swap payloads mid-mission at a remote site without manufacturer guidance on the specific combination being used. What must be verified first?
choices: No verification is needed since all payloads are universally interchangeable

That the specific payload swap is within manufacturer-approved configurations (or otherwise properly assessed for weight/balance/performance impact) before resuming flight, since operating outside approved configurations creates real risk
Only the payload's own weight matters, regardless of manufacturer guidance
Payload swaps never require any reassessment of aircraft performance
questions.rationale: Operating with an unapproved or unassessed payload configuration risks unknown weight/balance/performance issues; verification against manufacturer guidance (or proper assessment) is required before flight.

questions.question: An operator argues that since their RPA passed all pre-flight checks and has multiple redundant systems, a total loss-of-control incident is 'basically impossible.' Why is this reasoning flawed from a systems safety perspective?
choices: It is correct; redundancy and pre-flight checks together eliminate all possible failure modes

Redundancy reduces but does not eliminate risk; shared failure points, latent defects, cascading failures, and environmental/human factors can still combine to defeat redundancy, so absolute claims of impossibility are unwarranted
Pre-flight checks alone are always sufficient regardless of system design
Total loss-of-control incidents are impossible for any properly registered aircraft
questions.rationale: Redundancy and pre-flight checks meaningfully reduce risk but don't eliminate it; shared failure points, latent defects, and combined human/environmental factors can still defeat safeguards, so absolute safety claims are unwarranted.
questions.source: TP 15530 – systems safety and residual risk

questions.question: What is the primary source of maintenance instructions a pilot/operator should follow for an RPA?
choices: The manufacturer's maintenance instructions/manual
General internet forums
The pilot's personal preference regardless of manufacturer guidance
No maintenance instructions exist for RPAS
questions.rationale: Manufacturer instructions are the primary authoritative source for maintenance requirements on a given RPA.

questions.question: When might independent verification of maintenance work be required, per manufacturer instructions?
choices: Never; self-verification by the same person is always sufficient regardless of task
When the manufacturer's instructions specifically call for independent verification of certain critical maintenance tasks, to reduce the risk of an undetected error
Only if the maintenance was performed by a certified aircraft maintenance engineer for manned aircraft
Independent verification is only relevant for maintenance costing over a specific dollar amount
questions.rationale: Manufacturer instructions may specifically require independent verification for certain critical tasks, reducing the risk of an undetected single-person error.

questions.question: A technician performs a critical control-surface maintenance task that the manufacturer's manual specifies requires independent verification, but skips this step due to time pressure. What is the risk?
choices: No risk; independent verification is merely a suggestion with no real safety value
An undetected installation/assembly error (e.g., incorrect torque, reversed connection) could go unnoticed without a second qualified check, potentially leading to an in-flight failure
Skipping this step always improves overall efficiency with no downside
Independent verification is only relevant for engine work, never control surfaces
questions.rationale: Independent verification exists specifically to catch errors a single person might miss; skipping it for a critical task increases the risk of an undetected defect causing an in-flight failure.
questions.source: TP 15530 – risk of skipping independent verification

questions.question: What is a basic purpose of maintaining RPAS maintenance records?
choices: To document work performed, supporting airworthiness tracking and regulatory compliance
Only to satisfy the pilot's personal curiosity
Maintenance records serve no practical purpose
To replace the need for pre-flight inspections
questions.rationale: Maintenance records document work performed, supporting ongoing airworthiness tracking and regulatory compliance.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – maintenance recordkeeping

questions.question: Why is it important to record the specific parts/components replaced during RPAS maintenance, not just that 'maintenance was performed'?
choices: Detailed records support traceability (e.g., identifying if a specific part/batch is later found to be defective) and more accurate airworthiness assessment going forward
Detailed part records serve no practical safety purpose
Only the date of maintenance matters, never the specific work performed
Detailed records are only useful for warranty claims, not safety
questions.rationale: Detailed maintenance records support traceability and more accurate ongoing airworthiness assessment, which is valuable if defects are later identified.

questions.question: A manufacturer issues a recall/service bulletin for a specific motor batch. An operator's maintenance records only note 'motor replaced' without batch/serial details. What problem does this create?
choices: No problem; the recall doesn't require any records at all
The operator cannot easily determine whether their aircraft's replaced motor is part of the affected batch, potentially missing a critical safety recall action
Recalls never apply to RPAS components
This level of detail is never necessary regardless of circumstances
questions.rationale: Without specific batch/serial information in records, an operator cannot easily determine if their aircraft is affected by a targeted recall, risking a missed critical safety action.
questions.source: TP 15530 – recordkeeping detail for recall traceability

questions.question: What should a pilot do if a pre-flight inspection reveals something 'out of order' with the RPA?
choices: Assess whether the finding affects airworthiness, and not fly if there is doubt about safety
Always fly regardless of findings if the mission is important
Only address findings after the flight is complete
Ignore minor findings without any assessment
questions.rationale: Pilots must assess pre-flight findings for airworthiness impact and should not fly if there's genuine doubt about safety.

questions.question: A pre-flight inspection reveals a small crack in a propeller blade that the pilot judges to be 'probably fine.' What is the appropriate course of action?
choices: Fly as planned since the crack is small

Treat any crack in a critical rotating component like a propeller as a potential airworthiness concern and replace/inspect it properly before flight, rather than relying on a subjective 'probably fine' judgment
Only replace the propeller if it fails completely during the flight
Cracks in propellers are never a safety concern for small RPAS
questions.rationale: Cracks in critical rotating components like propellers pose a real failure risk and should be properly assessed/addressed rather than dismissed based on a subjective judgment.

questions.question: An operator's fleet-wide trend review shows repeated minor propeller damage across multiple aircraft, always after transport in a specific type of case. What should this trigger?
choices: No action; minor propeller damage is always just normal wear with no underlying cause

An investigation into the transport case design/procedure as a potential root cause, potentially leading to a corrective action (e.g., improved packing procedure or case redesign) under the operator's safety management process
Immediate replacement of all propellers with no further investigation into the cause
Ignoring the pattern since each individual incident was minor
questions.rationale: A recurring pattern across multiple aircraft tied to a specific cause (transport case) should trigger investigation and corrective action under a proper safety management process.
questions.source: AC 107-002 / SMS – trend analysis and corrective action
questions.knowledgeArea: RPA airframes, power plants, propulsion and systems

questions.question: What does 'airworthy' generally mean for an RPA?
choices: The aircraft is in a condition safe for the intended flight, consistent with its design/manufacturer specifications
The aircraft has a current insurance policy
The pilot holds a valid certificate, regardless of the aircraft's condition
The aircraft has never had any maintenance performed
questions.rationale: Airworthiness refers to the aircraft's condition being safe for the intended flight, consistent with its design specifications.

questions.question: Why does an aircraft's airworthiness need to be assessed before each flight, rather than relying solely on its condition at time of purchase?
choices: Airworthiness never changes after purchase
Wear, damage, and component degradation can accumulate over time and use, meaning a previously airworthy aircraft may no longer be airworthy without ongoing inspection/maintenance
Only the manufacturer needs to worry about ongoing airworthiness, not the operator/pilot
Pre-flight assessment is only a formality with no real safety value
questions.rationale: Wear and degradation accumulate over time, meaning airworthiness must be continually reassessed rather than assumed based on original condition.

questions.question: An RPA has accumulated flight hours well beyond the manufacturer's suggested inspection interval for a critical component, but has never shown any visible defects. What is the appropriate approach?
choices: Continue flying indefinitely since no visible defects have appeared
Follow the manufacturer's inspection schedule regardless of visible symptoms, since some failure modes (e.g., fatigue, internal wear) may not be visually apparent until they cause a failure
Assume the manufacturer's schedule is overly conservative and can be safely ignored
Only perform the inspection if a customer specifically requests it
questions.rationale: Manufacturer inspection intervals often account for failure modes not visually apparent (like fatigue), so schedules should be followed regardless of the absence of visible symptoms.

questions.question: What environmental factor is commonly highlighted as a risk to electrical components in RPAS?
choices: Moisture, temperature extremes, and other conditions outside manufacturer specifications
Only extremely high altitude flight above FL600
The color of the aircraft's exterior
Only radio frequency interference, never moisture or temperature
questions.rationale: Moisture and temperature extremes outside manufacturer specifications are commonly cited risks to electrical components.

questions.question: What does an RPAS 'waterproof rating' (e.g., an IP rating) typically indicate, and what is an important limitation to understand?
choices: It indicates a specific level of protection against dust/water ingress under defined test conditions, but real-world conditions (e.g., prolonged exposure, high-pressure water) may exceed what the rating was tested for
It means the aircraft can be fully submerged indefinitely with no risk
Waterproof ratings apply universally regardless of test conditions or duration
IP ratings have no relevance to RPAS operations
questions.rationale: IP/waterproof ratings indicate protection under specific tested conditions; real-world exposure exceeding those conditions (duration, pressure) may exceed the rating's actual protection.

questions.question: An RPA has an IP43 rating (limited splash protection), but an operator plans to fly it in sustained moderate rain for an extended period. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: IP43 provides full protection against any rain condition regardless of duration or intensity

IP43's limited splash protection likely does not cover sustained moderate rain exposure, so the planned operation exceeds the aircraft's tested water protection capability and creates real risk of water ingress/damage
IP ratings are irrelevant to RPAS since they were designed for consumer electronics only
The mission should proceed since any IP rating above zero guarantees full weather protection
questions.rationale: A limited splash-protection rating like IP43 likely does not cover sustained moderate rain exposure, meaning the planned operation would exceed the aircraft's tested protection and risk water damage.
questions.source: TP 15530 – interpreting specific IP rating limitations

questions.question: How can a pilot determine battery consumption during flight?
choices: By monitoring telemetry data (e.g., voltage, current draw, remaining capacity estimates) provided by the aircraft/ground control station
By guessing based on flight duration alone with no telemetry
Battery consumption cannot be monitored during flight
Only by checking the battery after landing
questions.rationale: Telemetry data such as voltage, current draw, and remaining capacity estimates allow pilots to monitor battery consumption during flight.

questions.question: Why should a pilot plan for a battery reserve beyond the estimated minimum needed to complete a mission?
choices: A reserve accounts for unexpected conditions (e.g., headwinds, contingency maneuvers) that could increase actual power consumption beyond the nominal estimate
Reserves are unnecessary since battery consumption estimates are always perfectly accurate
Reserves are only relevant for fuel-powered RPA, never battery-powered
Reserve planning only matters for missions longer than one hour
questions.rationale: A battery reserve provides margin for unexpected conditions that increase actual consumption beyond the nominal estimate, protecting against running out of power.

questions.question: A mission plan calculates just enough battery for the nominal flight plus a fixed 10% reserve, without considering that a stronger-than-forecast headwind on the return leg could significantly increase consumption. What is the risk?
choices: No risk; a fixed percentage reserve always covers any wind condition

The fixed reserve may be inadequate if actual conditions (like a stronger headwind) increase power consumption beyond what the reserve was sized for, risking a power-related emergency before completing the flight
Wind conditions never affect battery consumption in any way
This scenario only matters for fixed-wing aircraft, never multirotor
questions.rationale: A fixed reserve percentage may not adequately cover larger-than-expected consumption increases from conditions like stronger headwinds, risking a power-related emergency.
questions.source: TP 15530 – dynamic reserve planning under variable conditions

questions.question: What is a general hazard associated with fuel systems on larger fuel-powered RPAS?
choices: Fire/explosion risk from fuel leaks, improper storage, or grounding/bonding failures
Fuel systems present no meaningful hazards on any RPAS
Only battery-powered RPAS have any relevant hazards
Fuel hazards only exist during flight, never during ground handling
questions.rationale: Fuel systems carry fire/explosion risks from leaks, improper storage, or grounding/bonding failures, relevant during both ground handling and flight.

questions.question: Why is proper grounding/bonding technique important during fuel handling for RPAS?
choices: It reduces the risk of static electricity discharge igniting fuel vapors during handling/transfer
Grounding/bonding has no safety purpose during fuel handling
It only matters for large aircraft, never small RPAS
Grounding/bonding is only relevant to electrical system maintenance, not fuel handling
questions.rationale: Proper grounding/bonding reduces static discharge risk, which could otherwise ignite flammable fuel vapors during handling or transfer.

questions.question: A ground crew refuels a fuel-powered RPA without following proper grounding/bonding procedures, in dry, low-humidity conditions. What elevated risk does this create?
choices: No elevated risk; grounding/bonding is only a formality with no real safety benefit
Dry, low-humidity conditions increase the likelihood of static charge buildup, and without proper grounding/bonding, this raises the risk of a static discharge igniting fuel vapors during refueling
This scenario only matters in high-humidity conditions, not dry conditions
Refueling procedures are never relevant to RPAS since they use less fuel than manned aircraft
questions.rationale: Dry, low-humidity conditions increase static buildup risk, and skipping grounding/bonding procedures raises the risk of a static discharge igniting fuel vapors during refueling.
questions.source: TP 15530 – static discharge risk in dry conditions

questions.question: What is the general purpose of an autopilot's automated flight management system on an RPA?
choices: To assist with navigation, stabilization, and executing pre-programmed flight plans or responses
To replace the need for any pilot certification
To handle only payload camera operation
To manage RPAS registration paperwork
questions.rationale: Automated flight management systems assist with navigation, stabilization, and execution of programmed flight plans/responses.

questions.question: What precaution should a pilot take when programming an automated flight management system for a new mission?
choices: Carefully verify waypoints, altitudes, and parameters before launch, since programming errors can directly translate into unsafe flight behaviour
No verification is needed since autopilots always self-correct programming errors
Only verify programming after the flight has already begun
Programming precautions only matter for missions longer than 30 minutes
questions.rationale: Careful pre-launch verification of programmed parameters is essential, since errors can directly translate into unsafe flight behaviour once executed.

questions.question: A pilot copies a previous mission's flight plan for reuse at a new site without re-verifying waypoint altitudes against the new site's terrain/obstacles. What risk does this create?
choices: No risk; flight plans are always safe to reuse at any location without modification
Waypoint altitudes appropriate for the original site's terrain/obstacles may be unsafe at the new site if not re-verified, potentially resulting in a controlled flight into terrain or obstacle strike
This risk only applies to fixed-wing aircraft, never multirotor
Reused flight plans automatically adjust themselves to new terrain
questions.rationale: Reusing a flight plan without re-verifying waypoint altitudes against new terrain/obstacles risks a mismatch that could result in a terrain or obstacle strike.

questions.question: What is the purpose of identifying 'danger areas' associated with launch and recovery operations?
choices: To recognize zones of elevated risk (e.g., propeller arcs, catapult paths) where personnel/bystanders should not be positioned during launch/recovery
To mark areas exclusively reserved for RPAS storage
To identify areas requiring special insurance coverage only
Danger areas are irrelevant to launch and recovery operations
questions.rationale: Danger areas identify zones of elevated risk during launch/recovery (e.g., propeller arcs, catapult paths) where personnel should not be positioned.

questions.question: Why might a mobile launch platform introduce additional risk considerations compared to a fixed launch site?
choices: Mobile platforms never introduce any additional risk considerations
Movement of the platform itself, its stability, and coordination with personnel around a moving system introduce additional hazards not present at a fixed site
Mobile platforms are always inherently safer than fixed sites
Mobile launch platforms are prohibited under all circumstances
questions.rationale: A mobile launch platform introduces additional hazards related to its own movement/stability and coordination with personnel, not present at a fixed site.

questions.question: During a catapult-launched fixed-wing RPA operation, a bystander unexpectedly enters the danger area moments before a scheduled launch. What is the critical priority action?
choices: Proceed with the launch as scheduled since stopping mid-sequence is disruptive
Immediately abort/hold the launch sequence until the bystander is clear of the danger area, prioritizing personnel safety over mission timing
Only abort if the bystander is directly in the flight path, not just the danger area
Continue the countdown and warn the bystander verbally without stopping the sequence
questions.rationale: Personnel safety takes priority; the launch sequence should be immediately halted until the bystander is clear of the danger area.

questions.question: What does 'weight and balance' assessment generally verify for an RPA?
choices: That the aircraft's weight and center of gravity are within manufacturer-approved limits for safe flight
Only the aircraft's total weight, never its center of gravity
Only the pilot's own body weight
Weight and balance has no relevance to RPAS since they are remotely piloted
questions.rationale: Weight and balance assessment confirms both total weight and center of gravity are within manufacturer-approved limits for safe flight.

questions.question: What is the 'circular envelope' concept referenced for multirotor vertical-lift weight and balance?
choices: A tolerable range/zone for center of gravity deviation, generally described as a circular area around the aircraft's designed center point for multirotor configurations
A term describing the flight envelope's speed limits
A synonym for the aircraft's total flight envelope regardless of weight distribution
A regulatory requirement unrelated to weight and balance
questions.rationale: The circular envelope concept describes a tolerable zone of center-of-gravity deviation around a multirotor's designed center point.

questions.question: An operator adds an asymmetric payload mount to a multirotor without recalculating center of gravity, assuming 'multirotors are always stable regardless of loading.' What is the flaw in this assumption?
choices: There is no flaw; multirotors are immune to center of gravity effects by design
Even multirotor aircraft have tolerable center of gravity deviation limits (the circular envelope); an asymmetric payload could exceed this tolerance, degrading stability or control authority
Center of gravity only matters for fixed-wing aircraft, never multirotor
Payload mounts never affect an aircraft's center of gravity
questions.rationale: Multirotor aircraft still have a tolerable center-of-gravity deviation limit; an asymmetric payload could exceed that tolerance and degrade stability or control authority.

questions.question: What are 'OEM recommendations' generally referring to?
choices: Guidance and limitations provided by the Original Equipment Manufacturer for safe use/maintenance of their product
A term for recommendations made by regulatory bodies exclusively
Recommendations made by other RPAS operators, unrelated to the manufacturer
A synonym for aftermarket modification guides
questions.rationale: OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) recommendations refer to the manufacturer's own guidance and limitations for safe use/maintenance.

questions.question: What must an operator consider when making changes to an RPA beyond OEM recommendations?
choices: That such changes could affect airworthiness, declaration validity, or warranty, and should be carefully assessed/documented before being implemented
OEM recommendations are purely optional suggestions with no practical significance
Any change is automatically safe as long as the aircraft still flies afterward
Only cost should be considered when deviating from OEM recommendations
questions.rationale: Deviating from OEM recommendations can affect airworthiness, declaration validity, or warranty, and should be carefully assessed and documented.
questions.source: TP 15530 – operator changes vs OEM recommendations

questions.question: An operator installs an aftermarket component not listed in the manufacturer's approved parts list, reasoning that it is 'functionally equivalent.' What is the key risk in this reasoning?
choices: No risk exists since 'functionally equivalent' components are always identical in every relevant respect to OEM parts

Unapproved components may differ in ways not immediately apparent (tolerances, material properties, failure modes), and using them outside OEM approval could invalidate declarations and introduce unassessed risk
Aftermarket components are always superior to OEM parts
This reasoning is always valid as long as the component looks similar
questions.rationale: Unapproved 'equivalent' components may differ in ways not immediately obvious, introducing unassessed risk and potentially invalidating declarations tied to OEM-approved configurations.
questions.source: TP 15530 – risk of unapproved component substitution

questions.question: What does 'aircraft critical surface contamination' generally refer to?
choices: Contaminants (e.g., ice, frost, dirt, moisture) on aerodynamically critical surfaces that can degrade performance or safety
A term for contamination of the ground control station's software only
Contamination of the pilot's personal protective equipment
A regulatory classification unrelated to aircraft surfaces
questions.rationale: Critical surface contamination refers to contaminants on aerodynamically important surfaces that can degrade performance or safety.

questions.question: How might frost on a fixed-wing RPA's wing surface affect flight, even in small amounts?
choices: Frost has no aerodynamic effect regardless of amount
Even light frost can disrupt smooth airflow over the wing, reducing lift and potentially degrading stall margins
Frost only affects the aircraft's paint appearance, not performance
Frost improves aerodynamic performance by smoothing the surface
questions.rationale: Even light frost can disrupt smooth airflow over a wing, reducing lift and degrading stall margins, similar to well-known effects on manned aircraft.

questions.question: A pilot notices light frost on a fixed-wing RPA's wings before a scheduled morning flight and considers flying anyway since 'it's such a small amount.' What is the correct response?
choices: Proceed with the flight since small amounts of frost are always negligible

Remove all frost/contamination from critical surfaces before flight, since even small amounts can meaningfully disrupt airflow and reduce safety margins, consistent with established aviation practice for contamination
Frost only matters for aircraft heavier than 25 kg
Frost concerns only apply to rotary-wing RPAS, never fixed-wing
questions.rationale: Established aviation practice treats even small amounts of surface contamination like frost as a safety concern requiring removal before flight, given its disproportionate effect on airflow.

questions.question: What should be done if an RPA's user manual and a third-party maintenance guide conflict on a specific procedure?
choices: Follow the manufacturer's official instructions as the authoritative source
Always follow the third-party guide since it may be more detailed
Follow whichever source is more convenient at the time
Ignore both sources and improvise
questions.rationale: Manufacturer instructions are the authoritative source and should be followed when conflicts arise with third-party guidance.

questions.question: Why should maintenance actions performed be recorded even for a hobbyist-level RPAS not used commercially?
choices: Recordkeeping has no value for any non-commercial operation
Good recordkeeping habits support tracking component life, identifying recurring issues, and maintaining an accurate airworthiness picture over time, regardless of whether the use is commercial
Only commercial operators are ever expected to maintain any records
Records are only useful if requested by a customer
questions.rationale: Good recordkeeping supports tracking component life and identifying recurring issues, providing safety value regardless of commercial status.

questions.question: An operator's maintenance log shows a component was 'replaced' three times in six months without ever investigating why it kept failing. What does this indicate from an SMS perspective?
choices: This is normal and requires no further investigation as long as replacement parts are available
A repeated failure pattern like this should trigger a root-cause investigation rather than simply continuing to replace the symptom, since an underlying systemic issue may remain unaddressed
This pattern only matters if the aircraft is grounded permanently
Recordkeeping alone (without investigation) is always sufficient to satisfy safety management obligations
questions.rationale: A recurring failure without root-cause investigation suggests an unaddressed systemic issue, which a proper safety management approach should identify and resolve.
questions.source: AC 107-002 / SMS – root cause analysis for recurring failures
questions.knowledgeArea: RPA airframes, power plants, propulsion and systems

questions.question: What is the purpose of a manufacturer's suggested component life/replacement interval?
choices: To provide a data-informed guideline for replacing components before they are likely to fail due to wear/fatigue
To generate additional revenue for the manufacturer with no safety basis
To indicate the minimum time a component must remain installed regardless of condition
Component life intervals are arbitrary and can be safely ignored
questions.rationale: Suggested replacement intervals are generally based on data about wear/fatigue characteristics, aiming to replace components before likely failure.

questions.question: What is a 'contingency procedure' in RPAS operations?
choices: A pre-planned response to an abnormal but manageable situation, intended to keep the aircraft within a safe area while the issue is addressed
A procedure used only after an accident has already occurred
A synonym for a standard normal-operations checklist
A procedure that only applies to fixed-wing aircraft
questions.rationale: Contingency procedures address abnormal but manageable situations, aiming to keep the aircraft safely contained while the issue is resolved.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – contingency procedures

questions.question: What is 'flight termination' generally intended to achieve?
choices: A deliberate, controlled ending of flight (e.g., forced descent/landing) used as a last resort to prevent a greater hazard
A routine end-of-mission landing under normal conditions
A procedure used only for battery charging
A term unrelated to safety procedures
questions.rationale: Flight termination is a deliberate, controlled action used as a last resort to prevent a greater hazard when other contingencies aren't sufficient.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – flight termination

questions.question: How should a 'flight termination route/point' be selected during mission planning?
choices: Randomly, with no specific planning required
By identifying locations where a forced termination would minimize risk to people/property, ideally away from populated areas, roads, and other aircraft
Always at the exact center of the planned flight geography, regardless of terrain below
Flight termination points are unnecessary if the aircraft has a parachute
questions.rationale: Flight termination points/routes should be planned to minimize risk to people and property, considering terrain and surrounding hazards.

questions.question: During a BVLOS mission, a pilot must choose between continuing toward a marginal lost-link RTH point over a small crowd, or triggering flight termination over an open field with no people. What is the safer decision-making principle?
choices: Always prioritize aircraft recovery over any other consideration
Prioritize the option that minimizes risk to people, even if it means intentionally sacrificing the aircraft via flight termination over the safer open area
Choose whichever option preserves the most video footage
Flight termination should never be used regardless of the situation
questions.rationale: Safety-first decision-making prioritizes minimizing risk to people, even at the cost of the aircraft, consistent with the purpose of flight termination as a last-resort safety action.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TP 15530 – termination decision priority

questions.question: What is the recommended pilot response upon losing GPS signal during flight, assuming the RPA has a manual control mode?
choices: Assess the situation and be prepared to switch to manual/alternate control mode if GPS-dependent modes are no longer reliable
Immediately shut off all power to the aircraft
Ignore the loss since GPS is never actually needed for flight
Always land immediately regardless of aircraft behaviour or altitude
questions.rationale: Losing GPS may require switching to a manual/alternate control mode if GPS-dependent automated modes become unreliable, based on the specific situation.

questions.question: A pilot loses GPS signal during a BVLOS mission with no direct visual contact with the aircraft. What is a critical challenge this creates?
choices: No challenge; BVLOS missions never rely on GPS
Without GPS and without direct visual contact, the pilot may have very limited means to determine the aircraft's actual position, complicating both normal recovery and any needed contingency actions
GPS loss only affects camera footage, not aircraft control
This situation is automatically resolved by the aircraft's autopilot with no pilot action needed
questions.rationale: Combined GPS and visual contact loss during BVLOS severely limits the pilot's ability to determine aircraft position, complicating recovery and contingency response.

questions.question: A BVLOS operation's risk assessment did not specifically address a combined GPS-loss-and-lost-link scenario, treating each as independent risks with separate mitigations. Why is this a gap?
choices: It is not a gap; independent risks never need to be considered in combination

Combined/compounding failures can create a worse scenario than either failure alone, and a thorough risk assessment should specifically consider how mitigations perform when multiple systems fail together
GPS loss and lost link can never occur simultaneously in any real scenario
This combination is irrelevant since flight termination will always resolve it automatically
questions.rationale: Compounding failures can create scenarios worse than any single failure alone; thorough risk assessment should consider how mitigations hold up when multiple systems fail together.

questions.question: What is the recommended immediate pilot priority if a mid-air control anomaly (e.g., unexpected pitch/roll) is detected?
choices: Regaining and maintaining safe control of the aircraft as the top priority, before addressing secondary tasks
Immediately posting about the issue on social media
Ignoring the anomaly if it seems minor at first glance
Prioritizing continued data collection over aircraft control
questions.rationale: Regaining and maintaining safe aircraft control is the top priority when a control anomaly is detected, before addressing any secondary task.

questions.question: Why is it valuable for a pilot to have pre-briefed, memorized immediate actions for common abnormal situations (e.g., lost link, low battery warning)?
choices: Pre-briefed actions are unnecessary since pilots should always improvise in the moment
Having memorized immediate actions reduces response time and decision load during a high-stress abnormal event, improving the likelihood of an effective response
Memorized actions are only useful for written exams, not real operations
Pre-briefed actions eliminate all need for situational judgment
questions.rationale: Memorized immediate actions reduce response time and decision load during high-stress events, improving the likelihood of an effective, timely response.

questions.question: A pilot follows a memorized immediate action for a low-battery warning, but the situation involves an additional complicating factor (nearby people) not covered in the memorized procedure. What should the pilot do?
choices: Only ever follow the memorized procedure exactly as written, regardless of any additional factors present

Use the memorized procedure as a starting point while applying situational judgment to adapt the response given the additional complicating factor (e.g., choosing a termination/landing option that also avoids the nearby people)
Ignore the complicating factor entirely since it wasn't part of the original training
Abandon all procedures and improvise entirely from scratch
questions.rationale: Memorized procedures provide a starting framework, but situational judgment should adapt the response to address additional complicating factors not covered by the standard procedure.
questions.source: TP 15530 – adapting procedures to actual conditions

questions.question: What should a pilot do immediately after a reportable RPAS accident/incident, regarding the aircraft/data?
choices: Preserve relevant evidence/records (e.g., logs, wreckage, telemetry) to support investigation and reporting requirements
Immediately delete all flight logs to simplify things
Modify or repair the aircraft immediately before any review
No preservation of evidence is ever required
questions.rationale: Preserving relevant evidence and records supports accurate investigation and fulfillment of reporting requirements after an incident.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – post-incident evidence preservation

questions.question: Why is prompt, accurate post-incident reporting valuable beyond just regulatory compliance?
choices: It has no value beyond simply satisfying a legal requirement
It supports broader aviation safety by allowing lessons learned to inform future risk mitigation, both within the operator's own organization and potentially industry-wide
Reporting only serves to assign blame to individuals
Reporting is only useful if the incident involved a fatality
questions.rationale: Prompt, accurate reporting supports broader safety learning, helping identify and mitigate risks both organizationally and industry-wide.
questions.source: AC 107-002 / SMS – value of incident reporting

questions.question: After a minor incident with no injuries or significant damage, an operator considers not reporting it since 'nothing serious happened.' What is the flaw in this reasoning from a safety management perspective?
choices: There is no flaw; only serious incidents with injuries need ever be reported or reviewed
Minor incidents can reveal underlying systemic issues or near-miss patterns that, if left unreported and unreviewed, could later contribute to a more serious event
Reporting minor incidents always creates unnecessary legal liability with no safety benefit
Only incidents witnessed by Transport Canada inspectors need to be reported
questions.rationale: Minor incidents/near-misses can reveal systemic issues that, if unaddressed, may contribute to a future, more serious event; proper reporting/review helps catch these patterns early.

questions.question: What is the general purpose of practicing abnormal/emergency procedures during training, rather than only reading about them?
choices: Hands-on practice builds muscle memory and familiarity, improving real-world response speed and effectiveness under stress
Practicing procedures has no benefit over simply reading about them
Practice is only useful for procedures that will never actually be needed
Practicing abnormal procedures is prohibited by regulation
questions.rationale: Hands-on practice builds familiarity and muscle memory, improving real-world response effectiveness under the stress of an actual abnormal event.
questions.source: TP 15530 – value of practicing abnormal procedures

questions.question: Why might a pilot's response to a rare, high-stress emergency differ from their performance during a calm training simulation of the same scenario?
choices: Performance is always identical regardless of stress level

Real emergencies introduce physiological/psychological stress responses (e.g., tunnel vision, elevated heart rate) that can degrade performance compared to a calm training environment, making realistic stress-inoculation training valuable
Training simulations are always harder than real emergencies
Stress has no measurable effect on human performance in aviation contexts
questions.rationale: Real emergencies can trigger stress responses that degrade performance compared to calm training; realistic stress-inoculation training helps prepare for this gap.

questions.question: An operator's emergency training consists solely of reading the procedures manual with no simulated practice. What gap does this create, and how should it be addressed?
choices: No gap exists; reading alone is always fully equivalent to practiced training

Reading alone doesn't build the muscle memory/stress resilience that practiced scenarios provide; the operator should incorporate realistic simulated practice (e.g., tabletop or simulator exercises) into training
This gap can only be addressed by experiencing a real emergency
Emergency training gaps are irrelevant as long as procedures are documented
questions.rationale: Reading alone doesn't build the practical response capability that simulated practice provides; incorporating realistic exercises addresses this training gap.

questions.question: What should a crew do if a fire is detected in the ground control station or associated equipment?
choices: Follow established fire safety procedures (e.g., power isolation, appropriate extinguishing method, evacuation if needed) rather than improvising
Ignore small fires since they always self-extinguish
Always use water on any type of fire regardless of source
Continue operating the equipment normally despite the fire
questions.rationale: Established fire safety procedures (appropriate to the specific hazard, e.g., electrical/battery fire) should be followed rather than improvised responses.

questions.question: Why is water generally inappropriate for a lithium battery fire?
choices: Water reacts poorly with certain battery chemistries and doesn't effectively address the self-sustaining thermal runaway reaction; specific extinguishing agents/procedures are recommended instead
Water is always the single best method for any fire type
Lithium battery fires are impossible, so this scenario is moot
Water has no interaction with any type of battery fire
questions.rationale: Lithium battery fires involve a self-sustaining thermal runaway reaction that water doesn't effectively address and may interact poorly with; appropriate specific agents/procedures are recommended.

questions.question: A damaged LiPo battery begins swelling and emitting smoke after a hard landing. What is the safest immediate crew response?
choices: Immediately pick up the battery with bare hands to move it indoors quickly

Move to a safe distance, avoid direct contact, and follow established procedures for a suspected thermal runaway event (e.g., isolating the area, using appropriate fire response resources, and monitoring from a safe distance)
Continue mission operations while ignoring the smoking battery
Immediately submerge the entire aircraft and battery in a large quantity of gasoline
questions.rationale: A swelling, smoking battery indicates likely thermal runaway; the safest response is maintaining distance, avoiding direct contact, and following the established emergency response procedure.

questions.question: What is the purpose of identifying alternate landing sites during flight planning?
choices: To have pre-assessed safe options available if the primary landing/recovery site becomes unusable during the mission
Alternate sites are never useful since the primary site should always be used
To increase the total flight distance unnecessarily
Only relevant for manned aircraft, never RPAS
questions.rationale: Pre-identifying alternate landing sites ensures safe options are available if the primary site becomes unusable during the mission.

questions.question: Why should alternate landing sites be identified before flight, rather than selected reactively during an emergency?
choices: Reactive selection during an actual emergency, under time pressure and stress, is less reliable than a pre-assessed option chosen calmly during planning
There is no difference between reactive and pre-planned site selection
Alternate sites are only useful for BVLOS operations, never VLOS
Pre-identifying sites is prohibited by regulation
questions.rationale: Selecting a site reactively under emergency time pressure and stress is inherently less reliable than a calmly pre-assessed option identified during planning.
questions.source: TP 15530 – proactive vs reactive site selection

questions.question: A pre-identified alternate landing site is later found to be temporarily unusable (e.g., a parked vehicle now occupies it) just before an emergency occurs. What does this scenario highlight about contingency planning?
choices: Pre-identified alternates are useless since conditions can change

Contingency plans should be periodically reviewed/updated for currency, and pilots should maintain flexible situational judgment to identify a new safe option in real time if a pre-planned site becomes unavailable
This scenario proves emergency planning is pointless
Only a single alternate site should ever be identified, with no backup options
questions.rationale: This highlights the value of periodically reviewing plans for currency, while also maintaining the situational judgment to adapt in real time if a pre-planned option is no longer viable.

questions.question: What generally distinguishes an 'emergency' from a 'contingency' in RPAS operational terminology?
choices: An emergency typically represents a more severe situation requiring an immediate, potentially non-standard response, while a contingency is a planned response to a foreseeable abnormal but manageable event
There is no meaningful distinction between the two terms
Emergencies only apply to manned aircraft, contingencies only to RPAS
Contingencies are always more severe than emergencies
questions.rationale: Emergencies generally represent more severe situations requiring immediate response, while contingencies address foreseeable, more manageable abnormal events with planned procedures.

questions.question: A minor contingency (e.g., brief signal degradation) escalates into a true emergency (e.g., complete lost link with no recovery). What should the crew's response reflect?
choices: The crew should continue applying only the original contingency-level response indefinitely
The crew should recognize the escalation and transition their response to the more severe emergency procedure appropriate to the worsened situation
Escalating situations should always be treated identically to their initial, less severe state
Only the pilot's personal preference should determine how to respond, regardless of severity level
questions.rationale: As a situation escalates in severity, the crew's response should transition to match the more severe emergency procedure appropriate to the worsened conditions.
questions.source: TP 15530 – escalating response to worsening conditions

questions.question: A crew successfully resolves what initially appeared to be a routine contingency, but analysis afterward reveals it was only moments away from becoming a serious emergency due to a nearly exhausted battery reserve. What should the post-flight process address?
choices: Nothing further is needed since the flight ultimately ended safely

A thorough debrief/review identifying the near-miss nature of the event and any contributing factors (e.g., reserve margins, decision timing), feeding into safety management corrective action even though no actual harm occurred
Only actual accidents warrant any post-flight review, never near-misses
The crew should be commended with no further analysis, since the outcome was ultimately successful
questions.rationale: Even successfully resolved near-misses should be reviewed to identify contributing factors and feed into safety management improvements, since they reveal real underlying risk.
questions.source: AC 107-002 / SMS – near-miss debrief and review

questions.question: What is the general purpose of a 'site survey' in RPAS flight planning?
choices: To systematically identify hazards, obstacles, population density, and other risk factors relevant to the intended operating area before flight
To determine the aircraft's paint scheme
To calculate the pilot's certificate renewal date
A site survey is only relevant for indoor operations
questions.rationale: A site survey systematically identifies hazards, obstacles, population density, and other relevant risk factors for the intended operating area.
questions.source: TP 15530 / CARs Part IX – Site Survey + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Site survey requirements (p. 220-235)

questions.question: Why should a site survey be updated close to the actual flight date rather than relying solely on an assessment from months earlier?
choices: Conditions (e.g., new obstacles, changes in population density, seasonal factors) can change over time, so a stale survey may no longer accurately reflect current risk
Site surveys never need to be updated once completed
Only weather needs to be rechecked; other survey elements never change
Updating the survey is only required for VLOS operations, never BVLOS
questions.rationale: Conditions can change over time, so a stale site survey may not accurately reflect current risk; updates close to the flight date help ensure accuracy.
questions.source: TP 15530 / CARs Part IX – operational volume suitability determination + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Pre-flight survey procedures (p. 220-235)

questions.question: What does 'time/distance/energy/endurance' calculation generally support in flight planning?
choices: Determining whether the aircraft has sufficient power/fuel/battery capacity to safely complete the planned mission, including reserves
Only determining the aircraft's top speed
Only calculating insurance premiums
These calculations are irrelevant to RPAS flight planning
questions.rationale: These calculations support determining whether the aircraft has sufficient endurance/energy to safely complete the mission, including appropriate reserves.
questions.source: TP 15530 – flight planning calculations + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.2 Energy Planning - Time, distance, endurance calculations (p. 235-250)

questions.question: How does wind affect groundspeed calculations relevant to endurance planning?
choices: A headwind reduces groundspeed (increasing time/energy needed to cover a given distance), while a tailwind increases groundspeed (reducing time/energy needed)
Wind has no effect on groundspeed, only on altitude
Headwinds always increase groundspeed
Wind only matters for return-to-home calculations, never outbound legs
questions.rationale: Headwinds reduce groundspeed (requiring more time/energy for a given distance), while tailwinds increase groundspeed, directly affecting endurance planning.
questions.source: TP 15530 – wind effect on groundspeed + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.2 Energy Planning - Wind effects on groundspeed (p. 235-250)

questions.question: A mission plan calculates adequate endurance assuming calm winds for both outbound and return legs, but the forecast shows a strengthening headwind expected specifically for the return leg. What planning error does this represent?
choices: No error; wind conditions never need to be considered separately for each leg

Failing to account for asymmetric wind conditions between legs can result in an inaccurate endurance estimate, since the return leg may require significantly more energy than the calm-wind assumption suggests
This is not an error since headwinds only affect outbound legs
Endurance calculations are always conservative enough to cover any wind scenario automatically
questions.rationale: Assuming uniform calm winds when conditions actually differ between legs can produce an inaccurate endurance estimate, risking insufficient reserve for a more demanding return leg.
questions.source: TP 15530 – asymmetric wind planning error + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.2 Energy Planning - Endurance and battery planning (p. 235-250)

questions.question: What is a 'critical point' (or point of no return) in flight planning?
choices: The point along a route beyond which it becomes more efficient/necessary to continue to the destination rather than return to the departure point
The point where the RPA reaches maximum altitude
A synonym for the RPA's launch point
A term unrelated to endurance/route planning
questions.rationale: The critical point/point of no return marks where continuing to the destination becomes more efficient/necessary than returning, based on fuel/battery and distance considerations.
questions.source: TP 15530 – critical point calculation + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.3 Risk Assessment - Hazard identification (p. 250-265)

questions.question: Why is calculating a critical point especially relevant for a long BVLOS mission with limited alternate landing options?
choices: It has no particular relevance to BVLOS missions
It helps the pilot understand at what point continuing forward vs turning back becomes the safer/more efficient option, informing real-time decisions if conditions change mid-mission
Critical points only matter for missions under 10 minutes long
Critical point calculations replace the need for any battery reserve planning
questions.rationale: Understanding the critical point helps inform real-time decisions about whether to continue or turn back if conditions change during a long mission with limited alternates.
questions.source: TP 15530 – critical point relevance for BVLOS + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.3 Risk Assessment - Mitigation strategies (p. 250-265)

questions.question: A pilot's planned critical point assumed calm winds, but a headwind emerges on the outbound leg, extending the time/energy needed to reach the original critical point location. What must the pilot do in real time?
choices: Ignore the wind change and stick to the original planned critical point location and timing
Recalculate or reassess the critical point based on actual observed conditions, since the original calm-wind assumption may no longer accurately reflect the safest decision point
Always continue to the destination regardless of any recalculation
Critical point calculations cannot be adjusted once a flight has begun
questions.rationale: Real-time conditions differing from the original planning assumptions should prompt reassessment of the critical point to ensure it still reflects the safest actual decision point.
questions.source: TP 15530 – in-flight critical point reassessment + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Obstacle identification (p. 220-235)

questions.question: What is a Digital Surface Model (DSM) generally used for in flight planning?
choices: Representing the elevation of the terrain including features like buildings and vegetation, useful for obstacle/terrain awareness
Representing only bare-earth terrain with no surface features
Tracking the RPA's battery voltage over time
A term unrelated to terrain/obstacle data
questions.rationale: A DSM represents surface elevation including features like buildings and vegetation, useful for obstacle/terrain awareness during planning.
questions.source: TP 15530 – Digital Surface Model + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.4 Weather Considerations - Wind limits and operations (p. 265-280)

questions.question: How does a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) differ from a Digital Surface Model (DSM)?
choices: A DEM typically represents bare-earth terrain elevation, while a DSM includes surface features like buildings/vegetation on top of the terrain
They are identical datasets with different names
A DEM includes buildings and trees, while a DSM represents only bare earth
Neither model is relevant to RPAS flight planning
questions.rationale: A DEM typically represents bare-earth elevation, while a DSM includes surface features like buildings and vegetation, an important distinction for obstacle clearance planning.
questions.source: TP 15530 – DEM vs DSM distinction + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Clearance requirements (p. 220-235)

questions.question: A pilot uses only a DEM (bare-earth) dataset to plan minimum safe altitude over a forested area with tall trees. What risk does this create?
choices: No risk; DEM data always accounts for vegetation height

The DEM's bare-earth elevation excludes the actual height of the trees, meaning the planned altitude could be dangerously low relative to the true surface (including vegetation) if a DSM isn't also consulted
This risk only applies to urban areas, never forested terrain
DEM and DSM data are functionally interchangeable for this purpose
questions.rationale: A DEM excludes vegetation height, so relying on it alone over forested terrain risks planning an altitude that doesn't actually clear the true surface height including trees; a DSM should be consulted for that purpose.
questions.source: TP 15530 – terrain/obstacle model selection risk + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Restricted and prohibited zones (p. 220-235)

questions.question: Why should a pilot check for other airspace users (e.g., gliders, ultralights, parasailing areas) during flight planning?
choices: To identify additional potential traffic/conflict risks in the planned operating area beyond standard aerodrome-based traffic
These users are never relevant since they don't use standard aerodromes
Only powered aircraft need to be considered during planning
This consideration is only relevant for operations above 1000 ft AGL
questions.rationale: Non-standard airspace users like gliders or parasailing areas represent additional traffic/conflict risks that should be identified during planning.
questions.source: TP 15530 – other airspace user awareness + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.3 Risk Assessment - Environmental hazards (p. 250-265)

questions.question: Why might glider operations pose a unique detection challenge for RPAS pilots and DAA systems compared to powered aircraft?
choices: Gliders are always required to carry the same equipment as powered aircraft, eliminating any detection difference
Gliders can be quiet, may lack certain electronic conspicuity equipment, and can occupy unconventional altitude/position profiles, making them harder to detect via sound or some sensor types
Gliders never operate at altitudes relevant to RPAS
Gliders are prohibited in Canadian airspace, so this scenario doesn't apply
questions.rationale: Gliders can be quiet and may lack certain conspicuity equipment, posing a unique detection challenge for both human observers and some DAA sensor types.
questions.source: TP 15530 – detection challenges with gliders + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.2 Energy Planning - Reserve fuel calculations (p. 235-250)

questions.question: A site survey reveals a nearby glider operating area but the pilot's DAA system is vision-based only, with no proven detection performance against gliders specifically. What is a reasonable mitigation?
choices: No mitigation needed; vision-based DAA always reliably detects all aircraft types equally well

Increase reliance on additional mitigations (e.g., coordination with the glider operation, visual observers, or schedule/route adjustments) to compensate for the DAA system's uncertain performance against this specific traffic type
Assume gliders never actually pose a real collision risk to RPAS
Cancel all future operations near any airspace with recreational aviation activity
questions.rationale: Given uncertain DAA performance against a specific traffic type, additional mitigations like coordination, visual observers, or schedule/route adjustments help compensate for that gap.
questions.source: TP 15530 – mitigating DAA detection gaps + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.4 Weather Considerations - Density altitude effects (p. 265-280)

questions.question: Why should an RPAS pilot consider environmental factors like noise and wildlife encounters during flight planning?
choices: These factors can have real impacts (disturbance, harm, complaints) that should be considered as part of responsible and compliant operations
Environmental factors are never relevant to RPAS flight planning
Only wildlife factors matter; noise is never a planning consideration
These considerations only apply to operations over water
questions.rationale: Noise and wildlife disturbance are real potential impacts that responsible flight planning should consider, alongside regulatory compliance.
questions.source: TP 15530 – environmental planning considerations + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Access and entry routes (p. 220-235)

questions.question: An RPAS survey mission is planned near a known bird nesting area during breeding season. What should the flight plan address?
choices: No special consideration is needed regarding wildlife under any circumstances
Potential disturbance to nesting wildlife, possibly adjusting altitude, timing, or routing to minimize impact, consistent with responsible environmental practice
Wildlife considerations are only relevant for operations below 50 ft AGL
The mission should always proceed exactly as originally planned regardless of wildlife presence
questions.rationale: Responsible planning should consider potential wildlife disturbance and adjust the operation (altitude, timing, routing) to minimize impact where practical.
questions.source: TP 15530 – wildlife disturbance mitigation + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.3 Risk Assessment - Mitigation plan documentation (p. 250-265)

questions.question: A pilot's planned low-altitude survey route directly overflies a sensitive wildlife area, and no adjustment is made because 'the mission requires that exact altitude and route for data quality.' What should be reconsidered?
choices: Nothing; data quality requirements always override any other consideration automatically

Whether alternate methods (different sensor, altitude, timing, or route) could achieve acceptable data quality while reducing wildlife disturbance, since responsible planning should attempt to balance mission objectives with environmental impact
Wildlife impact is never a legitimate factor to weigh against mission requirements
The mission should be cancelled permanently with no further consideration of alternatives
questions.rationale: Responsible planning should explore whether adjustments to method, altitude, timing, or route could reduce environmental impact while still meeting mission objectives, rather than assuming no trade-off is possible.
questions.source: TP 15530 – balancing mission objectives and environmental impact + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.2 Energy Planning - Altitude effect on performance (p. 235-250)

questions.question: What is a CONOPS (Concept of Operations) intended to describe?
choices: An overview document describing how a specific RPAS operation will be conducted, including objectives, procedures, and key considerations
A synonym for the RPA's user manual
A financial budget document for the mission
A regulatory certificate issued by Transport Canada
questions.rationale: A CONOPS describes how a specific operation will be conducted, covering objectives, procedures, and key considerations.
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.4 Weather Considerations - Visibility requirements (p. 265-280)

questions.question: Why is a well-developed CONOPS particularly important for a Level 1 Complex BVLOS operation compared to a simple VLOS flight?
choices: CONOPS documents are never useful for any type of operation
The increased complexity and risk of BVLOS operations benefits from a clearly documented plan covering procedures, roles, and contingencies, supporting consistent, well-considered execution
CONOPS is only a regulatory formality with no operational value
Simple VLOS flights always require a more detailed CONOPS than complex BVLOS operations
questions.rationale: Increased operational complexity and risk benefit from a clearly documented CONOPS covering procedures, roles, and contingencies to support consistent execution.
questions.source: TP 15530 – CONOPS value for complex operations + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Local traffic patterns (p. 220-235)

questions.question: An operator reuses the same generic CONOPS template for every mission regardless of site-specific conditions. What is the risk of this approach?
choices: No risk; a single generic CONOPS is always sufficient regardless of context

A generic, unadapted CONOPS may fail to address site-specific hazards, terrain, population density, or other unique factors relevant to a particular mission, undermining its value as a genuine risk-management tool
CONOPS documents are only useful if they are extremely long and detailed regardless of relevance
Site-specific factors are never relevant to CONOPS development
questions.rationale: A generic, unadapted CONOPS may fail to capture site-specific hazards and factors, undermining its effectiveness as a genuine risk-management tool for that particular mission.
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.3 Risk Assessment - Contingency planning (p. 250-265)

questions.question: What is a 'terrain model' generally used for in flight planning?
choices: Representing ground elevation/features to support altitude planning and obstacle/terrain avoidance
Representing the aircraft's internal wiring diagram
Calculating battery charge cycles
A term unrelated to flight planning
questions.rationale: Terrain models represent ground elevation/features to support altitude planning and terrain/obstacle avoidance.
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.2 Energy Planning - Wind correction headings (p. 235-250)

questions.question: Why must minimum and maximum AGL limits be carefully considered together with terrain modeling in mountainous terrain?
choices: AGL limits are unaffected by terrain and remain constant regardless of elevation changes

Rapid changes in ground elevation mean a fixed altitude reference (e.g., ASL) can result in wildly varying actual AGL clearance, so terrain-aware planning is needed to maintain consistent, safe AGL limits throughout the route
Mountainous terrain eliminates the need for any AGL limit consideration
Only maximum AGL matters in mountainous terrain, never minimum AGL
questions.rationale: Rapidly changing terrain elevation means a fixed altitude reference can produce widely varying actual AGL clearance; terrain-aware planning helps maintain consistent, safe AGL limits.
questions.source: TP 15530 – terrain-aware altitude planning + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.4 Weather Considerations - Fog and low cloud limits (p. 265-280)

questions.question: A mission plans a constant ASL cruise altitude across a route with a 500 ft elevation rise partway through. If the plan doesn't account for this, what is the risk?
choices: No risk; ASL altitude is always a safe reference regardless of terrain changes

The aircraft's actual AGL clearance would decrease significantly as terrain rises, potentially violating minimum AGL limits or reducing obstacle clearance margins without the pilot realizing it if only ASL was being monitored
This only matters if the elevation change occurs at the very end of the route
Terrain elevation changes never affect AGL clearance calculations
questions.rationale: A constant ASL altitude across rising terrain results in progressively reduced actual AGL clearance, which could violate minimum AGL requirements or safety margins if not properly planned for.
questions.source: TP 15530 – ASL vs AGL planning risk in variable terrain + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.1 Site Survey - Emergency landing sites (p. 220-235)

questions.question: What frequency should a pilot determine is appropriate to monitor during a flight, based on the operating area?
choices: The relevant MF, ATF, or other applicable frequency for the area, determined from charts/CFS during planning
Any random frequency, since monitoring isn't important
Only international distress frequencies, regardless of local area
Frequency monitoring is irrelevant to RPAS operations
questions.rationale: The appropriate frequency to monitor (MF, ATF, or other) should be determined from charts/CFS data relevant to the specific operating area during planning.
questions.source: TP 15530 – frequency determination in planning + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.3 Risk Assessment - Witness and documentation (p. 250-265)

questions.question: Why is it important to reconcile and validate nonofficial data sources (e.g., a hobbyist map or app) against official ones during flight planning?
choices: Nonofficial sources are always fully accurate and require no validation
Nonofficial sources may contain errors, omissions, or outdated information, so cross-checking against official/current publications helps ensure planning is based on accurate, authoritative data
Official sources are never necessary if a convenient app is available
Reconciliation is only relevant for BVLOS missions, never VLOS
questions.rationale: Nonofficial sources may contain errors or outdated data; cross-checking against official publications helps ensure planning relies on accurate, authoritative information.
questions.source: TP 15530 – validating nonofficial data sources + RPAS 101 Chapter 5
questions.rpas101_reference: 5.2 Energy Planning - Cruise vs descent rates (p. 235-250)

questions.question: What is the general requirement to legally operate a VHF aviation radio in Canada?
choices: Holding an appropriate radio operator certificate (e.g., Restricted Operator Certificate – Aeronautical)
No certificate is required to operate any aviation radio
Only a driver's license is required
Only RPAS pilots with an Advanced certificate may use radios, regardless of other certification
questions.rationale: Operating a VHF aviation radio generally requires an appropriate radio operator certificate, such as the Restricted Operator Certificate – Aeronautical (ROC-A).

questions.question: What is standard phraseology in aviation radio communication intended to achieve?
choices: Clear, concise, and unambiguous communication using standardized terms understood by all pilots/controllers
Allowing pilots to use casual conversational language freely
Encouraging pilots to use as many words as possible for clarity
Standard phraseology is only used internationally, never domestically
questions.rationale: Standard phraseology exists to ensure clear, concise, and unambiguous communication understood consistently by all pilots and controllers.

questions.question: A pilot uses non-standard, casual phrasing to report position at an uncontrolled aerodrome (e.g., 'just kinda near the runway, gonna land soon'). What is the risk?
choices: No risk; casual phrasing is always equally clear as standard phraseology
Ambiguous, non-standard phrasing may not clearly convey the pilot's actual position/intentions to other pilots, increasing the risk of misunderstanding and potential conflict
Casual phrasing is always preferred by ATC for efficiency
Standard phraseology is only relevant for controlled airspace, never uncontrolled aerodromes
questions.rationale: Ambiguous phrasing risks other pilots misunderstanding actual position/intentions, increasing conflict risk; standard phraseology reduces this ambiguity.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology Guide – importance of standard terms

questions.question: An RPAS pilot without an operating radio is at a site where several manned aircraft are actively using ATF procedures. The pilot wants to still gain situational awareness. What is a reasonable compromise?
choices: Give up on gaining any situational awareness since no radio is present
Have another crew member (e.g., a properly certified visual observer or dedicated radio monitor) equipped with a radio to monitor ATF traffic and relay relevant information to the pilot
Assume the lack of a radio makes ATF traffic irrelevant to the RPAS operation
Only fly at times when no manned traffic could possibly be present
questions.rationale: Having another crew member monitor the relevant frequency and relay information is a practical way to gain situational awareness even if the pilot's own equipment lacks radio capability.
questions.source: TP 15530 – radio monitoring workaround + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does the phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, etc.) help accomplish in radio communication?
choices: Reducing ambiguity when spelling out letters/identifiers over radio, especially in poor signal conditions
Making radio calls sound more formal with no practical benefit
Replacing the need for standard phraseology entirely
Only used for weather reporting, never aircraft identification
questions.rationale: The phonetic alphabet reduces ambiguity when spelling out letters/identifiers over radio, particularly valuable in poor signal or noisy conditions.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology Guide – phonetic alphabet

questions.question: Why might correctly using the phonetic alphabet be especially important when relaying a call sign over a degraded radio link?
choices: It isn't important; degraded links never cause confusion regardless of phrasing
Degraded signal quality increases the risk of misheard letters/numbers, and the phonetic alphabet reduces this risk by making each letter more distinct and recognizable
The phonetic alphabet is only used for numbers, never letters
Call signs are never spelled out using the phonetic alphabet
questions.rationale: Degraded signal quality increases the chance of misheard letters; the phonetic alphabet's distinct word-per-letter system reduces this risk.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology Guide – phonetic alphabet value

questions.question: What is the general purpose of a radio check?
choices: To confirm the radio equipment is functioning and the signal is being clearly received by the intended party
To request permission to enter controlled airspace
To report weather conditions
To file a flight plan
questions.rationale: A radio check confirms equipment function and clear reception before relying on the radio for operational communication.
questions.source: TC AIM – radio check procedure + NAV CANADA

questions.question: Why is it good practice to perform a radio check before a mission relying on radio communication for coordination near an aerodrome?
choices: Radio checks are unnecessary since radios never fail
Confirming the radio is working properly before departure helps avoid discovering a communication failure only after it becomes operationally critical
Radio checks are only performed after landing, never before
This practice only applies to manned aircraft, never RPAS
questions.rationale: Confirming radio function before departure helps avoid discovering a critical communication failure only once it's operationally significant.
questions.source: TP 15530 – pre-flight radio verification practice + NAV CANADA

questions.question: A pilot's pre-flight radio check succeeds, but 20 minutes into the flight, radio calls appear to go unanswered. What should the pilot consider?
choices: Assume the radio is definitely broken since it worked earlier and take no further action

Consider multiple possibilities (e.g., radio malfunction, wrong frequency, being out of range of the intended recipient, or simply no traffic present to respond) and try to verify which applies, such as attempting a fresh radio check or trying an alternate frequency
Immediately terminate the flight regardless of any other information available
A successful earlier radio check guarantees continued function for the rest of the flight with no further concern
