questions.rationale: Multiple explanations are possible for unanswered calls; the pilot should try to diagnose (e.g., fresh radio check, alternate frequency) rather than assume a single cause without verification.
questions.source: TP 15530 – in-flight radio troubleshooting + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does 'roger' mean in standard aviation phraseology?
choices: Message received and understood
A request for the other party to repeat their message
An affirmative response meaning 'yes, I will comply'
A distress call indicator
questions.rationale: 'Roger' specifically means the message was received and understood; it does not necessarily indicate agreement or compliance.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology Guide – standard terms

questions.question: A pilot says 'roger' in response to an instruction that actually requires a specific compliance action. Why might this be problematic phraseology?
choices: It is never problematic since 'roger' always implies compliance

'Roger' only confirms the message was received/understood, not that the pilot will comply; using 'wilco' or a specific readback may be more appropriate to confirm actual compliance with an instruction
'Roger' is not a real aviation term and should never be used
'Roger' should only be used for weather-related communications
questions.rationale: 'Roger' only confirms receipt/understanding, not compliance; instructions requiring action are better acknowledged with 'wilco' or a specific readback.
questions.source: TC AIM – roger vs wilco distinction + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does 'say again' mean in standard phraseology?
choices: A request for the other party to repeat their last transmission
A confirmation that the message was fully understood
An instruction to stop transmitting entirely
A distress signal
questions.rationale: "Say again" is standard phraseology requesting the other party repeat their last transmission.

questions.question: Why is it preferable to use 'say again' rather than simply 'what?' or 'huh?' in aviation radio communication?
choices: There is no meaningful difference; both are equally acceptable standard terms

'Say again' is standardized, unambiguous phraseology universally recognized by pilots/controllers, while casual terms may not be clearly understood or may add ambiguity, especially across a degraded link
'Say again' is only used by air traffic controllers, never pilots
'What?' is actually the preferred, official term instead of 'say again'
questions.rationale: Standardized phraseology like 'say again' is universally recognized and unambiguous, unlike casual terms that could be misunderstood, especially over a degraded radio link.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology Guide – standardized terms

questions.question: What does the term 'standby' typically mean in radio communication?
choices: The requested action/response will follow shortly; wait for further communication
An immediate refusal of the request
A request to switch frequencies immediately
An emergency declaration
questions.rationale: 'Standby' indicates a brief wait is needed before a follow-up response, not a refusal or emergency indicator.

questions.question: A VO says 'standby' in response to a pilot's urgent request for a traffic update. What should the pilot understand from this?
choices: The VO is refusing to provide any traffic information at all
The VO needs a brief moment before responding (e.g., to visually reacquire or assess the traffic) and will follow up shortly, so the pilot should not assume the request was ignored
The pilot should immediately terminate the flight
'Standby' has no defined meaning in this context
questions.rationale: 'Standby' indicates a brief delay before a full response is given, not that the request is being ignored or refused.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology Guide – standby usage

questions.question: What is the general purpose of using a specific 'call sign' or aircraft identifier during radio communication?
choices: To clearly identify which aircraft/station is transmitting or being addressed, reducing confusion in shared-frequency environments
Call signs are purely decorative with no functional purpose
Call signs are only used for military aircraft
Call signs replace the need for standard phraseology entirely
questions.rationale: Call signs clearly identify the transmitting/addressed station, reducing confusion when multiple aircraft share a frequency.
questions.source: TC AIM – call sign usage + NAV CANADA

questions.question: Why should an RPAS crew member relaying information over radio clearly identify themselves and the aircraft they represent?
choices: Identification is unnecessary since context always makes it obvious who is speaking
Clear identification helps other frequency users correctly attribute the transmission to a specific aircraft/operation, supporting accurate situational awareness for everyone listening
Identification is only required for controlled airspace communications
Only pilots may ever transmit; other crew members should never use the radio
questions.rationale: Clear identification helps other frequency users correctly attribute transmissions, supporting accurate shared situational awareness.
questions.source: TC AIM / TP 15530 – radio identification practice + NAV CANADA

questions.question: An RPAS operator wants a ground crewmember (not a certified pilot) to make position reports on the ATF for a Level 1 Complex operation. What should be verified first?
choices: Nothing; anyone may transmit on any frequency regardless of certification

That the crewmember holds the appropriate radio operator certificate and is trained on correct phraseology/procedures for that frequency, since operating a radio has its own certification requirement independent of RPAS pilot certification
Only the pilot's certificate matters; crew members never need their own radio certification
ATF communication never requires any certification for any user
questions.rationale: Operating an aviation radio has its own certification requirement (e.g., ROC-A) independent of RPAS pilot certification, so this should be verified for anyone transmitting.
questions.source: RIC-21 – radio operator certification requirement + NAV CANADA

questions.question: What does 'over' signify at the end of a radio transmission?
choices: The transmission is complete and a response is expected/invited
The conversation is entirely finished with no further reply expected
An emergency condition exists
A request to repeat the message
questions.rationale: 'Over' signals the transmission is complete and invites a response, distinct from 'out' which indicates the conversation is finished.

questions.question: Why might omitting 'over' or an equivalent handoff cue create confusion during a busy ATF period?
choices: It never creates confusion since all pilots always know when someone finishes speaking
Without a clear handoff cue, other pilots may be uncertain whether the transmission is complete, potentially leading to overlapping transmissions ('stepping on' each other) on a shared frequency
'Over' is an outdated term no longer used in any modern communication
This only matters for controlled airspace, never uncontrolled ATF communication
questions.rationale: Without a clear handoff cue, other frequency users may be uncertain if a transmission is complete, increasing risk of overlapping transmissions on a shared frequency.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology Guide – transmission handoff clarity

questions.question: What does a VNC (VFR Navigation Chart) primarily support?
choices: Visual navigation by depicting terrain, obstacles, airspace, and other features relevant to VFR flight
Only weather forecasting
Only aircraft maintenance scheduling
A VNC only depicts controlled airspace with no other information
questions.rationale: VNCs support visual navigation by depicting terrain, obstacles, airspace, and other relevant features for VFR flight. [RPAS 101, Chapter 4: Navigation Systems] VNC chart interpretation (p. 145-160)
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.1 VFR Navigation Charts - VNC chart interpretation (p. 145-160)

questions.question: What is the general purpose of a VTA (VFR Terminal Area) chart compared to a VNC?
choices: A VTA provides a more detailed view of busier terminal airspace around major airports, typically at a larger scale than a VNC
A VTA covers the entire country at a single small scale
A VTA is used exclusively for weather reporting
There is no difference between a VTA and a VNC
questions.rationale: VTAs provide a more detailed, larger-scale view of busier terminal airspace compared to the broader-scale VNC. [RPAS 101, Chapter 4: Navigation Systems] VTA terminal area charts (p. 145-160)
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.1 VFR Navigation Charts - VTA terminal area charts (p. 145-160)

questions.question: Why might a VTA be more useful than a VNC for planning an RPAS operation near a busy terminal area?
choices: VTAs are never more useful than VNCs for any purpose
The larger scale and greater detail of a VTA can more clearly show the specific airspace segments, floors, and features relevant to operating safely in a complex terminal environment
VTAs do not include any airspace information, unlike VNCs
VNCs always provide more relevant detail for terminal areas than VTAs
questions.rationale: A VTA's larger scale and detail level can more clearly depict specific airspace segments and features relevant to complex terminal-area operations. [RPAS 101, Chapter 4: Navigation Systems] Chart selection and use (p. 145-160)
questions.source: NAV CANADA VTA – use case + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.1 VFR Navigation Charts - Chart selection and use (p. 145-160)

questions.question: A pilot plans a mission that starts within VTA-chart coverage near a terminal area, but the flight extends beyond the VTA's edge into VNC-only coverage. What must the pilot ensure?
choices: Nothing special; the VTA alone is always sufficient for any distance of flight
Both charts are consulted as needed so the entire route is covered, ensuring no gap in awareness of airspace/obstacles as the flight transitions from VTA to VNC coverage
Only the initial VTA chart matters; features beyond its edge can be ignored
VNC charts and VTA charts can never be used together for a single mission
questions.rationale: Both charts should be consulted as relevant to ensure complete coverage and awareness as the flight transitions between VTA and VNC chart areas.
questions.source: TP 15530 – multi-chart route planning + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.2 Airspace Identification - Chart airspace markings (p. 160-175)

questions.question: How is latitude/longitude typically depicted on an aeronautical chart?
choices: As a grid of lines with labeled values, allowing a specific point to be plotted using its coordinates
Latitude/longitude are never shown on aeronautical charts
Only as a single reference point in the corner of the chart
Only relevant for oceanic charts, never for VNC/VTA
questions.rationale: Latitude/longitude are depicted as a labeled grid, allowing pilots to plot and identify specific coordinate points.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VNC – coordinate grid + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.3 Coordinate Systems - Latitude and longitude (p. 175-190)

questions.question: A pilot is given a coordinate for a planned operating area in decimal degrees, but their chart uses degrees/minutes/seconds. What must the pilot do?
choices: Assume the two formats are always identical numerically with no conversion needed
Convert between the coordinate formats correctly before plotting the location, since a format mismatch could result in plotting the wrong location if not properly converted
Ignore the coordinate since format differences make it unusable
Only use whichever format seems more convenient without converting
questions.rationale: Correctly converting between coordinate formats (e.g., decimal degrees vs degrees/minutes/seconds) is necessary to avoid plotting an incorrect location. [RPAS 101, Chapter 4: Navigation Systems] Scale interpretation (p. 145-160)
questions.source: TP 15530 – coordinate format conversion + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.1 VFR Navigation Charts - Scale interpretation (p. 145-160)

questions.question: A pilot mis-converts a coordinate, resulting in a plotted point several kilometres from the intended location, though still within a generally similar area. What is the most significant risk of this kind of error?
choices: No risk; being in a 'generally similar area' is always close enough for safe operations
The site survey, hazard assessment, and airspace/obstacle checks may have been performed for the wrong actual location, meaning real hazards at the true intended site could be completely missed
Coordinate conversion errors only affect chart aesthetics, not actual safety
This type of error is not possible with modern charts and coordinates
questions.rationale: A coordinate error means all subsequent site survey and hazard assessment work may apply to the wrong location, potentially missing real hazards at the true intended site.
questions.source: TP 15530 – consequences of coordinate errors + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.3 Coordinate Systems - Grid systems and UTM (p. 175-190)

questions.question: How can ground elevation generally be determined from a topographic or aeronautical chart?
choices: Using contour lines and/or spot elevation figures depicted on the chart
Ground elevation is never shown on any chart
Only by physically visiting the site with survey equipment
Only from weather reports, never from charts
questions.rationale: Contour lines and spot elevation figures on charts allow determination of ground elevation at a given location.
questions.source: TC AIM – chart elevation representation + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: RPAS 101 Chapter 4: Navigation Systems - Ground elevation representation on charts

questions.question: Why is understanding ground elevation important when calculating a safe RPAS operating altitude in varied terrain?
choices: Ground elevation has no bearing on operating altitude calculations

Since operating altitude limits (e.g., 400 ft AGL) are relative to the ground directly below the aircraft, knowing local ground elevation is necessary to correctly translate between AGL and ASL references as terrain varies
Ground elevation only matters for aircraft flying above 10,000 ft ASL
AGL limits apply uniformly regardless of actual ground elevation
questions.rationale: AGL-based limits depend on local ground elevation directly below the aircraft, so understanding elevation is necessary to correctly translate between AGL and ASL as terrain varies.
questions.source: TP 15530 – AGL/ASL and terrain relationship + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.3 Coordinate Systems - Map datum considerations (p. 175-190)

questions.question: A route crosses terrain that rises 300 ft over a short horizontal distance. If the pilot maintains a constant ASL altitude throughout, what happens to the AGL clearance, and what should the pilot do?
choices: AGL clearance stays exactly the same; no action is needed
AGL clearance decreases as terrain rises beneath a constant ASL altitude; the pilot should adjust the planned ASL altitude (climb) to maintain safe/legal AGL clearance across the rising terrain
AGL clearance increases as terrain rises; the pilot should descend
This scenario is impossible since ASL and AGL are always identical
questions.rationale: As terrain rises beneath a constant ASL altitude, actual AGL clearance decreases; the pilot should climb (increase ASL altitude) as needed to maintain safe/legal AGL clearance. [RPAS 101, Chapter 4: Navigation Systems] Distance and scale measurement (p. 145-160)
questions.source: TP 15530 – maintaining AGL clearance over rising terrain + RPAS 101 Chapter 4
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.1 VFR Navigation Charts - Distance and scale measurement (p. 145-160)

questions.question: What is the purpose of using the CFS alongside a VNC/VTA to identify airport operators and ATC agencies?
choices: The CFS provides detailed textual facility information (contacts, frequencies, services) that complements the chart's visual depiction
The CFS replaces the need for any chart entirely
The CFS only lists weather stations, not airport operator information
The CFS is irrelevant to identifying airport operators
questions.rationale: The CFS provides detailed textual facility information that complements the visual chart depiction, useful for identifying airport operators and relevant ATC agencies.
questions.source: NAV CANADA CFS – complementary use with charts

questions.question: A pilot identifies an aerodrome on a VNC but needs the specific frequency/contact for coordination. What should the pilot do?
choices: Guess a plausible frequency and use it without verification
Cross-reference the CFS entry for that specific aerodrome to obtain the correct, current frequency/contact information
Assume all aerodromes share the same standard frequency nationwide
Frequency information cannot be found in any official publication
questions.rationale: The CFS provides the specific, current frequency/contact details for a given aerodrome, complementing the chart's visual location depiction.

questions.question: A pilot finds an aerodrome depicted on a VNC but no corresponding entry in the current CFS edition. What should the pilot conclude and do?
choices: Assume the aerodrome doesn't actually exist and disregard the chart symbol entirely

Recognize a possible discrepancy (e.g., aerodrome status change, closure, or publication lag) and seek to verify current status through other means (e.g., contacting relevant authorities or checking NOTAMs) rather than assuming either source is definitively correct
Always trust the VNC over the CFS without further verification
This scenario is impossible and indicates a corrupted chart
questions.rationale: A discrepancy between sources should prompt further verification of current status rather than assuming either source is automatically correct.

questions.question: What is the purpose of plotting latitude and longitude on an aeronautical chart during flight planning?
choices: To precisely locate a specific point of interest (e.g., operating area boundary) referenced by coordinates
Plotting coordinates has no practical planning use
Only used for international flights, never domestic operations
Coordinates are only relevant for weather reporting, not chart plotting
questions.rationale: Plotting coordinates allows precise location of specific points of interest referenced by latitude/longitude during planning.

questions.question: Why might GPS-based digital tools be preferred over manual chart plotting for precise coordinate work, while still keeping a chart as backup?
choices: Digital tools are always completely infallible and charts are never needed
Digital tools can improve precision and speed for coordinate work, but maintaining chart/manual skills and a physical backup provides resilience if digital tools fail or are unavailable
Manual chart plotting is always faster and more accurate than any digital tool
Charts serve no purpose once digital tools are available
questions.rationale: Digital tools can improve precision/speed, but maintaining chart skills and a backup provides resilience against digital tool failure or unavailability.
questions.source: TP 15530 – digital tool and manual skill balance

questions.question: A pilot's flight planning software crashes just before a mission, and the pilot has only practiced digital coordinate plotting, never manual chart plotting. What risk does this reveal?
choices: No risk; digital tool failure never actually affects real mission capability

Over-reliance on a single digital tool without a practiced manual backup skill leaves the pilot unable to complete essential planning tasks if that tool becomes unavailable, a risk that basic chart/manual proficiency helps mitigate
This scenario indicates the mission should always be flown without any planning at all
Digital tools never fail, so this scenario is purely hypothetical with no real relevance
questions.rationale: Relying solely on a digital tool without practiced manual backup skills creates a real vulnerability if that tool becomes unavailable; basic manual proficiency mitigates this risk.

questions.question: What does 'determining validity of an aeronautical publication' generally involve?
choices: Confirming the publication is the current edition and hasn't been superseded or affected by more recent NOTAMs/updates
Checking only the publication's price
Assuming all aeronautical publications remain valid indefinitely once purchased
Validity checks are unnecessary for official publications
questions.rationale: Confirming currency (correct edition, not superseded, checked against recent NOTAMs) is essential to properly rely on an aeronautical publication.

questions.question: A pilot uses a VNC purchased two years ago for current flight planning. What should the pilot verify?
choices: Nothing; charts never need updating once purchased
Whether a newer edition has since been published and whether any relevant changes (e.g., new obstacles, airspace changes) have occurred that the older chart wouldn't reflect
Only the chart's physical condition, not its content currency
Chart currency is only relevant for controlled airspace areas
questions.rationale: Charts are periodically updated; an older edition may not reflect newer obstacles or airspace changes, so currency should be verified before relying on it.

questions.question: A pilot's outdated VNC doesn't show a newly constructed 400 ft tower that has been added since the chart's publication, though a NOTAM did announce it before construction was complete. What layered failure does this scenario illustrate?
choices: No failure; outdated charts and missed NOTAMs are both irrelevant to actual flight safety

A compounded failure: relying on an outdated chart without recognizing its limitations, combined with not properly incorporating the NOTAM into planning, together create a real risk of an undetected obstacle hazard
This scenario indicates all charts are permanently unreliable and should never be used
This is solely the fault of the tower construction company with no pilot responsibility involved
questions.rationale: This illustrates a compounded planning failure — relying on outdated static data while also failing to properly incorporate available NOTAM information — creating real risk of an undetected hazard.

questions.question: What is dead reckoning navigation generally based on?
choices: Estimating position using known heading, speed, elapsed time, and wind correction, without direct reference to satellite positioning
Exclusively relying on GPS satellite data
A method only usable at night
A term unrelated to navigation, referring to aircraft maintenance
questions.rationale: Dead reckoning estimates position using heading, speed, time, and wind correction, independent of satellite positioning.

questions.question: Why might dead reckoning skills remain relevant for an RPAS pilot despite heavy reliance on GNSS?
choices: Dead reckoning is entirely obsolete and irrelevant to any modern RPAS operation
As a conceptual backup understanding, dead reckoning principles help a pilot reason about aircraft position/behaviour if GNSS becomes degraded or unavailable during flight
Dead reckoning is only relevant to fixed-wing aircraft, never multirotor
Dead reckoning replaces the need for any pre-flight planning
questions.rationale: Understanding dead reckoning principles provides a conceptual backup for reasoning about aircraft position if GNSS becomes degraded or unavailable.

questions.question: During a GNSS outage NOTAM period, a pilot's RPA loses satellite positioning mid-flight over a large open area with clear landmarks. What is a practical approach the pilot can apply given basic dead reckoning understanding?
choices: Immediately assume the aircraft is lost with no way to estimate position

Use known heading, elapsed time, approximate speed, and visible landmarks to estimate the aircraft's approximate position and make an informed decision about a course of action (e.g., continue toward a known visual reference or execute a planned contingency)
GNSS loss always means immediate uncontrolled flight regardless of other available information
Dead reckoning principles are irrelevant to a real GNSS outage scenario
questions.rationale: Basic dead reckoning principles (heading, time, speed, and visual reference) can help estimate position and inform a safe course of action during a GNSS outage.
questions.source: TP 15530 – applying dead reckoning during GNSS loss

questions.question: What do GNSS augmentation systems generally aim to improve?
choices: The accuracy/reliability of satellite-based positioning beyond standard GNSS alone
The RPA's battery charging speed
The visual clarity of onboard camera footage
Augmentation systems have no relevance to RPAS navigation
questions.rationale: GNSS augmentation systems aim to improve positioning accuracy/reliability beyond standard, unaugmented satellite positioning.

questions.question: Why might solar activity affect GNSS signal reliability?
choices: Solar activity has no relationship to GNSS signals whatsoever
Increased solar activity (e.g., geomagnetic storms) can disturb the ionosphere, degrading GNSS signal propagation and positioning accuracy
Solar activity only affects radio communication, never satellite positioning
Solar activity always improves GNSS accuracy
questions.rationale: Increased solar activity can disturb the ionosphere, degrading GNSS signal propagation and positioning accuracy.
questions.source: TP 15530 – solar activity effects on GNSS

questions.question: A geomagnetic storm forecast coincides with a planned high-precision BVLOS survey mission relying heavily on GNSS accuracy. What should the pilot do?
choices: Proceed as planned since geomagnetic storms never actually affect real-world GNSS performance
Consider rescheduling the mission or having contingencies ready for potential degraded GNSS accuracy/reliability during the forecast storm period, given the known risk to signal quality
Geomagnetic storm forecasts are irrelevant to any RPAS mission planning
Increase RPA altitude to avoid all geomagnetic storm effects
questions.rationale: Given the known risk of degraded GNSS during geomagnetic storms, rescheduling or preparing specific contingencies is a prudent response for a mission relying on high-precision GNSS.
questions.source: TP 15530 – geomagnetic storm mission planning impact

questions.question: What is the general right-of-way principle between an RPAS and a manned aircraft?
choices: The RPAS pilot is generally responsible for avoiding manned aircraft, giving way as needed to maintain safety
Manned aircraft must always give way to RPAS regardless of circumstance
Right-of-way rules never apply to RPAS since they are unmanned
Right-of-way is determined solely by which aircraft is larger
questions.rationale: RPAS pilots generally bear responsibility for avoiding manned aircraft, consistent with the added flexibility/maneuverability expected of the smaller, remotely piloted aircraft.
questions.source: CARs Part IX / TC AIM – right-of-way principles
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot spots a manned aircraft on a potential collision course during a VLOS flight. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Continue on the current flight path since the manned aircraft should give way
Take timely evasive action to avoid the manned aircraft, since RPAS pilots bear responsibility for maintaining separation from manned traffic
Wait for radio confirmation from the manned aircraft before taking any action
Ignore the aircraft unless it is within 50 ft of the RPA
questions.rationale: RPAS pilots should proactively take evasive action to maintain safe separation, given their general responsibility to avoid manned traffic.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – RPAS collision avoidance responsibility
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An RPAS pilot's DAA system detects converging traffic and recommends an evasive maneuver that would take the RPA closer to a group of bystanders on the ground. What should the pilot do?
choices: Always follow the DAA-recommended maneuver exactly regardless of the ground risk it creates

Weigh both risks (air collision vs ground risk to bystanders) and select the maneuver/response that best manages the combined risk, which might mean a modified avoidance path rather than the exact DAA recommendation
Ignore the DAA recommendation entirely and take no action of any kind
Ground risk is never relevant when responding to an air traffic conflict
questions.rationale: A sound safety decision weighs both air and ground risk together, potentially modifying the exact automated recommendation to avoid trading one hazard for another.
questions.source: TP 15530 – balancing air and ground risk in avoidance decisions

questions.question: What is the general goal of 'public safety' considerations in RPAS operations?
choices: Minimizing risk of injury or harm to uninvolved members of the public from the RPAS operation
Maximizing operational efficiency regardless of public risk
Public safety only applies to operations near aerodromes
Public safety considerations only apply to operations over 25 kg
questions.rationale: Public safety considerations aim to minimize risk of injury or harm to uninvolved bystanders from an RPAS operation.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – public safety objective
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why does CARs Part IX generally require greater distance from uninvolved people for Basic Operations compared to the reduced distances allowed under Advanced Operations?
choices: There is no meaningful distinction between the two operation types regarding distance from people

Advanced Operations pilots have additional certification/knowledge and may operate aircraft meeting specific technical standards (Standard 922), justifying reduced distances under appropriately managed conditions
Basic Operations always allows closer proximity to people than Advanced Operations
Distance requirements are identical regardless of certificate type or aircraft standard
questions.rationale: Advanced Operations privileges (including reduced distance from people) are tied to additional pilot certification and aircraft technical standards (Standard 922) that justify the increased proximity allowance.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – distance requirements rationale
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An Advanced Operations pilot operates an RPA that does not meet Standard 922 but assumes the reduced-distance privilege still applies because they hold the Advanced certificate. Why is this incorrect?
choices: It is correct; holding the Advanced certificate alone is always sufficient for reduced-distance operations regardless of aircraft standard

The reduced-distance privilege depends on both the pilot certificate and the aircraft meeting the applicable declared technical standard (Standard 922); lacking the aircraft-side compliance means the reduced distance doesn't apply
Standard 922 only applies to Level 1 Complex operations, never standard Advanced Operations
Aircraft technical standards are irrelevant to distance-from-people privileges
questions.rationale: The reduced-distance privilege requires both appropriate pilot certification and aircraft compliance with the relevant technical standard; missing the aircraft-side requirement means the privilege doesn't apply.
questions.source: CARs Part IX Standard 922 – combined certificate/aircraft requirement

questions.question: What is a 'bystander' generally understood to be in the context of RPAS operations?
choices: A person not involved in or necessary to the RPAS operation who happens to be near the operating area
Any member of the RPAS crew
Only law enforcement personnel
A synonym for the pilot's employer
questions.rationale: A bystander is a person not involved in the operation, distinguished from crew members who are part of the mission.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is the distinction between 'crew member' and 'bystander' operationally important for distance-from-people rules?
choices: There is no distinction; all people near the operation are treated identically under distance rules

Crew members are trained, briefed, and knowingly accept operational risk, while bystanders have not, which is why distance-from-people rules specifically protect bystanders rather than treating everyone the same
Crew members are always required to maintain greater distance than bystanders
This distinction is only relevant for Level 1 Complex operations
questions.rationale: Crew members are trained and knowingly accept operational risk, unlike bystanders, which is why distance-from-people protections specifically focus on protecting uninvolved bystanders.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – rationale for bystander protection

questions.question: A property owner grants verbal permission for an RPAS operation over their private event but has not been briefed on any operational risks or safety procedures. Should this person be treated as a 'crew member' for distance purposes?
choices: Yes, simply granting permission is always sufficient to reclassify someone as a crew member
No; without proper briefing/training and an understanding of the operational risks and their role, this person should generally still be treated as a bystander for distance-from-people purposes
Permission-granting always eliminates any distance requirement regardless of training
This distinction is irrelevant since property owners are automatically exempt from all safety rules
questions.rationale: Merely granting permission doesn't confer 'crew member' status; without proper briefing on operational risks/procedures, the person should still be treated as a bystander requiring appropriate distance protection.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – crew member status criteria
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the general purpose of maintaining a safe distance from moving vehicles/roadways during an RPAS operation?
choices: To reduce risk of distraction to drivers and potential collision/interference with vehicle traffic
Roadway proximity has no safety relevance to RPAS operations
Only relevant for operations occurring at night
Only relevant if the RPAS itself is capable of driving on roads
questions.rationale: Maintaining safe distance from roadways reduces the risk of driver distraction and potential vehicle interference/collision.

questions.question: Why might a low-altitude RPAS hovering directly above a busy highway pose a distraction risk to drivers even without any direct collision occurring?
choices: Drivers are never distracted by anything occurring outside their vehicle
An unusual and visible object like a hovering RPA could draw driver attention away from the road, increasing the risk of a vehicle collision unrelated to the RPA itself
Distraction risk only applies to pedestrians, never drivers
This risk only exists if the RPA is flying above 400 ft AGL
questions.rationale: An unusual, visible object like a hovering RPA could draw driver attention away from the road, creating an indirect but real collision risk unrelated to the RPA striking a vehicle.

questions.question: A site survey identifies a busy highway near a planned RPAS survey route. The RPA's flight geography avoids directly overflying the highway, but the ground risk buffer overlaps it. What should the risk assessment conclude?
choices: No further consideration is needed since the flight geography itself avoids the highway

The overlap of the ground risk buffer with the highway still represents a meaningful risk (deviation potential, driver distraction) that should be addressed through mitigation (e.g., increased buffer margin, alternate routing, or timing adjustments)
Highways are never relevant to ground risk buffer considerations
This scenario should always result in outright cancellation with no other mitigation options considered
questions.rationale: Ground risk buffer overlap with a busy highway represents meaningful residual risk that should be addressed through appropriate mitigation, even if the nominal flight path avoids direct overflight.
questions.source: TP 15530 – ground risk buffer and roadway risk

questions.question: What general precaution should be taken regarding RPAS operations near schools or playgrounds?
choices: Extra caution and distance/timing considerations should be applied given the higher concentration of children and potential unpredictability of behaviour in these areas
No special precautions are needed near schools/playgrounds
Schools and playgrounds are automatically exempt from all RPAS-related risk considerations
Only aerodrome proximity matters; population-sensitive sites are irrelevant
questions.rationale: Areas with higher concentrations of children, who may behave less predictably, warrant extra caution regarding distance and operational timing.

questions.question: Why might children specifically present a different risk profile compared to adult bystanders in an RPAS operation?
choices: Children behave identically to adults in every situation with no meaningful difference
Children may be less predictable, more curious about the RPA, and less likely to recognize or respond appropriately to hazards, warranting extra caution/distance
Children are always naturally more cautious around aircraft than adults
This distinction is irrelevant to RPAS risk assessment
questions.rationale: Children may behave less predictably and be less likely to recognize/respond to hazards appropriately, warranting extra caution in risk assessment.

questions.question: A pilot plans an operation timed to avoid school recess/dismissal times to reduce risk near a school, but the mission unexpectedly runs long into the dismissal window due to a delay. What should occur?
choices: Continue the mission exactly as planned since the original timing was carefully chosen
Reassess the situation in real time as conditions change (increasing bystander presence), and be prepared to adjust or terminate the mission if the actual risk now exceeds what was planned for
Timing considerations are irrelevant once a mission has already begun
Only the pre-flight plan matters; real-time conditions never need to be reconsidered
questions.rationale: Good risk management requires real-time reassessment as conditions change, adjusting or terminating the mission if actual risk exceeds original planning assumptions.
questions.source: TP 15530 – dynamic risk reassessment during timing changes

questions.question: What is the general purpose of establishing a cordon or controlled perimeter for certain RPAS operations?
choices: To physically limit bystander access to a defined safe area, reducing the risk of uninvolved people entering the operational hazard zone
Cordons have no safety value in RPAS operations
Cordons are only used for weather monitoring equipment
Cordons are required only for RPAS heavier than 150 kg
questions.rationale: A cordon/controlled perimeter physically limits bystander access to a defined safe area, reducing the risk of uninvolved people entering the hazard zone.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – sheltered/cordon risk reduction concept
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might a cordon alone not be sufficient to fully mitigate public safety risk if not actively monitored?
choices: A cordon by itself always guarantees complete safety with no further action needed
Without active monitoring/enforcement, people could still inadvertently or deliberately cross the cordon boundary, undermining its intended protective function
Cordons are never crossed by anyone under any circumstances
Monitoring is only relevant for cordons used at night
questions.rationale: Without active monitoring/enforcement, a cordon boundary could still be crossed, undermining its intended protective function.

questions.question: An operator establishes a cordon for a public demonstration flight but assigns no one specifically to monitor it, assuming signage alone will keep people out. A bystander later crosses into the area unnoticed. What safety management lesson does this illustrate?
choices: Signage alone is always fully sufficient and no further action is ever needed
Passive mitigations like signage should be paired with active monitoring/enforcement for genuinely effective risk reduction, since signage alone may not reliably prevent access
This incident proves cordons are useless and should never be attempted
Bystanders never cross cordons regardless of monitoring level
questions.rationale: Passive mitigations like signage should be paired with active monitoring for genuinely effective risk reduction, since signage alone doesn't reliably prevent all access.

questions.question: What is the general purpose of maintaining liability insurance for RPAS operations?
choices: To provide financial protection/coverage in the event of damage or injury resulting from the operation
Insurance has no practical relevance to RPAS safety
Insurance is only relevant for operations under an SFOC-RPAS
Insurance replaces the need for any other safety mitigation
questions.rationale: Liability insurance provides financial protection/coverage in case of damage or injury resulting from the operation, though it doesn't replace operational safety practices.
questions.source: General RPAS operational practice – insurance purpose
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is insurance coverage not a substitute for good operational risk management?
choices: Insurance and risk management are functionally identical concepts

Insurance addresses financial consequences after an incident occurs, while risk management aims to prevent the incident in the first place; relying on insurance alone doesn't reduce actual safety risk to people
Insurance always prevents incidents from occurring in the first place
Risk management is unnecessary if adequate insurance coverage is held
questions.rationale: Insurance addresses financial consequences after an incident, while risk management aims to prevent the incident itself; insurance doesn't reduce actual physical safety risk.
questions.source: TP 15530 / SMS – insurance vs risk prevention distinction

questions.question: What is the general concept behind 'as low as reasonably practicable' (ALARP) risk management?
choices: Reducing risk to the lowest level reasonably achievable, balancing safety benefit against practical cost/effort of further mitigation
Accepting any level of risk as long as it doesn't cause an obvious immediate accident
ALARP means risk must always be reduced to exactly zero regardless of cost
ALARP is a term unrelated to safety management
questions.rationale: ALARP involves reducing risk to the lowest level reasonably achievable, balancing safety benefit against the practical cost/effort of further mitigation. ALARP is a widely used SMS best-practice concept (per AC 107-002 guidance) rather than a specific CARs Part IX "shall" clause for Basic/Advanced RPAS operations; the closest regulatory hooks are the risk-assessment content required in an SFOC application (CAR 903.02) and the risk-based safety-assurance framework for declared RPAS (Standard 922).
questions.source: AC 107-002 (SMS Development Guide) – ALARP concept; general aviation SMS guidance, not a CARs Part IX mandate. Free full text/PDF at tc.canada.ca; see Appendix J (Risk Acceptability Matrix) for the ALARP wording.

questions.question: An operator identifies an additional mitigation that would reduce residual risk slightly but at very high cost/impracticality relative to the benefit. How does ALARP thinking apply here?
choices: The mitigation must always be implemented regardless of cost, since any risk reduction is mandatory

ALARP allows for a reasoned judgment that the mitigation may not be required if its cost/impracticality is grossly disproportionate to the marginal safety benefit, provided existing risk is already acceptably low
ALARP means no further mitigation is ever required once any risk reduction has been achieved
Cost is never a legitimate factor in any safety risk decision
questions.rationale: ALARP permits a reasoned judgment that further mitigation may not be required if its cost is grossly disproportionate to the marginal safety benefit, given already-acceptable residual risk. This is SMS best-practice guidance (AC 107-002), not a CARs Part IX "shall" provision for Basic/Advanced operations; CAR 903.02 (SFOC risk-assessment content) and Standard 922 (declared-RPAS safety assurance) are the applicable regulatory risk-management hooks.
questions.source: AC 107-002 (SMS Development Guide) – ALARP proportionality principle; general aviation SMS guidance, not a CARs Part IX mandate. Free full text/PDF at tc.canada.ca; see Appendix J (Risk Acceptability Matrix) for the ALARP wording.

questions.question: An operator dismisses a low-cost, easily implementable additional mitigation, citing ALARP as justification since 'some risk reduction has already been achieved.' Why is this application of ALARP flawed?
choices: It is not flawed; any level of existing mitigation always satisfies ALARP regardless of further options available

ALARP requires genuinely weighing the cost/practicality against the benefit for each specific additional mitigation; dismissing an easy, low-cost, meaningful risk reduction without genuine justification misapplies the principle
ALARP only applies to mitigations costing over a specific dollar threshold
ALARP is not a legitimate safety management concept and should never be used
questions.rationale: ALARP requires a genuine cost/benefit weighing for each specific mitigation option; dismissing an easy, low-cost, meaningful improvement without real justification misapplies the principle. ALARP itself is SMS best-practice guidance (AC 107-002), not a codified CARs Part IX "shall" requirement for Basic/Advanced RPAS operations; CAR 903.02 and Standard 922 are the regulatory risk-management hooks that do apply (to SFOC and declared-RPAS operations respectively).
questions.source: AC 107-002 (SMS Development Guide) – proper ALARP application; general aviation SMS guidance, not a CARs Part IX mandate. Free full text/PDF at tc.canada.ca; see Appendix J (Risk Acceptability Matrix) for the ALARP wording.

questions.question: What is a 'hazard' as distinguished from a 'risk' in safety management terminology?
choices: A hazard is a potential source of harm, while risk is the combination of the likelihood and severity of harm resulting from that hazard
Hazard and risk are identical terms with no meaningful distinction
A hazard only refers to weather conditions
Risk always refers only to financial loss, never physical harm
questions.rationale: A hazard is a potential source of harm, while risk combines the likelihood and severity of harm actually resulting from that hazard.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An operator identifies a hazard (e.g., nearby high-tension power lines) but doesn't formally assess the associated risk level for a specific planned flight. What gap does this represent?
choices: No gap; identifying the hazard alone is always fully sufficient for safety management purposes
Hazard identification without a corresponding risk assessment (likelihood/severity for the specific operation) fails to determine whether mitigation is actually needed and to what degree
Power lines are never actually a real hazard to RPAS operations
Risk assessment is only required for hazards involving other aircraft
questions.rationale: Identifying a hazard without assessing its actual risk (likelihood/severity for the specific operation) fails to determine whether and how much mitigation is needed.
questions.source: AC 107-002 – hazard identification vs risk assessment
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Two operations both identify the same hazard (nearby power lines), but one has a much higher likelihood of proximity due to its flight geography. Why might their assessed risk levels differ despite the identical hazard?
choices: Risk levels must always be identical whenever the same hazard is present, regardless of context

Risk depends on both the hazard and the specific likelihood/severity in context; a flight geography bringing the aircraft closer to the power lines increases likelihood of an encounter, resulting in a higher assessed risk for that specific operation
Only severity matters in risk assessment, never likelihood
The specific flight geography has no bearing on assessed risk level
questions.rationale: Risk depends on both the hazard and context-specific likelihood/severity; a flight geography with greater proximity to the hazard increases likelihood, resulting in a higher assessed risk for that specific operation.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the general purpose of a 'safety culture' within an RPAS operating organization?
choices: Fostering shared values and behaviours that prioritize safety, encourage reporting, and support continuous improvement
A safety culture is a purely symbolic concept with no practical operational effect
Safety culture only applies to large commercial airlines, never small RPAS operators
Safety culture means avoiding all operational risk entirely, never conducting any flights
questions.rationale: A safety culture fosters shared values/behaviours prioritizing safety, encouraging reporting, and supporting continuous improvement across the organization.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why might a 'blame culture' (punishing every reported error harshly) undermine an organization's actual safety performance?
choices: Blame culture always improves reporting rates and safety performance

Harsh punishment for every reported error discourages people from reporting mistakes/near-misses, reducing the organization's ability to learn from and correct underlying issues before a serious incident occurs
Blame culture has no effect on reporting behaviour whatsoever
Reporting rates and safety performance are entirely unrelated concepts
questions.rationale: Harsh punishment for every reported error discourages future reporting, reducing the organization's ability to learn from and correct issues before a serious incident occurs.
questions.source: AC 107-002 – blame culture vs just culture
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An organization wants to build a 'just culture' that balances accountability with encouraging open reporting. What core principle should guide how they respond to reported errors?
choices: Every error, regardless of cause, should be met with identical disciplinary action

Distinguish between honest mistakes/system failures (which should be treated as learning opportunities) and genuinely reckless or deliberate violations (which may warrant accountability measures), rather than treating all errors identically
No error should ever result in any accountability measure under any circumstance
Reporting should be discouraged entirely to avoid the complexity of managing a just culture
questions.rationale: A just culture distinguishes between honest mistakes/system failures (treated as learning opportunities) and reckless/deliberate violations (which may warrant accountability), rather than a uniform punitive or permissive approach.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: What is the general purpose of a 'go/no-go' decision process before an RPAS flight?
choices: Systematically evaluating whether conditions/factors support proceeding with the planned flight or whether it should be delayed/cancelled
A go/no-go process is purely a formality with no operational value
Go/no-go decisions are only relevant for BVLOS operations, never VLOS
The process only considers weather, ignoring all other factors
questions.rationale: A go/no-go process systematically evaluates whether conditions support proceeding, considering multiple relevant factors, not just weather.

questions.question: Why should a go/no-go decision process include criteria beyond just weather (e.g., crew fitness, NOTAMs, aircraft status)?
choices: Weather is the only factor that ever actually matters for flight safety
A comprehensive go/no-go process considers all relevant risk factors together, since a flight could still be unsafe due to non-weather factors even if weather alone seems acceptable
Including additional criteria always makes the process unnecessarily complicated with no safety benefit
Crew fitness and aircraft status are never relevant to a go/no-go decision
questions.rationale: A comprehensive process considers all relevant risk factors together, since a flight could be unsafe due to non-weather factors even with acceptable weather.

questions.question: A pilot's go/no-go checklist gives a 'go' result based purely on a scoring system, but the pilot has a strong personal unease about an unquantified factor (e.g., an unusual crowd gathering nearby). What should the pilot do?
choices: Always follow the checklist's scored result exactly, ignoring any personal unease not captured by the scoring system

Treat professional judgment and situational awareness as complementary to, not fully replaced by, any structured checklist; a 'go' score shouldn't override a pilot's well-founded specific safety concern
Personal unease should never factor into any go/no-go decision under any circumstances
Checklists should always be discarded in favor of pure intuition with no structured criteria at all
questions.rationale: Structured checklists support but don't fully replace professional judgment; a well-founded specific safety concern shouldn't be overridden by a scored 'go' result that may not capture every relevant factor.
questions.source: TP 15530 / SMS – judgment complementing structured processes

questions.question: What does 'operational risk assessment' (e.g., per AC 903-001) generally involve for an RPAS mission?
choices: A structured process to identify hazards, assess risk levels, and determine appropriate mitigations before conducting the operation
A financial audit of the operator's business finances
A test of the pilot's certificate validity only
A weather-only assessment with no other risk factors considered
questions.rationale: Operational risk assessment is a structured process to identify hazards, assess risk, and determine mitigations before conducting an operation.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Why is a documented operational risk assessment valuable even for a routine, frequently repeated RPAS mission?
choices: Documentation has no value for routine missions since risk is assumed to be understood implicitly
Documenting the assessment ensures consistency, provides a record for review/audit, and helps catch any change in circumstances that might affect an otherwise 'routine' mission's actual risk profile
Routine missions never actually carry any risk, making assessment unnecessary
Documented assessments are only required for missions using an SFOC-RPAS
questions.rationale: Documentation ensures consistency, supports review/audit, and helps catch changes in circumstances that could affect the risk profile of an otherwise routine mission.
questions.source: AC 903-001 / SMS – value of documented risk assessment
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An operator's routine weekly inspection flight has used the identical risk assessment for over a year without any review, despite gradual residential development occurring near the site. What safety management failure does this illustrate?
choices: No failure; a single risk assessment is always valid indefinitely regardless of any changes near the site
Failing to periodically review and update a risk assessment as surrounding conditions change (e.g., new development) can result in an outdated assessment that no longer reflects actual current risk
This scenario indicates risk assessments are entirely pointless as a safety tool
Development near a site is never relevant to a flight's risk assessment
questions.rationale: CAR 901.27 requires a pilot to determine the operational volume is suitable via a site survey, including the proximity of people, obstacles and other factors; a static risk assessment that is never revisited will not reflect changes such as new residential development near the site, so periodic review/update is required to keep the assessment current.
questions.source: CAR 901.27 – site survey / operational volume suitability, reassessed as surrounding conditions change
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: When contacting an ATF for the first time, what basic information should be included in your initial transmission?
choices: Just say 'Hello' to check if the frequency is active
Aircraft/RPAS type, call sign, location, and what you intend to do (e.g., 'Drone One, small RPAS, south of the field, practicing circuits')
Your personal name and hometown
A request for clearance to land immediately
questions.rationale: Initial ATF contacts should include aircraft/RPAS type, call sign, location, and intention. This gives other frequency users essential information to understand your operation and potential conflicts.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology – Initial Contact Procedures, RPAS 101 Radio Chapter

questions.question: What does the acronym ATIS stand for, and when is it typically used?
choices: Automatic Threat Information Service; used for hazard warnings
Automatic Terminal Information Service; used to receive continuous airport status info (weather, active runway, etc.)
Airborne Traffic Identification System; used for collision avoidance
Automated Time Information Signal; used for synchronizing clocks
questions.rationale: ATIS broadcasts continuous airport information (weather, QNH, active runway, etc.) allowing pilots to plan their approach and reduce frequency congestion.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology, RPAS 101 Radiotelephony

questions.question: A ground operator transmits to an RPAS ATF: 'Drone Two, descend to 200 ft and reduce speed to 5 knots.' When should the pilot read back this clearance?
choices: Never, because ground operators don't issue clearances
Immediately, by reading back the altitude and speed: 'Drone Two, descending to 200 ft, reducing to 5 knots'
Only if they disagree with the instruction
After completing the maneuver
questions.rationale: Read-backs of critical instructions (altitude, speed, heading changes) confirm mutual understanding and prevent misinterpretation, especially in busy frequency environments.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology – Read-Back Procedures

questions.question: What is meant by the radio term 'Roger' when an ATF controller uses it in a transmission?
choices: The controller is asking a question that requires a response
The controller has received and understood your transmission
The controller is granting you permission to land
The controller is denying your request
questions.rationale: 'Roger' confirms receipt and understanding of a transmission. It does not imply approval; use 'Wilco' to indicate compliance with an instruction.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology – Standard Radio Terminology

questions.question: An ATF operator says, 'Drone Three, this frequency is now closed.' What action should the RPAS pilot take?
choices: Continue transmitting but use shorter messages
Continue monitoring the frequency but cease any operational transmissions; switch to a backup frequency or contact a different facility
Immediately land the RPAS wherever it is
Request a ten-minute extension to finish the operation
questions.rationale: When an ATF closes, cease transmitting unless in an emergency. Switch to a backup frequency, move to a different facility's coverage, or land to await reopening.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology, RPAS 101 Procedures

questions.question: How should an RPAS pilot report an in-flight emergency to an ATF?
choices: Wait until landing to submit a written incident report
Immediately declare 'MAYDAY' (or 'PAN' for urgency), state the aircraft type/call sign, nature of emergency, and request assistance
Use normal radio procedure since it's just an RPAS
Turn off the radio to avoid confusion and land quickly
questions.rationale: Emergency declarations must be immediate and clear. 'MAYDAY' signals life-threatening danger; 'PAN' signals urgent but non-life-threatening situations. State your call sign, aircraft type, nature of emergency, and assistance needed.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology – Emergency Procedures, CARs Part IX

questions.question: What is the standard format for reading back a heading instruction from ATF, and why is this important?
choices: 'Understood, heading.' No specific format is necessary.
'[Call sign], heading [number], [date]' to confirm the exact heading and prevent confusion with other aircraft
'[Call sign], turning [direction] to heading [number]' to confirm understanding of the direction and specific heading value
Headings do not require read-backs; they're assumed to be correct
questions.rationale: Read-backs must confirm the call sign, direction of turn, and exact heading number to eliminate ambiguity, especially in congested frequency environments.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology – Heading Instructions

questions.question: An RPAS is operating near an aerodrome with an active ATF. The pilot wishes to transition through the area but is unsure about procedures. What is the first step?
choices: Just fly through; as long as you're below 400 ft, no radio contact is needed
Contact the ATF early, state your position and intention (e.g., transiting north at 150 ft), and listen for any traffic advisories or restrictions
Wait until you're within 1 km of the aerodrome, then call for clearance
Bypass the ATF area entirely by flying much lower
questions.rationale: Early contact (5+ km away) allows the ATF to provide traffic advisories and coordinate your transition safely. State your position, altitude, and direction clearly.
questions.source: CARs Part IX Aerodrome Procedures, NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology

questions.question: What does 'QNH' refer to, and why would an RPAS pilot need to know this value?
choices: A type of RPAS battery; irrelevant to radio communication
The altimeter setting; used to set your altimeter to indicate height above mean sea level, ensuring accurate altitude reporting to ATF
A frequency code unique to each airfield
A weather warning code indicating thunderstorms
questions.rationale: QNH is the altimeter setting (atmospheric pressure at sea level). Setting your altimeter to QNH ensures your altitude reports match those of manned aircraft, critical for separation and safety.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology, RPAS 101 Radio Procedures

questions.question: During a radio transmission, the RPAS pilot's voice is unclear or broken. How should the ATF controller or other pilots typically respond?
choices: Ignore the transmission and wait for the next one
Use the term 'Say again' (or 'Repeat') to request the pilot to retransmit the message
Assume they understood and proceed normally
Immediately declare an emergency
questions.rationale: 'Say again' is the standard phraseology requesting a full retransmission of a garbled or unclear message. Using this term prevents misunderstandings in critical operations.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology – Clarity and Confirmation

questions.question: When should an RPAS operator monitor the local ATF frequency if one is active in the area?
choices: Only when planning to transmit
Continuously, to be aware of other traffic and potential instructions or restrictions
Never; ATF is only for manned aircraft
Only during night operations
questions.rationale: Continuous monitoring of the active ATF frequency provides situational awareness of other aircraft, potential traffic conflicts, and any advisories affecting your operation.
questions.source: CARs Part IX – Operational Procedures, NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology

questions.question: An RPAS pilot reports to an ATF: 'Descending through 250 ft.' What critical information is missing from this transmission?
choices: The aircraft type (nothing is missing for an RPAS)
The call sign; 'Descending through 250 ft' is ambiguous without identifying which aircraft
The direction of descent
The wind speed
questions.rationale: All radio transmissions must include a call sign so the controller and other frequency users know who is transmitting. 'Drone One, descending through 250 ft' is proper format.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology – Transmission Format

questions.question: What is 'stepped on' communication, and why is it a hazard?
choices: A normal radio procedure where one pilot steps to the side while transmitting
When two transmissions overlap on the same frequency at the same time, making both messages garbled and unreadable
A procedure used only in emergencies
When a pilot transmits too slowly, allowing time for others to interrupt
questions.rationale: Stepped-on transmissions occur when two pilots transmit simultaneously, resulting in overlapping signals that are unintelligible to receivers. This hazard is prevented by proper frequency discipline and listening before transmitting.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VFR Phraseology, RPAS 101 Procedures

questions.question: Which coordinate system is explicitly identified in the Advanced navigation knowledge requirements for locating a position?
choices: Latitude and longitude
UTM easting and northing only
A radio frequency and an aerodrome identifier
A runway designator and magnetic variation
questions.rationale: TP 15263, Section 5, lists 'Locating position by latitude and longitude' in the Maps and charts knowledge area. This requirement focuses on identifying an operating location using the geographic coordinates shown on aeronautical charts.
questions.source: TP 15263, Section 5 - Navigation: Maps and charts, 'Locating position by latitude and longitude'; NAV CANADA VNC - geographic graticule
questions.rpas101_reference: Navigation charts - latitude and longitude

questions.question: What is magnetic variation, and why does it matter for RPAS navigation?
choices: Magnetic variation is irrelevant to RPAS operations since they use GPS
It is the difference between True North and Magnetic North; important when converting between map headings (True) and compass headings (Magnetic)
Magnetic variation is a constant value worldwide
It only affects compass readings; GPS does not require correction for magnetic variation
questions.rationale: Magnetic variation changes with geographic location and year. When planning RPAS routes on maps (True North), pilots must convert to magnetic headings for compass/navigation systems. The formula is: Magnetic Heading = True Heading ± Variation.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Navigation, RPAS 101 Navigation Fundamentals
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.3 Coordinate Systems - Latitude and longitude (p. 175-190)

questions.question: A chart shows magnetic variation of 'W 12°' for your operating area. If you need to fly a True heading of 090°, what is the corresponding Magnetic heading?
choices: 090° (magnetic variation is not applied to headings)
Cannot be calculated without knowing the latitude
questions.rationale: When variation is WEST, subtract from True to get Magnetic: 090° – 12° = 078° Magnetic. Mnemonic: 'West is Best' (subtract), 'East is Least' (add). [RPAS 101, Chapter 4: Navigation Systems] Scale interpretation (p. 145-160)
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Navigation Calculations, RPAS 101 Magnetic Correction
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.1 VFR Navigation Charts - Scale interpretation (p. 145-160)

questions.question: What is a datum, and how does it affect GPS coordinates?
choices: A datum is a time zone; GPS coordinates are independent of time zones
A datum is a mathematical model of Earth's shape; different datums produce different lat/long coordinates for the same physical location
All GPS units automatically use the same datum, so datum selection is never necessary
A datum only affects marine navigation, not RPAS operations
questions.rationale: Common datums include WGS84 and NAD83. A GPS unit set to the wrong datum may display coordinates several hundred meters off. Always verify your GPS unit is set to the same datum as your maps.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Coordinate Systems, RPAS 101 GPS Fundamentals
questions.rpas101_reference: Navigation charts - latitude and longitude

questions.question: What is the difference between ground speed and airspeed?
choices: They are identical terms for the same measurement
Ground speed is your actual speed over land (affected by wind); airspeed is your speed through the air (not affected by wind)
Airspeed is only relevant for manned aircraft, not RPAS
Ground speed is only relevant over water
questions.rationale: Ground Speed = Airspeed ± Wind. If flying into a 10 kt headwind at 20 kt airspeed, ground speed is only 10 kt. This affects flight time calculations and fuel/battery planning.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Wind Effects, RPAS 101 Flight Planning
questions.rpas101_reference: RPAS 101 Chapter 4: Navigation Systems - Airspeed and ground speed relationships

questions.question: An RPAS is planned to fly 10 km against a 5 kt headwind at a cruise speed of 15 kt airspeed. How long will the flight segment take?
choices: 30 minutes (10 km ÷ 20 kt)
40 minutes (10 km ÷ 15 kt)
50 minutes (10 km ÷ 12 kt, which is the ground speed: 15 kt – 5 kt headwind = 10 kt... wait, 10 km ÷ 10 kt = 1 hour = 60 minutes)
Cannot be calculated without knowing the wind direction
questions.rationale: Ground Speed = Airspeed – Headwind = 15 kt – 5 kt = 10 kt. Time = Distance ÷ Speed = 10 km ÷ 10 kt ≈ 60 minutes (1 hour). Note: 1 kt ≈ 1.85 km/h, so 10 kt ≈ 18.5 km/h.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Wind Calculation, RPAS 101 Navigation Math
questions.rpas101_reference: 4.3 Coordinate Systems - Map datum considerations (p. 175-190)

questions.question: Why must a pilot verify that the aeronautical chart used for a planned Advanced operation is current?
choices: A current chart is required to identify applicable airspace, aerodromes, obstacles, and other information at the intended operating location.
Chart currency matters only for flights above 18,000 feet ASL.
A chart remains current permanently once it has been purchased.
Current charts are useful only for filing a flight plan.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 identifies determining the validity and currency of aeronautical charts as an Advanced navigation objective. A current chart supports correct assessment of the planned location, including airspace and nearby aerodromes.
questions.source: TP 15263, Section 5 - Navigation: Maps and charts, 'Locating position by latitude and longitude' - determine the validity/currency of aeronautical charts; NAV CANADA VNC/VTA - current edition
questions.rpas101_reference: Navigation charts - chart currency

questions.question: How is track made good (TMG) different from heading?
choices: They are the same measurement
Heading is the direction the aircraft is pointed; TMG is the actual path over ground (affected by wind and drift)
TMG is only used for water navigation
Heading is the actual path; TMG is what the pilot intends
questions.rationale: If wind drifts an aircraft sideways, the heading (direction pointed) differs from TMG (actual ground path). Pilots use wind corrections to align TMG with the desired track.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Wind Correction, RPAS 101 Flight Planning

questions.question: What is a waypoint, and how is it used in RPAS mission planning?
choices: A waypoint is the same as a checkpoint; both refer to the destination
A waypoint is a predetermined geographic location, such as one recorded by latitude and longitude, used as a navigation reference; multiple waypoints form a flight path or mission plan
Waypoints are only used for manned aircraft, not RPAS
A waypoint is a point where fuel must be loaded
questions.rationale: A waypoint is a predetermined location used to define a route or flight path. TP 15263 requires pilots to locate positions by latitude and longitude and use aeronautical charts for pilot navigation; those skills support accurate waypoint planning.
questions.source: TP 15263, Section 5 - Navigation: 'Locating position by latitude and longitude' and 'Pilot navigation'; NAV CANADA VNC - geographic graticule

questions.question: During a pre-flight, an RPAS operator discovers the chart datum is NAD83 but the GPS is set to WGS84. What is the likely impact on accuracy?
choices: No impact; all GPS systems use the same datum
Potential error of tens to hundreds of meters, depending on location; the coordinates read by the GPS may not match the map
A minor error of <1 meter; not significant for RPAS operations
The GPS will not function at all
questions.rationale: In Canada, WGS84 and NAD83 differ by ~10–20 meters in many areas. A mismatch can cause significant errors in navigation. Always ensure GPS datum matches the chart datum before flying.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Datum Selection, RPAS 101 GPS Setup

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a VNC (VFR Navigation Chart) scale?
choices: To measure wind speed
To convert map distances to real-world distances; a VNC typically uses a scale like 1:500,000
To indicate the altitude available for flight
To show the magnetic variation directly
questions.rationale: A VNC scale (e.g., 1:500,000) means 1 cm on the chart represents 500,000 cm (5 km) in reality. Pilots use a scale ruler or dividers to measure distances on the chart.
questions.source: NAV CANADA VNC Chart Interpretation, RPAS 101 Navigation Charts

questions.question: Why is true airspeed (TAS) different from indicated airspeed (IAS), and when does this difference become significant for RPAS missions?
choices: TAS and IAS are always the same; there is no difference
TAS is the actual speed through the air; IAS is what instruments show due to air density changes; for RPAS flying low and slow, the difference is minimal but increases with altitude
IAS is only used for helicopters
TAS only applies to fuel consumption, not navigation
questions.rationale: At sea level and low altitudes (typical for RPAS), IAS ≈ TAS. At higher altitudes (if RPAS can climb), air density decreases, IAS remains constant but TAS increases. For most RPAS missions (<500 ft), the difference is negligible.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 5 – Airspeed Concepts, RPAS 101 Aerodynamics Basics

questions.question: Under CARs 901.27, what is the primary purpose of a site survey for an RPAS operation?
choices: To obtain weather forecasts for the week
To identify potential hazards, obstacles, and environmental factors that could affect flight safety
To estimate the cost of operations
To locate the nearest emergency landing zone
questions.rationale: A site survey (901.27) must identify obstacles, terrain, emergency procedures, and potential hazards specific to the operating area. This information forms the basis for safe operation planning.
questions.source: CARs 901.27 + TP 15263 Section 6 – Site Survey Requirements, RPAS 101 Pre-Flight Planning

questions.question: When conducting a site survey, which of the following must be documented?
choices: Only the longitude of the site
Hazards, obstacles, terrain, weather patterns, emergency procedures, and any restrictions (airspace, land use)
The color of the vegetation in the area
The names of all birds in the area
questions.rationale: Site survey documentation must include hazards (power lines, trees), terrain features, weather exposure, emergency procedures, and airspace/land use restrictions. This informs the Operational Risk Assessment.
questions.source: CARs 901.27, TP 15263 Section 6 – Site Survey Documentation

questions.question: An RPAS operator plans to fly in an area with multiple obstacles (trees, power lines) and variable wind exposure. How should this inform the operation?
choices: Obstacles and wind exposure don't affect RPAS operations; ignore them
Adjust flight altitude, speed, and emergency procedures based on the hazards; establish no-fly zones and wind-hold criteria
Only concern yourself with obstacles above 100 ft AGL
Increase the RPAS weight to maintain stability in wind
questions.rationale: Site hazards determine operational limits (wind speed limits, altitude restrictions, no-fly zones). Wind exposure and obstacle proximity directly affect control authority and emergency procedures.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 6 – Hazard Assessment + AIM RPA Chapter, RPAS 101 Risk Management

questions.question: What is weight and balance, and why is it critical for RPAS operations?
choices: Weight and balance refers only to how heavy an RPAS is; it doesn't affect performance
The distribution of weight in the aircraft; critical because improper balance affects control, stability, and flight performance
A regulatory inspection process unrelated to flight safety
Only relevant for large manned aircraft, not RPAS
questions.rationale: Weight affects battery life, climb performance, and max speed. Balance (CG location) affects control authority and stability. Outside acceptable limits, the RPAS may be uncontrollable.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 2 – Aircraft Systems + Section 6 Flight Operations, RPAS 101 Aircraft Fundamentals

questions.question: An RPAS has an empty weight of 500g and maximum takeoff weight of 750g. If the operator adds a 100g camera payload, what is the current total weight?
choices: 500g (empty weight is all that matters)
750g (always at maximum)
Cannot be determined without knowing the propeller weight
questions.rationale: Total weight = empty weight + payload. At 600g, the RPAS is within limits (750g max). Knowing actual weight is essential for battery life calculations and performance predictions.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 2 – Weight Calculations, RPAS 101 Aircraft Performance

questions.question: An RPAS is loaded beyond its specified center-of-gravity (CG) envelope. What operational consequence is most likely?
choices: The RPAS will fly slightly faster
No effect; CG is irrelevant to small RPAS
The RPAS may be difficult or impossible to control; it could pitch up uncontrollably
It will use less battery power
questions.rationale: Forward CG (nose-heavy) may cause nose-down pitch requiring constant elevator correction. Aft CG (tail-heavy) can cause pitch oscillations or even a stall. Always verify weight distribution before flight.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 2 – Aircraft Stability + Section 7 Flight Dynamics, RPAS 101 Aerodynamics
