questions.question: After modifying a declared RPA, a pilot wants to use it for an operation listed in CARs 901.69. What must the pilot be able to demonstrate to the Minister?
choices: That the modified system continues to meet the applicable Standard 922 technical requirements.
That the modification reduced the RPA's weight.
That the modification was completed more than 30 days before flight.
That the pilot has flown the original RPA model for at least 10 hours.
questions.rationale: Under CARs 901.70(1)(a), a modified RPAS used for an operation described in 901.69 must still meet the applicable Standard 922 technical requirements. CARs 901.70(1)(b) also requires applicable modification instructions to be followed.
questions.knowledgeArea: RPA airframes, power plants, propulsion and systems

questions.question: When requested by the air traffic services provider for a proposed Advanced RPAS flight in controlled airspace, which information must the pilot provide?
choices: The operation's date, time and duration; aircraft details; vertical and horizontal boundaries; pilot details; lost-link and emergency procedures; and termination process/time.
Only the pilot's certificate number and home address.
Only the desired altitude and a copy of the weather forecast.
Only the RPAS registration number.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.71(1)(a)-(k) specifies the information that must be provided if requested by the ATS provider, including operating-area boundaries, lost command-and-control link procedures, emergency procedures, and termination process/time.
questions.source: CARs 901.71(1)(a)-(k); TC AIM RPA chapter - Controlled airspace operations
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An Advanced RPAS authorization permits controlled-airspace flight, but the pilot cannot readily produce it during the operation. Is that compliant?
choices: No. The authorization must be easily accessible to the pilot during the operation.
Yes. The authorization only needs to be available after landing.
Yes, if the RPAS remains below 400 ft AGL.
No. The authorization must be carried only by a visual observer.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.71(3) requires the authorization for controlled-airspace operation to be easily accessible to the pilot throughout the operation.
questions.source: CARs 901.71(3); TC AIM RPA chapter - Controlled airspace operations
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: ATC issues an instruction directly to an RPAS pilot operating in controlled airspace under Division V. What is the pilot's obligation?
choices: Comply with the instruction.
Comply only if the instruction was included in the original authorization.
Treat the instruction as advisory because the aircraft is remotely piloted.
Wait for the RPAS manufacturer to approve the instruction.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.72 requires a pilot operating a remotely piloted aircraft in controlled airspace under Division V to comply with all ATC instructions directed at that pilot.
questions.source: CARs 901.72; TC AIM RPA chapter - Air traffic services and controlled airspace
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: An Advanced VLOS operation is planned 2 NM from an airport centre. Which condition permits the operation under Division V?
choices: It is conducted in accordance with the established RPAS safe-use procedure applicable to that airport.
The pilot announces the flight on social media before launch.
The RPA remains below 100 ft AGL.
The pilot has logged at least 24 months of flight time.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.73 prohibits a Division V operation less than 3 NM from an airport centre, or less than 1 NM from a heliport centre, unless it follows the established RPAS safe-use procedure applicable to that airport or heliport.
questions.source: CARs 901.73; TC AIM RPA chapter - Operations near airports and heliports
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: Which condition is required for an extended VLOS operation under CARs 901.74?
choices: The RPA must remain no more than 2 NM from the pilot, control station, and visual observer at all times.
The RPA may be any distance from the visual observer if it has a camera.
The pilot may operate from a moving vehicle during launch and recovery.
The operation may be conducted directly over uninvolved persons if it remains below 400 ft AGL.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.74(1)(b) limits the RPA to no more than 2 NM from the pilot, control station, and visual observer. Sections 901.74(1)(a) and (c) also set location and 30 m separation conditions.

questions.question: For an extended VLOS operation, what must the visual observer maintain unaided visual contact with?
choices: The airspace in which the RPA operates, sufficiently to detect conflicting traffic and other hazards and take avoidance action.
Only the RPA's video feed.
Only the pilot at the control station.
Only the RPA during takeoff and landing.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.74(2) requires a visual observer in an extended VLOS operation to maintain unaided visual contact with the operating airspace sufficient to detect conflicting air traffic and other hazards and take action to avoid them.

questions.question: Which qualification is acceptable for a visual observer supporting an extended VLOS operation under Division V?
choices: A Basic, Advanced, or Level 1 Complex RPAS pilot certificate, provided the other visual-observer conditions are met.
No qualification is needed if the observer has a smartphone.
Only an Advanced Operations pilot certificate is acceptable.
Only a manned-aircraft commercial pilot licence is acceptable.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.75(a) accepts a Basic, Advanced, or Level 1 Complex RPAS pilot certificate. The observer must also maintain the required unaided visual contact and stay within 2 NM of the RPA under CARs 901.75(b)-(c).

questions.question: An RPAS becomes uncontrolled and inadvertently enters, or is likely to enter, Class F Special Use Restricted airspace. What must occur immediately?
choices: Notify the appropriate ATS unit or user agency.
Wait until the RPAS lands, then include it in the flight log.
Notify only the RPAS manufacturer.
Continue monitoring; notification is only required after a collision.
questions.rationale: CARs 900.07 requires immediate notification of the appropriate ATS unit or user agency when an uncontrolled RPA inadvertently enters, or is likely to enter, Class F Special Use Restricted airspace. The DAH identifies the affected areas and responsible agencies.
questions.source: CARs 900.07; CARs 601.04(2); NAV CANADA Designated Airspace Handbook, Class F Special Use Airspace
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures

questions.question: In the March 19, 2026 TC AIM RPA chapter, Transport Canada uses “should” and “shall” differently. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Both words identify mandatory regulatory requirements
“Should” is encouraged practice; “shall” indicates a mandatory procedure supported by regulation
“Should” is mandatory; “shall” is advisory
Neither word has regulatory significance in the TC AIM
questions.rationale: TC AIM RPA 1.0 uses 'should' for encouraged practice and 'shall' for a procedure that is mandatory because it is supported by regulation.
questions.learningObjective: Understand TC AIM convention for 'should' versus 'shall'.

questions.question: A crew member consumed an alcoholic beverage 11 hours and 45 minutes before a planned RPAS flight and is otherwise unimpaired. Under CAR 901.19, may that person act as a crew member?
choices: Yes, because observable impairment is the only restriction
Yes, if the pilot-in-command approves
No, because fewer than 12 hours have elapsed
No, because the required interval is 24 hours
questions.rationale: CAR 901.19 prohibits acting as an RPAS crew member within 12 hours after consuming an alcoholic beverage. At 11 h 45 min, the restriction still applies.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: Apply the crew-fitness prohibitions, including the 12-hour alcohol restriction.

questions.question: Icing is reported along the intended RPAS route. Under CAR 901.35, which condition can permit the operation with respect to the forecast icing provision?
choices: The aircraft remains below 400 ft AGL
The pilot shortens the flight to less than 15 minutes
The aircraft has de-icing or anti-icing equipment, or the pilot has a means to detect icing
A visual observer watches the propellers continuously
questions.rationale: CAR 901.35 prohibits flight when icing is observed, reported or likely along the route unless the aircraft has de-icing/anti-icing equipment or the pilot has a means to detect icing. Other icing restrictions still apply.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: Apply the icing restrictions and identify the equipment/means that can satisfy the regulatory exception.

questions.question: An Advanced RPAS pilot successfully completed an accepted recurrent training activity 23 months ago. Under CAR 901.65, what is the effect on recency for an Advanced operation today?
choices: The pilot remains current because the activity occurred within the preceding 24 months
The pilot is not current because recurrent training is valid for only 12 months
The pilot must complete another flight review before every Advanced flight
Recency never expires once an Advanced certificate has been issued
questions.rationale: CAR 901.65 requires a qualifying recency event within the 24 months preceding the flight. A qualifying activity 23 months earlier remains inside that window.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: Apply the 24-month recency requirement for holders of an Advanced Operations pilot certificate.

questions.question: The TC AIM notes that expanded RPAS regulations effective November 4, 2025 gave Advanced pilots additional privileges. Which is one of those privileges identified by Transport Canada?
choices: Unrestricted operations anywhere in Canada
Sheltered operations in any airspace and EVLOS operations in uncontrolled airspace, subject to applicable requirements
Automatic authorization to enter every CYR restricted area
Exemption from the site-survey requirement for EVLOS operations
questions.rationale: TP 15263 and CAR 901.74 include EVLOS and sheltered-operation knowledge for Advanced pilots. TC AIM 2026-1 explains the expanded privileges and their operating context.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.knowledgeTopic: CAR 901.74 — Extended VLOS and sheltered operations
questions.learningObjective: Identify permitted Advanced EVLOS and sheltered operations and their applicable operating limitations.
questions.source: CAR 901.74; TP 15263 Sections 1 and 6; TC AIM 2026-1 RPA

questions.question: A VLOS RPA operation is planned 2.5 NM from the centre of an aerodrome operated under the authority of the Minister of National Defence. An established civilian RPAS procedure exists for a nearby airport. What authorization is specifically required by CAR 901.47(4)?
choices: Authorization from the Department of National Defence
Only compliance with the nearby civilian airport procedure
Only an Advanced pilot certificate
No authorization because the operation is more than 1 NM away
questions.rationale: CAR 901.47(4) requires Department of National Defence authorization for an operation less than 3 NM from the centre of an aerodrome operated under the authority of the Minister of National Defence.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.knowledgeTopic: CAR 901.47 — Operations at or near aerodromes, airports or heliports
questions.learningObjective: Apply the special authorization requirement for operations near aerodromes operated under the authority of the Minister of National Defence.

questions.question: A pilot plans an Advanced VLOS operation 1.1 NM from the centre of a heliport listed in the CFS. The route would cross the established helicopter traffic pattern. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Being beyond 1 NM automatically makes the operation compliant.
The operation must still be planned so it does not interfere with aircraft operating in the established traffic pattern.
Heliport traffic patterns are relevant only inside 1 NM.
The RPA has priority because it is conducting an Advanced operation.
questions.rationale: CAR 901.47(1) separately prohibits operating at or near a listed aerodrome in a manner that could interfere with an aircraft in the established traffic pattern. Being outside the less-than-1-NM heliport distance threshold does not remove that independent requirement.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: Apply the traffic-pattern interference prohibition independently from the numerical airport/heliport distance thresholds.

questions.question: A crew has programmed a lost-command-and-control procedure that climbs before returning home. A newly issued airspace restriction now affects part of that contingency trajectory. What should the crew do before launch?
choices: Launch because emergency programming overrides temporary airspace restrictions.
Reassess and, where necessary, revise the contingency procedure so the foreseeable lost-link trajectory remains compatible with current airspace constraints.
Disable all lost-link behaviour and allow the RPA to continue indefinitely if the link fails.
Ignore the restriction because a lost command-and-control event is unlikely.
questions.rationale: CAR 901.23 requires emergency procedures for loss of command and control and requires operations to be conducted in accordance with those procedures. TP 15263 also expects Advanced pilots to assess lost-link behaviour, emergency procedures and current operating conditions. A contingency trajectory must therefore be suitable for the actual airspace environment before launch.
questions.knowledgeTopic: Emergency procedures — lost command and control / current airspace constraints
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a programmed lost-link procedure remains safe and compliant when the operating environment or airspace constraints change.
questions.source: CAR 901.23; TP 15263 Section 6 — RPAS operations and emergency procedures

questions.question: A warm, humid afternoon produces a substantially higher density altitude than the cool morning conditions used for the original performance calculation. What operational effect should the pilot expect?
choices: Performance margins may decrease, requiring reassessment of payload, endurance, launch/climb and manoeuvre capability.
Performance must improve because warmer air always increases lift.
Density altitude affects only crewed piston aircraft.
Only GNSS accuracy changes with density altitude.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 requires pilots to recall factors affecting density altitude and assess density altitude for anticipated performance and flight-envelope limitations. Higher density altitude generally reduces aerodynamic and propulsion performance margins.
questions.knowledgeTopic: Meteorological aspects of altimetry — density altitude
questions.learningObjective: Assess weather and density altitude for anticipated aircraft performance and flight-envelope limitations.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 4 — Density altitude; Section 6 — Aircraft performance

questions.question: A pilot has been troubleshooting a recurring warning and becomes convinced it is a harmless sensor glitch. A second crew member points out evidence that it could indicate a flight-critical fault. Which response best reflects sound Advanced-pilot decision-making?
choices: Continue because the pilot's initial diagnosis should not be challenged once made.
Seek disconfirming evidence, use the crew member's input, and reassess the aircraft's serviceability before launch.
Clear the warning and launch before it reappears.
Ignore the crew member because only the pilot can recognize technical hazards.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 Human Factors requires pilots to identify factors that interfere with effective decision-making, maintain situational awareness, manage risk and promote open crew communication. Actively testing an initial assumption and considering contrary evidence is the strongest response.
questions.knowledgeTopic: Aviation psychology — decision-making, situational awareness and risk management
questions.learningObjective: Recognize factors that interfere with effective decision-making and use crew input to manage operational risk.

questions.question: A single pilot wants to control exactly five RPA simultaneously from one control station. The operation is VLOS, the applicable manuals permit it, and the RPAS is designed for multiple-aircraft control. No SFOC-RPAS applies. Is this permitted under CAR 901.40?
choices: Yes; five is the maximum permitted under the ordinary multiple-RPA provision when all stated conditions are met.
No; ordinary operations are limited to two RPA.
No; any operation involving more than one RPA requires an SFOC-RPAS.
Yes, and the same ordinary conditions also permit six RPA.
questions.rationale: CAR 901.40 permits more than one RPA at a time when the operation is VLOS, the aircraft are operated in accordance with applicable manuals, the system is designed for multiple-aircraft control, and no more than five aircraft are operated at a time. More than five requires an SFOC-RPAS.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: State the conditions and maximum number of RPA that may be operated simultaneously under the ordinary multiple-RPA rule.

questions.question: An RPA is carrying a surveying sensor suspended beneath it by a line. The applicable operating manuals specifically provide procedures for carrying that payload by line, and the payload creates no other prohibited hazard. Which statement best applies CAR 901.43?
choices: A payload attached by a line is always prohibited without an SFOC-RPAS.
The operation may be permitted because the applicable operating manuals specifically support the line-attached payload.
The payload is permitted only if it weighs less than 250 g.
The payload is permitted only in Class G airspace.
questions.rationale: CAR 901.43(1)(d) prohibits a line-attached payload unless the operation is conducted in accordance with the operating manuals applicable to the system. Other payload prohibitions and SFOC provisions still apply.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: Apply the regulatory conditions governing payloads attached to an RPA by a line.

questions.question: An RPA lacks a transponder and automatic pressure-altitude reporting equipment, but the pilot wants to enter transponder airspace referred to in CAR 601.03. Under CAR 901.46, which combination can allow the operation?
choices: The pilot enters first and requests ATC authorization after establishing contact.
The responsible ATC unit provides service in that airspace, the request is made before entry, and aviation safety is not likely to be affected.
The RPA remains below 400 ft AGL and the pilot holds an Advanced certificate.
The operation is VLOS and a visual observer is present.
questions.rationale: CAR 901.46(2) allows an ATC unit to authorize an unequipped RPA when that unit provides ATC service for the airspace, the pilot requests authorization before entry, and aviation safety is not likely to be affected.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.knowledgeTopic: CAR 901.46 — Transponder and automatic pressure-altitude reporting equipment
questions.learningObjective: Apply the equipment requirement and the specific ATC authorization exception for entry into transponder airspace.

questions.question: Two qualified pilots intend to transfer control of an RPA from Pilot 1 to Pilot 2 during flight. Under CAR 901.42, what must exist before takeoff or launch?
choices: Only verbal agreement that a handover may occur.
A pre-arrangement between the pilots and a procedure to mitigate the risk of loss of control.
An SFOC-RPAS for every pilot handover.
Approval from the nearest ATC unit even in uncontrolled airspace.
questions.rationale: CAR 901.42 requires, before takeoff or launch, both a pre-arrangement concerning the handover and a procedure developed to mitigate the risk of loss of control.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: State the pre-flight conditions required before pilot responsibilities may be transferred during flight.

questions.question: A pilot conducts a night RPAS operation using night-vision goggles. The RPA's required lights are on. What additional requirement applies specifically to use of the goggles under CAR 901.39?
choices: The goggles must magnify the RPA by at least 2×.
The goggles must be capable of detecting all light within the visual spectrum, or the person must have another means of doing so.
The pilot must remain below 200 ft AGL.
A second pilot must be present.
questions.rationale: CAR 901.39(2) prohibits operation using night-vision goggles unless the goggles are capable of, or the person has another means of, detecting all light within the visual spectrum.
questions.knowledgeArea: Air law, air traffic rules and procedures
questions.learningObjective: State the additional visual-spectrum detection requirement when night-vision goggles are used.

questions.question: A multirotor's payload is moved substantially upward, raising the aircraft's centre of gravity. What operational consideration should the pilot make?
choices: The changed centre of gravity can alter stability and control margins, so the aircraft must remain within approved loading limits and performance must be reassessed.
Centre-of-gravity position has no effect on multirotor stability because flight-control software cancels all mass-distribution effects.
Raising the centre of gravity always increases passive stability.
Centre of gravity matters only during fixed-wing gliding flight.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 requires knowledge of locating centre of gravity, returning C of G within limits, the effects of external loads on performance and stability, and how C of G affects aircraft stability. Flight-control automation does not make mass distribution irrelevant.
questions.knowledgeTopic: Weight and balance — centre of gravity and external-load effects
questions.learningObjective: Assess how payload location and centre-of-gravity changes affect aircraft stability, control and operating limits.
questions.source: TP 15263 Section 6 — Weight and balance; Section 7 — Stability

questions.question: A pilot plans a VLOS small-RPA flight in Class C controlled airspace. Which statement best describes the regulatory starting point?
choices: The pilot must operate in accordance with an authorization from the air traffic control unit.
The pilot may enter Class C airspace if the RPA remains below 122 m AGL.
The pilot may enter Class C airspace after broadcasting intentions on 126.7 MHz.
The pilot may enter Class C airspace if a visual observer is used.
questions.rationale: Controlled-airspace RPAS operations are not made legal by altitude, blind broadcast, or use of an observer alone. CARs 901.14 requires the operation to be in accordance with the applicable ATC authorization.
questions.source: CARs 901.14; TP 15263, Section 1 - controlled airspace operating rules
questions.learningObjective: Describe the communication and authorization requirements for small-RPA VLOS operations in controlled airspace.

questions.question: During a flight near controlled airspace, the RPA loses command and control and is likely to enter the control zone. What is the immediate required action?
choices: Notify the appropriate ATS unit or user agency immediately.
Wait until the RPA lands, then enter the event in the flight log.
Continue the flight if the aircraft is still visible.
Notify Transport Canada within 30 days.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.15 requires immediate notification when an RPA is no longer under the pilot's control and inadvertently enters, or is likely to enter, controlled airspace.
questions.source: CARs 901.15; TP 15263, Section 1 - airspace and emergency procedures
questions.knowledgeTopic: Loss of control near controlled airspace
questions.learningObjective: Recall the immediate notification requirement when an uncontrolled RPA enters or may enter controlled airspace.

questions.question: An RPA is drifting toward Class F restricted airspace listed in the Designated Airspace Handbook after a command-link failure. What must the operator ensure?
choices: The appropriate ATS unit or user agency is notified immediately.
The operator waits for the airspace user agency to call first.
The event is reported only if another aircraft takes avoiding action.
The flight continues because Class F restrictions do not apply to small RPA.
questions.rationale: CARs 900.07 requires immediate notification if an RPA is no longer under control and inadvertently enters, or is likely to enter, Class F Special Use Restricted airspace.
questions.source: CARs 900.07; NAV CANADA DAH; TP 15263, Section 1 - Class F airspace
questions.knowledgeTopic: Class F Special Use Restricted airspace
questions.learningObjective: Recall the required action when an uncontrolled RPA enters or may enter Class F restricted airspace.

questions.question: A site survey shows a tower crane inside the planned lateral area, a nearby road with intermittent pedestrian traffic, and a possible emergency landing area. What is the best regulatory interpretation?
choices: The pilot must determine whether the operational volume is suitable before flight, taking relevant site-survey factors into account.
The pilot may ignore ground hazards if the RPA will remain more than 30 m from people.
The pilot only needs to confirm weather and battery state before launch.
The pilot may proceed if the RPA has a return-to-home function.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.27 requires the pilot to determine that the operational volume is suitable by conducting a site survey before the operation. Obstacles, bystanders, traffic, and emergency areas are operational suitability factors.
questions.source: CARs 901.27; TP 15263, Section 6 - site surveys and flight operations
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether the operational volume is suitable before commencing a small-RPA operation.

questions.question: A multirotor normally launches safely at sea level, but the planned site is hot, humid, and at a high field elevation. What is the key performance concern?
choices: Higher density altitude can reduce lift and power margin, increasing takeoff and climb risk.
Higher density altitude always improves propeller efficiency.
Humidity eliminates the need to consider battery temperature.
Field elevation matters only to crewed aircraft.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 meteorology and performance knowledge requires pilots to assess density altitude and weather effects against the aircraft's operating limitations before flight.
questions.source: TP 15263, Sections 4 and 6 - density altitude and aircraft performance
questions.learningObjective: Assess weather and density-altitude effects for anticipated launch and flight performance.

questions.question: A pilot has been scanning mostly through the control-station display and has not looked around the operating area for several minutes. Which human-factors risk is most directly involved?
choices: Reduced situational awareness from poor visual scanning.
Improved vigilance because instrument displays replace outside scanning.
A regulatory violation only if the RPA is above 122 m AGL.
A radio-phraseology issue rather than a human-factors issue.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 human-factors objectives include visual scanning and situational awareness. Display fixation can reduce the pilot's awareness of aircraft, people, obstacles, and changing conditions.
questions.source: TP 15263, Section 3 - visual scanning and situational awareness
questions.learningObjective: Describe good scanning techniques and factors that affect situational awareness.

questions.question: A visual observer is watching the RPA video feed from the passenger seat while also driving the support vehicle. Which statement best applies?
choices: The observer may not perform visual-observer duties while operating a moving vehicle.
This is permitted if the vehicle remains below 30 km/h.
This is permitted in uncontrolled airspace only.
This is permitted if the pilot and observer use radios.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.20 prohibits a visual observer from performing visual-observer duties while operating a moving vehicle, vessel, or aircraft.
questions.learningObjective: Apply visual-observer limitations and responsibilities to operational scenarios.

questions.question: An Advanced VLOS flight is planned 0.8 NM from the centre of a heliport. What condition must be satisfied under Division V?
choices: The operation must follow the established RPAS safe-use procedure applicable to that heliport.
The pilot may proceed if the RPA remains below rooftop height.
The pilot may proceed after notifying any nearby building owner.
No special condition applies because heliports are not airports.
questions.rationale: CARs 901.73 prohibits Division V operations less than 1 NM from the centre of a heliport unless the operation follows the established RPAS safe-use procedure for that heliport.
questions.source: CARs 901.73; TP 15263, Section 1 - aerodromes, airports, and heliports
questions.learningObjective: Apply airport and heliport proximity rules for Advanced small-RPA operations.

questions.question: When making an operational radio call, which information is most important for other aviation users to build traffic awareness?
choices: Who you are calling, who you are, where you are, altitude, intentions, and any relevant timing.
Only the pilot's name and phone number.
Only the RPA manufacturer's model name.
Only the battery percentage and camera heading.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 radiotelephony objectives require practical understanding of routine calls, position reports, common frequencies, and clear phraseology. A useful call identifies station, aircraft/pilot, position, altitude, and intentions.
questions.source: TP 15263, Section 8 - routine calls and radiotelephony
questions.learningObjective: List the contents of a routine call to ATC or an advisory broadcast.

questions.question: A NOTAM or chart reference gives a position in latitude and longitude. What core navigation skill is being tested when the pilot transfers it to a VNC or VTA?
choices: Operational understanding of coordinates and aeronautical-chart interpretation.
Radio reception troubleshooting.
Battery endurance calculation.
Manufacturer safety-assurance declaration review.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 navigation objectives include longitude/latitude understanding and using VNC/VTA charts to locate positions and interpret aeronautical chart information.
questions.source: TP 15263, Section 5 - coordinates and aeronautical charts
questions.learningObjective: Locate a position on an aeronautical chart using coordinate information.

questions.question: A fixed-wing RPA is loaded with the centre of gravity too far aft. Which effect is the best exam-style concern?
choices: Reduced longitudinal stability and more difficult pitch recovery.
Improved stability in all axes.
No effect because only total weight matters.
A radio interference hazard only.
questions.rationale: TP 15263 theory-of-flight objectives include stability and centre-of-gravity effects. An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can make recovery more difficult.
questions.source: TP 15263, Section 7 - stability and centre of gravity
questions.learningObjective: Explain how centre-of-gravity position affects longitudinal stability.

questions.question: A pilot finds swelling in one lithium battery pack during pre-flight. What is the best operational decision?
choices: Remove the battery from service and follow safe handling/disposal procedures.

questions.question: Before launch, forecast winds are within limits, but gusts at the site are increasing and exceed the aircraft manual's demonstrated limit. What should the pilot do?

questions.learningObjective: Use observed weather and performance limitations to make a safe go/no-go decision.

questions.question: What is the regulatory issue if a pilot flies so close to a helicopter that the helicopter pilot must manoeuvre to avoid conflict?

questions.source: CARs 901.18; TP 15263, Section 1 - right-of-way and collision avoidance
questions.learningObjective: Apply the prohibition against operating an RPA near another aircraft in a way that creates collision risk.

Runway marking recognition only.

questions.rationale: MAYDAY identifies distress: grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance.
questions.learningObjective: MAYDAY identifies distress: grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance.

questions.question: The urgency signal is:
choices: MAYDAY
SEELONCE MAYDAY
ROGER
PAN PAN
questions.rationale: PAN PAN identifies an urgent condition concerning safety without the immediate grave danger associated with distress.
questions.learningObjective: PAN PAN identifies an urgent condition concerning safety without the immediate grave danger associated with distress.

questions.question: A ROC-A holder should treat the certificate as:
choices: A personal radio operator qualification; current ISED requirements should be followed for issue/reprint and use
An ATC licence
An aircraft registration
A drone pilot certificate
questions.rationale: ROC-A is a radio operator certificate distinct from an RPAS pilot certificate.
questions.learningObjective: ROC-A is a radio operator certificate distinct from an RPAS pilot certificate.

questions.question: When broadcasting an urgency message to all stations, the address is:
choices: ANYONE LISTENING
ALL STATIONS, repeated as prescribed
EMERGENCY CENTRE
CONTROL ONLY
questions.rationale: RIC-21 provides standard addressing/order for urgency and distress transmissions.
questions.learningObjective: RIC-21 provides standard addressing/order for urgency and distress transmissions.

questions.question: The procedural word 'ROGER' means:
choices: Yes
I will comply
I have received all of your last transmission
End of transmission
questions.rationale: ROGER acknowledges receipt; it does not mean 'yes' or 'will comply'.
questions.learningObjective: ROGER acknowledges receipt; it does not mean 'yes' or 'will comply'.

questions.question: 'WILCO' means:
choices: I have received only
No
Repeat
I understand your message and will comply with it
questions.rationale: WILCO combines understanding with intent to comply.
questions.learningObjective: WILCO combines understanding with intent to comply.

questions.question: 'AFFIRM' means:
choices: Yes
No
Repeat
Wait
questions.rationale: AFFIRM is the standard affirmative response in aeronautical phraseology.
questions.learningObjective: AFFIRM is the standard affirmative response in aeronautical phraseology.

questions.question: 'NEGATIVE' means:
choices: Yes
No, or permission not granted/that is not correct
Message received
End of conversation
questions.rationale: NEGATIVE is used for denial or correction.
questions.learningObjective: NEGATIVE is used for denial or correction.

questions.question: 'SAY AGAIN' means:
choices: Speak louder
Cancel clearance
Repeat all or the specified part of your last transmission
End transmission
questions.rationale: SAY AGAIN requests repetition.
questions.learningObjective: SAY AGAIN requests repetition.

questions.question: 'STANDBY' means:
choices: End of conversation
Proceed immediately
Repeat
Wait and I will call you
questions.rationale: STANDBY tells the other station to wait for a later call.
questions.learningObjective: STANDBY tells the other station to wait for a later call.

questions.question: 'CORRECTION' is used when:
choices: An error has been made in the transmission and corrected information follows
The frequency is wrong
A distress exists
The message is complete
questions.rationale: Standard phraseology uses CORRECTION to repair a transmission error.
questions.learningObjective: Standard phraseology uses CORRECTION to repair a transmission error.

questions.question: 'READ BACK' is an instruction to:
choices: Transmit more slowly
Repeat specified information back for verification
End the call
Change frequency
questions.rationale: Readback verifies safety-critical instructions/information.
questions.learningObjective: Readback verifies safety-critical instructions/information.

questions.question: Good radio technique uses:
choices: Shouting rapidly
Long conversational wording
Clear, concise speech at a steady rate with the microphone close enough for intelligibility
Unnecessary filler words
questions.rationale: RIC-21 emphasizes clear articulation, normal tone and an appropriate speaking rate.
questions.learningObjective: RIC-21 emphasizes clear articulation, normal tone and an appropriate speaking rate.

questions.question: Before transmitting on a frequency, an operator should:
choices: Key the microphone immediately
Transmit a long test message
Use emergency priority
Listen to avoid interrupting another transmission
questions.rationale: Good radio discipline requires listening first and avoiding interference.
questions.learningObjective: Good radio discipline requires listening first and avoiding interference.

questions.question: The phonetic word for the letter A is:
choices: ALFA
ABLE
APPLE
ATLANTIC
questions.rationale: ICAO spelling alphabet uses ALFA.
questions.learningObjective: ICAO spelling alphabet uses ALFA.

questions.question: In ICAO radiotelephony, a decimal point is spoken as:
choices: POINT
DOT
DECIMAL
STOP
questions.rationale: DECIMAL is the prescribed spoken form to avoid ambiguity.
questions.learningObjective: DECIMAL is the prescribed spoken form to avoid ambiguity.

questions.question: The digit 3 is commonly pronounced in ICAO aviation speech as:
choices: THREE exactly as conversational English
TRI
TERA
TREE
questions.rationale: Standard radiotelephony pronunciation modifies some digits for intelligibility.
questions.learningObjective: Standard radiotelephony pronunciation modifies some digits for intelligibility.

questions.question: A routine initial radio call should normally include:
choices: Only your first name
A long weather report
Station called, your identification, position/intent or request as applicable
No identification
questions.rationale: TP 15263 requires pilots to know the contents of a routine ATC call; RIC-21 provides standard operating procedure.
questions.learningObjective: TP 15263 requires pilots to know the contents of a routine ATC call; RIC-21 provides standard operating procedure.

questions.question: If an RPAS flyaway creates an immediate collision hazard, an emergency broadcast should:
choices: Avoid giving position
Use only text messaging
Wait until the flight ends
Use clear priority language, identify the station/aircraft, location, altitude/direction and nature of the hazard as available
questions.rationale: TP 15263 specifically requires an example of an emergency flyaway broadcast; concise hazard information supports ATS/aircraft response.
questions.learningObjective: TP 15263 specifically requires an example of an emergency flyaway broadcast; concise hazard information supports ATS/aircraft response.

questions.question: 121.5 MHz is internationally recognized primarily as:
choices: The aeronautical emergency frequency
The universal MF frequency
The VFR transponder code
A weather radar channel
questions.rationale: 121.5 MHz is the principal VHF aeronautical emergency frequency.
questions.learningObjective: 121.5 MHz is the principal VHF aeronautical emergency frequency.

questions.question: In an MF area, the applicable frequency should be obtained from:
choices: Always 121.5 MHz
Current CFS/chart/aeronautical publication; do not assume one frequency for every MF area
Always 126.7 MHz
Any frequency selected by the pilot
questions.rationale: MF frequencies are published for each location; pilots must use current aeronautical information.
